abstract: Contour maps provide a general method for recognizing two-dimensional shapes. All but blank images give rise to such maps, and people are good at recognizing objects and shapes from them. The maps are encoded easily in long feature vectors that are suitable for recognition by an associative memory. These properties of contour maps suggest a role for them in early visual perception. The prevalence of direction-sensitive neurons in the visual cortex of mammals supports this view.

All but blank images give rise to such maps, and people are good at recognizing objects and shapes from them. The prevalence of direction-sensitive neurons in the visual cortex of mammals supports this view.

paragraphs: The paper proposes contour maps as a general representation for recognizing two-dimensional shapes. Its starting point is their broad applicability: any image other than a blank one can give rise to such a map. It also draws on the observation that people can recognize objects and shapes from contour information.

The computational proposal is to encode the maps as long feature vectors suitable for an associative memory. This creates a connection between a visual description of shape and a representation that a recognition system can use. The contour map supplies the shape information, and its vector encoding provides a way to present that information to the memory.

The authors suggest that these properties make contour maps relevant to early visual perception. They point to the abundance of direction-sensitive neurons in mammalian visual cortex as supporting this view. The argument combines representational usefulness, human recognition ability, and biological compatibility to motivate a possible role for contours in the initial processing of visual shape.
summary.tldr: Contour maps offer a broadly applicable shape representation that can be encoded for recognition by associative memory.

title: Contour-Map Encoding of Shape for Early Vision

abstract: We describe a number of learning rules that can be used to train un(cid:173) supervised parallel feature extraction systems. The learning rules are derived using gradient ascent of a quality function. We con(cid:173) sider a number of quality functions that are rational functions of higher order moments of the extracted feature values. We show that one system learns the principle components of the correla(cid:173) tion matrix. Principal component analysis systems are usually not optimal feature extractors for classification. Therefore we design quality functions which produce feature vectors that support unsu(cid:173) pervised classification. The properties of the different systems are compared with the help of different artificially designed datasets and a database consisting of all Munsell color spectra.

The learning rules are derived using gradient ascent of a quality function. We con(cid:173) sider a number of quality functions that are rational functions of higher order moments of the extracted feature values. We show that one system learns the principle components of the correla(cid:173) tion matrix. Principal component analysis systems are usually not optimal feature extractors for classification. paragraphs: This paper develops learning rules for systems that extract multiple features without supervision. The rules come from gradient ascent on explicit quality functions, meaning the learning updates seek to increase a defined measure of feature quality. The authors consider functions formed from ratios involving higher-order moments of the extracted feature values.

One resulting system learns the principal components of the correlation matrix. The paper then argues that principal components are usually not optimal features for classification. This motivates alternative quality functions intended to produce feature vectors that support unsupervised classification, making the desired use of the representation part of the objective’s design.

The authors compare the resulting systems on artificially designed datasets and a database containing all Munsell color spectra. These comparisons examine how different objectives shape the extracted features. The central contribution is a systematic route from a chosen quality measure to a learning rule, together with the distinction between recovering principal components and producing representations suited to separating classes without supervision.
summary.tldr: Explicit statistical quality functions yield unsupervised feature-learning rules, including alternatives to principal components aimed at classification.

title: Unsupervised Parallel Feature Extraction from First Principles

abstract: This paper presents ongoing work on a speaker independent visual speech recognition system. The work presented here builds on previous research efforts in this area and explores the potential use of simple hidden Markov models for limited vocabulary, speaker independent visual speech recognition. The task at hand is recognition of the first four English digits, a task with possible applications in car-phone images were modeled as mixtures of independent dialing. The Gaussian distributions, and the temporal dependencies were captured with standard left-to-right hidden Markov models. The results indicate that simple hidden Markov models may be used to successfully recognize relatively unprocessed image sequences. The system achieved performance levels equivalent to untrained humans when asked to recognize the fIrst four English digits.

paragraphs: The paper explores speaker-independent visual speech recognition using relatively unprocessed image sequences. The task is deliberately limited to recognizing the first four English digits, with car-phone dialing suggested as a possible application. The authors investigate whether simple probabilistic sequence models can extract enough information from visual speech to perform this task.

The system models images using mixtures of independent Gaussian distributions. Standard left-to-right hidden Markov models capture dependencies over time, representing how visual observations progress through an utterance. This separates the description of image appearance from the temporal organization needed to recognize a spoken sequence.

The reported system reaches performance equivalent to untrained humans asked to recognize the same four digits. This supports the feasibility of using simple hidden Markov models with minimally processed visual input in the stated limited-vocabulary setting. The finding is particularly relevant to the speaker-independent goal: the approach investigates recognition across speakers while relying on statistical appearance and timing models rather than a heavily processed visual representation.
summary.tldr: Simple hidden Markov models recognize four English digits from visual speech at performance levels comparable to untrained humans.

title: Visual Speech Recognition with Stochastic Networks

abstract: A method for incorporating context-dependent phone classes in a connectionist-HMM hybrid speech recognition system is intro(cid:173) duced. A modular approach is adopted, where single-layer networks discriminate between different context classes given the phone class and the acoustic data. The context networks are combined with a context-independent (CI) network to generate context-dependent (CD) phone probability estimates. Experiments show an average reduction in word error rate of 16% and 13% from the CI system on ARPA 5,000 word and SQALE 20,000 word tasks respectively. Due to improved modelling, the decoding speed of the CD system is more than twice as fast as the CI system.

A modular approach is adopted, where single-layer networks discriminate between different context classes given the phone class and the acoustic data. The context networks are combined with a context-independent (CI) network to generate context-dependent (CD) phone probability estimates. Experiments show an average reduction in word error rate of 16% and 13% from the CI system on ARPA 5,000 word and SQALE 20,000 word tasks respectively. Due to improved modelling, the decoding speed of the CD system is more than twice as fast as the CI system.

paragraphs: The paper adds context-dependent phone classes to a speech recognizer combining a neural network with a hidden Markov model. Phones are the speech sound units being classified. The approach allows their probability estimates to reflect context, extending a system whose neural predictions originally treated phone classes independently of that context.

The design is modular. Separate single-layer networks distinguish among context classes using both the phone class and acoustic observations. Their outputs are combined with those of a context-independent network to produce context-dependent phone probabilities. This gives the original phone model and the additional context models distinct responsibilities within the recognizer.

Experiments report average word error reductions of 16% on the ARPA 5,000-word task and 13% on the SQALE 20,000-word task, relative to the context-independent system. Decoding also becomes more than twice as fast, which the abstract attributes to improved modeling. The findings show that adding context through this modular construction improves both recognition accuracy and the speed of obtaining a transcription.
summary.tldr: Modular context networks improve a hybrid speech recognizer's word error rates and more than double its decoding speed.

title: Context-Dependent Classes in a Hybrid Recurrent Network-HMM Speech Recognition System

abstract: We propose a new method to compute prediction intervals. Especially for small data sets the width of a prediction interval does not only depend on the variance of the target distribution, but also on the accuracy of our estimator of the mean of the target, i.e., on the width of the confidence interval. The confidence interval follows from the variation in an ensemble of neural networks, each of them trained and stopped on bootstrap replicates of the original data set. A second improvement is the use of the residuals on validation patterns instead of on training patterns for estimation of the variance of the target distribution. As illustrated on a synthetic example, our method is better than existing methods with regard to extrapolation and interpolation in data regimes with a limited amount of data, and yields prediction intervals which actual confidence levels are closer to the desired confidence levels.

The confidence interval follows from the variation in an ensemble of neural networks, each of them trained and stopped on bootstrap replicates of the original data set. A second improvement is the use of the residuals on validation patterns instead of on training patterns for estimation of the variance of the target distribution. paragraphs: The paper develops prediction intervals that account for two sources of uncertainty. One is variation in the target distribution; the other is uncertainty in the estimated target mean. The authors emphasize that the second source matters especially with small datasets, where an estimated mean may itself be imprecise.

To estimate uncertainty in the mean, they use variation across an ensemble of neural networks trained and stopped on bootstrap replicates of the original data. They also estimate target variance from residuals on validation examples rather than training examples. These two choices address different contributions to the width of the final prediction interval.

On a synthetic example with limited data, the method improves over existing approaches for both interpolation and extrapolation. Its prediction intervals also achieve confidence levels closer to the intended levels. The result highlights that a useful interval must reflect uncertainty in the fitted predictor as well as variation around it, with validation residuals supplying a separate basis for estimating the latter contribution.
summary.tldr: Bootstrap neural-network ensembles and validation residuals produce better-calibrated prediction intervals in a limited-data synthetic example.

title: Practical Confidence and Prediction Intervals

abstract: We provide an analysis of the turbo decoding algorithm (TDA) in a setting involving Gaussian densities. In this context, we are able to show that the algorithm converges and that - somewhat surprisingly - though the density generated by the TDA may differ significantly from the desired posterior density, the means of these two densities coincide. 1
originalAbstract: We provide an analysis of the turbo decoding algorithm (TDA) in a setting involving Gaussian densities. In this context, we are able to show that the algorithm converges and that - somewhat surprisingly - though the density generated by the TDA may differ significantly from the desired posterior density, the means of these two densities coincide. 1

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the turbo decoding algorithm in a setting where the relevant probability densities are Gaussian. The central question is how the algorithm's output relates to the posterior density that inference is intended to recover. Restricting the analysis to this setting allows the authors to establish precise results about both convergence and the resulting estimate.

They show that the algorithm converges in the Gaussian setting they study. Convergence means its iterative computation reaches a limiting result, but that alone does not establish that the result is the desired posterior. The paper makes this distinction explicit: the density produced by the algorithm can differ substantially from the target density.

Despite that possible discrepancy, the two densities have the same mean. Thus, in this analysis, the algorithm recovers the posterior's average value even when it does not recover the entire distribution. The result separates accuracy of a particular summary from accuracy of a full probabilistic representation, and its stated scope remains the Gaussian setting.
summary.tldr: In the analyzed Gaussian setting, turbo decoding converges and recovers the correct posterior mean even when its density differs substantially.

title: An Analysis of Turbo Decoding with Gaussian Densities

abstract: 'Kernel' principal component analysis (PCA) is an elegant non(cid:173) linear generalisation of the popular linear data analysis method, where a kernel function implicitly defines a nonlinear transforma(cid:173) tion into a feature space wherein standard PCA is performed. Un(cid:173) fortunately, the technique is not 'sparse', since the components thus obtained are expressed in terms of kernels associated with ev(cid:173) ery training vector. This paper shows that by approximating the covariance matrix in feature space by a reduced number of exam(cid:173) ple vectors, using a maximum-likelihood approach, we may obtain a highly sparse form of kernel PCA without loss of effectiveness.

Un(cid:173) fortunately, the technique is not 'sparse', since the components thus obtained are expressed in terms of kernels associated with ev(cid:173) ery training vector. This paper shows that by approximating the covariance matrix in feature space by a reduced number of exam(cid:173) ple vectors, using a maximum-likelihood approach, we may obtain a highly sparse form of kernel PCA without loss of effectiveness.

paragraphs: Kernel principal component analysis extends ordinary PCA by using a kernel to define an implicit nonlinear feature space. Standard PCA is then performed in that space. The paper addresses a representation problem with this method: each resulting component depends on kernel evaluations associated with every training example.

The authors propose approximating the feature-space covariance matrix using a smaller collection of example vectors. They choose this approximation through a maximum-likelihood approach. Because the covariance matrix determines the principal components, changing its representation provides a route to components that depend on far fewer example vectors.

The paper reports that this can produce a highly sparse version of kernel PCA without losing effectiveness. Here, sparsity concerns the number of examples needed to express the components, rather than the number of original input coordinates. The contribution preserves the nonlinear feature-space approach while reducing its dependence on the complete training set, directly addressing the source of the original method's dense representation.
summary.tldr: A maximum-likelihood covariance approximation can make kernel PCA highly sparse without loss of effectiveness.

title: Sparse Kernel Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Given an N(cid:2)N grid of squares, where each square has a count and an un- derlying population, our goal is to ﬁnd the square region with the highest density, and to calculate its signiﬁcance by randomization. Any density measure D, dependent on the total count and total population of a re- gion, can be used. For example, if each count represents the number of disease cases occurring in that square, we can use Kulldorff’s spatial scan statistic DK to ﬁnd the most signiﬁcant spatial disease cluster. A naive approach to ﬁnding the maximum density region requires O(N 3) time, and is generally computationally infeasible. We present a novel algorithm which partitions the grid into overlapping regions, bounds the maximum score of subregions contained in each region, and prunes re- gions which cannot contain the maximum density region. For sufﬁciently dense regions, this method ﬁnds the maximum density region in optimal O(N2) time, in practice resulting in signiﬁcant (10-200x) speedups.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a spatial search problem: given a square grid containing counts and population totals, find the square region with the highest density score. For disease surveillance, the counts can represent cases and the populations provide context for interpreting them. Randomization is then used to assess the significance of the selected region.

The algorithm divides the grid into overlapping regions and calculates bounds on the scores their smaller regions could achieve. If a bound shows that a region cannot contain the best answer, that part of the search is discarded. This makes it possible to avoid evaluating every candidate square while still searching for the maximum.

The method accommodates density measures based on a region’s total count and population, including the stated spatial scan statistic. For sufficiently dense regions, the authors establish optimal quadratic running time instead of the naive cubic cost. They report practical speedups of 10–200 times; the quadratic guarantee specifically depends on the density condition.
summary.tldr: A search algorithm uses regional score bounds to find spatial clusters faster, with optimal quadratic time under a stated density condition.

title: A Fast Multi-Resolution Method for Detection of Significant Spatial Disease Clusters

abstract: We propose a generic algorithm for computation of similarity measures for se- quential data. The algorithm uses generalized sufﬁx trees for efﬁcient calculation of various kernel, distance and non-metric similarity functions. Its worst-case run-time is linear in the length of sequences and independent of the underlying embedding language, which can cover words, k-grams or all contained subse- quences. Experiments with network intrusion detection, DNA analysis and text processing applications demonstrate the utility of distances and similarity coefﬁ- cients for sequences as alternatives to classical kernel functions.
originalAbstract: We propose a generic algorithm for computation of similarity measures for se- quential data. The algorithm uses generalized sufﬁx trees for efﬁcient calculation of various kernel, distance and non-metric similarity functions. Its worst-case run-time is linear in the length of sequences and independent of the underlying embedding language, which can cover words, k-grams or all contained subse- quences. Experiments with network intrusion detection, DNA analysis and text processing applications demonstrate the utility of distances and similarity coefﬁ- cients for sequences as alternatives to classical kernel functions.

paragraphs: This paper presents a shared computational method for comparing sequential data. It covers several kinds of comparison: kernel functions, distances, and similarities that do not satisfy metric requirements. The aim is to support this range of measures through one generic algorithm rather than treating each type as an unrelated computational problem.

The algorithm uses generalized suffix trees to calculate the comparisons efficiently. Its stated worst-case running time is linear in sequence length and does not depend on the underlying embedding language. That language specifies the sequence elements being represented, which may include words, fixed-length k-grams, or all contained subsequences. The result connects a broad choice of representations with the same stated runtime behavior.

Experiments span network intrusion detection, DNA analysis, and text processing. They demonstrate the usefulness of sequence distances and similarity coefficients as alternatives to classical kernels. The contribution combines computational efficiency with flexibility in how sequences are compared, making the choice of similarity measure part of the modeling approach rather than restricting it to kernels alone.
summary.tldr: A generalized-suffix-tree algorithm computes diverse sequence similarities with worst-case runtime linear in sequence length.

title: Computation of Similarity Measures for Sequential Data using Generalized Suffix Trees

abstract: We introduce a hierarchical Bayesian model for the discovery of putative regulators from gene expression data only. The hierarchy incorporates the knowledge that there are just a few regulators that by themselves only regulate a handful of genes. This is implemented through a so-called spike-and-slab prior, a mixture of Gaussians with different widths, with mixing weights from a hierarchical Bernoulli model. For efficient inference we implemented expectation propagation. Running the model on a malaria parasite data set, we found four genes with significant homology to transcription factors in an amoebe, one RNA regulator and three genes of unknown function (out of the top ten genes considered).

The hierarchy incorporates the knowledge that there are just a few regulators that by themselves only regulate a handful of genes. This is implemented through a so-called spike-and-slab prior, a mixture of Gaussians with different widths, with mixing weights from a hierarchical Bernoulli model. For efficient inference we implemented expectation propagation. Running the model on a malaria parasite data set, we found four genes with significant homology to transcription factors in an amoebe, one RNA regulator and three genes of unknown function (out of the top ten genes considered).

paragraphs: This paper seeks candidate regulators using gene-expression data alone. Its hierarchical Bayesian model incorporates the idea that only a few genes act as regulators and that each regulates only a handful of other genes. That assumption shapes the search toward a small collection of regulators with sparse sets of targets.

The authors implement this structure with a spike-and-slab prior formed from Gaussian components of different widths. A hierarchical Bernoulli model controls the mixing weights, connecting the sparsity assumptions at different levels. Expectation propagation provides an efficient inference procedure for estimating the model from expression measurements.

Applied to malaria parasite data, the model identifies candidates with several kinds of biological relevance. Among the top ten genes considered, four have significant homology to transcription factors in an amoeba, one is an RNA regulator, and three have unknown function. These findings give the candidate list biological interest while retaining the paper’s distinction between putative regulators and experimentally established regulatory roles. The model is a discovery tool guided by an explicit sparse-regulation assumption.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical sparse Bayesian model uses malaria gene-expression data to identify putative regulators, including candidates related to known regulatory proteins.

title: Regulator Discovery from Gene Expression Time Series of Malaria Parasites: a Hierachical Approach

abstract: We develop a Bayesian sequential model for category learning. The sequential model updates two category parameters, the mean and the variance, over time. We define conjugate temporal priors to enable closed form solutions to be obtained. This model can be easily extended to supervised and unsupervised learning involving multiple categories. To model the spacing effect, we introduce a generic prior in the temporal updating stage to capture a learning preference, namely, less change for repetition and more change for variation. Finally, we show how this approach can be generalized to efficiently performmodel selection to decide whether observations are from one or multiple categories.

We define conjugate temporal priors to enable closed form solutions to be obtained. This model can be easily extended to supervised and unsupervised learning involving multiple categories. To model the spacing effect, we introduce a generic prior in the temporal updating stage to capture a learning preference, namely, less change for repetition and more change for variation. Finally, we show how this approach can be generalized to efficiently performmodel selection to decide whether observations are from one or multiple categories.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian model of category learning in which beliefs change as observations arrive. The model updates both a category's mean and its variance over time. These quantities describe the category's central tendency and its spread, allowing learning to alter both what is typical and how much variation belongs within the category.

The authors introduce conjugate temporal priors so the updates have closed-form solutions. To represent the spacing effect, they add a prior during temporal updating that expresses a particular learning preference: repetition produces less change, while variation produces more. The way observations unfold over time therefore becomes part of the model's account of learning.

The formulation can be extended to supervised and unsupervised learning with multiple categories. The authors also generalize it to efficient model selection, allowing a decision between explaining observations with one category or several. Together, these developments connect sequential parameter updating with the separate question of how many categories the observations should be assigned to.
summary.tldr: A sequential Bayesian category model represents spacing effects through updates that respond less to repetition and more to variation.

title: Modeling the spacing effect in sequential category learning

abstract: Search engines today present results that are often oblivious to recent shifts in intent. For example, the meaning of the query independence day shifts in early July to a US holiday and to a movie around the time of the box office release. While no studies exactly quantify the magnitude of intent-shifting traffic, studies suggest that news events, seasonal topics, pop culture, etc account for 1/2 the search queries. This paper shows that the signals a search engine receives can be used to both determine that a shift in intent happened, as well as find a result that is now more relevant. We present a meta-algorithm that marries a classifier with a bandit algorithm to achieve regret that depends logarithmically on the number of query impressions, under certain assumptions. We provide strong evidence that this regret is close to the best achievable. Finally, via a series of experiments, we demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms prior approaches, particularly as the amount of intent-shifting traffic increases.

This paper shows that the signals a search engine receives can be used to both determine that a shift in intent happened, as well as find a result that is now more relevant. paragraphs: The same search query can express different interests at different times. A phrase such as independence day may refer to a holiday or a film depending on current events. This paper studies how a search engine can recognize such changes and identify a result that has become more relevant.

The proposed meta-algorithm combines a classifier with a bandit algorithm. It uses signals received by the search engine both to detect a shift and to adapt result selection. Under certain assumptions, its regret grows only logarithmically with the number of query impressions. Regret describes the accumulated cost of imperfect decisions, so this bound addresses how that cost grows as the system handles more searches.

The authors provide strong evidence that the regret is close to the best achievable and report experimental improvements over prior approaches. Those improvements are particularly pronounced as intent-shifting traffic increases. The contribution connects detecting change with acting on it: recognizing that an old interpretation has become less relevant is useful only if the system can also identify a better result.
summary.tldr: A classifier-and-bandit algorithm detects changing search intent and adapts results, with logarithmic regret under stated assumptions.

title: Adapting to the Shifting Intent of Search Queries

abstract: Motivated by recent developments in manifold-valued regression we propose a family of nonparametric kernel-smoothing estimators with metric-space valued output including a robust median type estimator and the classical Frechet mean. Depending on the choice of the output space and the chosen metric the estimator reduces to partially well-known procedures for multi-class classification, multivariate regression in Euclidean space, regression with manifold-valued output and even some cases of structured output learning. In this paper we focus on the case of regression with manifold-valued input and output. We show pointwise and Bayes consistency for all estimators in the family for the case of manifold-valued output and illustrate the robustness properties of the estimator with experiments.
originalAbstract: Motivated by recent developments in manifold-valued regression we propose a family of nonparametric kernel-smoothing estimators with metric-space valued output including a robust median type estimator and the classical Frechet mean. Depending on the choice of the output space and the chosen metric the estimator reduces to partially well-known procedures for multi-class classification, multivariate regression in Euclidean space, regression with manifold-valued output and even some cases of structured output learning. In this paper we focus on the case of regression with manifold-valued input and output. We show pointwise and Bayes consistency for all estimators in the family for the case of manifold-valued output and illustrate the robustness properties of the estimator with experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops regression methods for outputs that belong to a metric space, where distances are available but ordinary numerical averaging may not be the appropriate operation. It proposes a family of nonparametric kernel-smoothing estimators that includes both a robust median-type estimator and the classical Fréchet mean.

The output space and its distance measure determine which prediction procedure results. Different choices connect the framework to multiclass classification, multivariate Euclidean regression, manifold-valued regression, and some structured-output problems. This gives several seemingly different tasks a shared formulation while allowing their output geometry to affect the estimator.

The authors focus their analysis on regression with manifold-valued inputs and outputs. For manifold-valued outputs, they establish pointwise and Bayes consistency for every estimator in the family. Experiments illustrate robustness properties of the estimator. The contribution combines a flexible construction for geometric outputs with theoretical consistency results in the manifold setting and empirical evidence about resistance to problematic observations.
summary.tldr: A family of distance-based regression estimators includes robust median prediction and has consistency guarantees for manifold-valued outputs.

title: Robust Nonparametric Regression with Metric-Space Valued Output

abstract: Non-parametric Bayesian techniques are considered for learning dictionaries for sparse image representations, with applications in denoising, inpainting and compressive sensing (CS). The beta process is employed as a prior for learning the dictionary, and this non-parametric method naturally infers an appropriate dictionary size. The Dirichlet process and a probit stick-breaking process are also considered to exploit structure within an image. The proposed method can learn a sparse dictionary in situ; training images may be exploited if available, but they are not required. Further, the noise variance need not be known, and can be non-stationary. Another virtue of the proposed method is that sequential inference can be readily employed, thereby allowing scaling to large images. Several example results are presented, using both Gibbs and variational Bayesian inference, with comparisons to other state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Sparse image representations describe an image using a limited selection of elements from a learned dictionary. This paper develops a nonparametric Bayesian approach that learns the dictionary and infers an appropriate size for it. The method is applied to denoising, filling in missing image information, and reconstruction in compressive sensing.

A beta-process prior supports dictionary learning, while a Dirichlet process and a probit stick-breaking process are considered for capturing structure within an image. The dictionary can be learned directly from the image being processed. Training images can contribute when available, but the method does not require them. It also accommodates unknown noise variance and noise that varies across the image.

The authors explain that sequential inference can be used to scale the approach to large images. They present example results using both Gibbs sampling and variational Bayesian inference, alongside comparisons with state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution brings several forms of flexibility into one modeling approach: adapting dictionary size, using internal image structure, estimating noise, and allowing learning without a separate training collection.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian sparse-image model infers dictionary size, can learn directly from an image, and accommodates unknown spatially varying noise.

title: Non-Parametric Bayesian Dictionary Learning for Sparse Image Representations

abstract: In many domains, humans appear to combine perceptual cues in a near-optimal, probabilistic fashion: two noisy pieces of information tend to be combined linearly with weights proportional to the precision of each cue. Here we present a case where structural information plays an important role. The presence of a background cue gives rise to the possibility of occlusion, and places a soft constraint on the location of a target – in effect propelling it forward. We present an ideal observer model of depth estimation for this situation where structural or ordinal information is important and then fit the model to human data from a stereo-matching task. To test whether subjects are truly using ordinal cues in a probabilistic manner we then vary the uncertainty of the task. We find that the model accurately predicts shifts in subject’s behavior. Our results indicate that the nervous system estimates depth ordering in a probabilistic fashion and estimates the structure of the visual scene during depth perception.

We present an ideal observer model of depth estimation for this situation where structural or ordinal information is important and then fit the model to human data from a stereo-matching task. To test whether subjects are truly using ordinal cues in a probabilistic manner we then vary the uncertainty of the task. We find that the model accurately predicts shifts in subject’s behavior. Our results indicate that the nervous system estimates depth ordering in a probabilistic fashion and estimates the structure of the visual scene during depth perception.

Here, a background cue also provides structural information: the possibility that something is hidden imposes a soft constraint on the target’s location, shifting its perceived position forward.

The authors develop an ideal-observer model that incorporates this structural or depth-ordering information and fit it to human performance in a stereo-matching task. They then change the task’s uncertainty to test whether people use ordinal cues probabilistically. This tests the model through predicted behavioral changes as the reliability of the available information changes.

The model accurately predicts shifts in participants’ behavior. The findings indicate that depth perception involves probabilistic estimates of which surfaces are in front of others, together with estimates of scene structure. The contribution is evidence that perceived depth depends on inferred relationships among scene elements as well as the precision of individual cues.
summary.tldr: An ideal-observer model predicts how possible occlusion and uncertainty shift human depth judgments.

title: Structural inference affects depth perception in the context of potential occlusion

abstract: This paper describes a probabilistic framework for studying associations between multiple genotypes, biomarkers, and phenotypic traits in the presence of noise and unobserved confounders for large genetic studies. The framework builds on sparse linear methods developed for regression and modified here for inferring causal structures of richer networks with latent variables. The method is motivated by the use of genotypes as ``instruments'' to infer causal associations between phenotypic biomarkers and outcomes, without making the common restrictive assumptions of instrumental variable methods. The method may be used for an effective screening of potentially interesting genotype phenotype and biomarker-phenotype associations in genome-wide studies, which may have important implications for validating biomarkers as possible proxy endpoints for early stage clinical trials. Where the biomarkers are gene transcripts, the method can be used for fine mapping of quantitative trait loci (QTLs) detected in genetic linkage studies. The method is applied for examining effects of gene transcript levels in the liver on plasma HDL cholesterol levels for a sample of sequenced mice from a heterogeneous stock, with $\sim 10^5$ genetic instruments and $\sim 47 \times 10^3$ gene transcripts.

title: Sparse Instrumental Variables (SPIV) for Genome-Wide Studies

abstract: We consider online learning in finite stochastic Markovian environments where in each time step a new reward function is chosen by an oblivious adversary. The goal of the learning agent is to compete with the best stationary policy in terms of the total reward received. In each time step the agent observes the current state and the reward associated with the last transition, however, the agent does not observe the rewards associated with other state-action pairs. The agent is assumed to know the transition probabilities. The state of the art result for this setting is a no-regret algorithm. In this paper we propose a new learning algorithm and assuming that stationary policies mix uniformly fast, we show that after T time steps, the expected regret of the new algorithm is O(T^{2/3} (ln T)^{1/3}), giving the first rigorously proved convergence rate result for the problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies an agent acting in a finite stochastic environment while the reward function changes at every step. An oblivious adversary selects these rewards. The agent knows the transition probabilities but observes only its current state and the reward from its latest transition, leaving rewards for other choices unseen.

The objective is to compete in total reward with the best stationary policy. This creates a learning problem with both state-dependent transitions and limited feedback. The proposed algorithm addresses this setting under the assumption that stationary policies mix uniformly quickly, meaning their state distributions settle rapidly in a uniform way.

Under that assumption, the authors prove an expected regret bound of O(T^(2/3)(ln T)^(1/3)) after T steps. Because this grows more slowly than T, the average reward shortfall against the comparator decreases over time. The contribution strengthens the earlier no-regret result with an explicit convergence rate, described by the authors as the first rigorously established rate for this problem.
summary.tldr: With known transitions and uniformly fast policy mixing, a new bandit-feedback MDP algorithm achieves an explicit sublinear expected regret bound.

title: Online Markov Decision Processes under Bandit Feedback

abstract: Since the discovery of sophisticated fully polynomial randomized algorithms for a range of #P problems (Karzanov et al., 1991; Jerrum et al., 2001; Wilson, 2004), theoretical work on approximate inference in combinatorial spaces has focused on Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Despite their strong theoretical guarantees, the slow running time of many of these randomized algorithms and the restrictive assumptions on the potentials have hindered the applicability of these algorithms to machine learning. Because of this, in applications to combinatorial spaces simple exact models are often preferred to more complex models that require approximate inference (Siepel et al., 2004). Variational inference would appear to provide an appealing alternative, given the success of variational methods for graphical models (Wainwright et al., 2008); unfortunately, however, it is not obvious how to develop variational approximations for combinatorial objects such as matchings, partial orders, plane partitions and sequence alignments. We propose a new framework that extends variational inference to a wide range of combinatorial spaces. Our method is based on a simple assumption: the existence of a tractable measure factorization, which we show holds in many examples. Simulations on a range of matching models show that the algorithm is more general and empirically faster than a popular fully polynomial randomized algorithm. We also apply the framework to the problem of multiple alignment of protein sequences, obtaining state-of-the-art results on the BAliBASE dataset (Thompson et al., 1999).

paragraphs: Probabilistic models over combinatorial objects must reason about possibilities such as matchings, partial orders, and sequence alignments. Randomized inference algorithms can offer strong theoretical guarantees, yet slow execution and restrictions on model potentials can hinder their use. This paper develops a variational alternative for a broad range of these structured spaces.

The framework relies on the existence of a tractable measure factorization. The authors show that this assumption holds in many examples, providing a foundation for constructing variational approximations over objects whose structure makes such approximations difficult to formulate. summary.tldr: A tractable measure factorization enables variational inference over combinatorial objects, with strong empirical results for matching and protein alignment.

title: Variational Inference over Combinatorial Spaces

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a popular algorithm that can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of machine learning tasks. Several researchers have recently proposed schemes to parallelize SGD, but all require performance-destroying memory locking and synchronization. This work aims to show using novel theoretical analysis, algorithms, and implementation that SGD can be implemented without any locking . We present an update scheme called Hogwild which allows processors access to shared memory with the possibility of overwriting each other's work. We show that when the associated optimization problem is sparse, meaning most gradient updates only modify small parts of the decision variable, then Hogwild achieves a nearly optimal rate of convergence. We demonstrate experimentally that Hogwild outperforms alternative schemes that use locking by an order of magnitude.

We present an update scheme called Hogwild which allows processors access to shared memory with the possibility of overwriting each other's work. paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent improves model parameters through successive updates. Running those updates on multiple processors introduces a coordination problem when they share the same parameters. Locking and synchronization protect shared memory, but they also impose overhead. This paper asks whether parallel optimization can work effectively without that protection.

The proposed scheme, Hogwild, lets processors update shared memory without acquiring locks. Processors may therefore overwrite one another's work. The authors support this design with theoretical analysis, algorithms, and an implementation. Their convergence result depends on sparsity: most gradient updates must change only a small portion of the decision variable. Under that condition, they establish a nearly optimal convergence rate.

Experiments show an order-of-magnitude advantage over alternative schemes that use locking. The finding combines a conditional mathematical result with a practical performance demonstration. Its significance is that preventing every conflicting update is not required for effective parallel SGD in the sparse setting analyzed, allowing the implementation to avoid expensive coordination.
summary.tldr: Hogwild removes locks from parallel SGD and achieves nearly optimal convergence when updates are sparse, with large experimental speedups.

title: Hogwild!: A Lock-Free Approach to Parallelizing Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: The representer theorem is a property that lies at the foundation of regularization theory and kernel methods. A class of regularization functionals is said to admit a linear representer theorem if every member of the class admits minimizers that lie in the finite dimensional subspace spanned by the representers of the data. A recent characterization states that certain classes of regularization functionals with differentiable regularization term admit a linear representer theorem for any choice of the data if and only if the regularization term is a radial nondecreasing function. In this paper, we extend such result by weakening the assumptions on the regularization term. In particular, the main result of this paper implies that, for a sufficiently large family of regularization functionals, radial nondecreasing functions are the only lower semicontinuous regularization terms that guarantee existence of a representer theorem for any choice of the data.

paragraphs: A linear representer theorem says that a regularized learning problem admits a minimizer in the finite-dimensional subspace spanned by the data’s representers. This property underlies regularization theory and kernel methods. It matters because the solution can be sought in a data-defined subspace even when the surrounding Hilbert space is much larger.

Earlier characterizations covered certain families with differentiable regularization terms. They linked the representer property for every possible dataset to penalties that are radial and nondecreasing: the penalty depends on distance from the origin and does not decrease as that distance grows. The paper weakens the assumptions needed for this characterization.

Its main result implies that, for a sufficiently large family of regularization functionals, radial nondecreasing penalties are the only lower semicontinuous regularization terms that guarantee a representer theorem for every dataset. The scope of the family and the requirement to cover all data choices are essential qualifications. The result extends the structural characterization beyond differentiable penalties and clarifies which penalty shapes can support this universal representer guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper extends representer-theorem characterizations to weaker regularity assumptions, identifying radial nondecreasing penalties as essential within its stated scope.

title: The representer theorem for Hilbert spaces: a necessary and sufficient condition

abstract: Distributions over exchangeable matrices with infinitely many columns are useful in constructing nonparametric latent variable models. However, the distribution implied by such models over the number of features exhibited by each data point may be poorly-suited for many modeling tasks. In this paper, we propose a class of exchangeable nonparametric priors obtained by restricting the domain of existing models. Such models allow us to specify the distribution over the number of features per data point, and can achieve better performance on data sets where the number of features is not well-modeled by the original distribution.

Such models allow us to specify the distribution over the number of features per data point, and can achieve better performance on data sets where the number of features is not well-modeled by the original distribution.

paragraphs: Nonparametric latent variable models can use exchangeable matrices with infinitely many columns to represent hidden features. Such a representation also implies a distribution over how many features each observation exhibits. This paper addresses situations where that implied feature-count distribution is poorly matched to the modeling task.

The authors construct a class of priors by restricting the domains of existing nonparametric models. The resulting priors retain exchangeability while allowing the modeler to specify the distribution of feature counts per observation. This separates the choice of how many features an individual data point uses from the broader availability of an unbounded collection of possible features.

The practical significance is greater control over an aspect of the model that may otherwise be dictated by the original prior. The authors state that these restricted models can perform better on datasets whose feature counts are not well described by the original distribution. The benefit is therefore connected to a specific modeling mismatch: imposing a more suitable count distribution can improve the resulting latent-feature model.
summary.tldr: Restricting existing exchangeable nonparametric priors allows explicit feature-count distributions and can improve performance when the original count model fits poorly.

title: Restricting exchangeable nonparametric distributions

abstract: We consider energy minimization for undirected graphical models, also known as MAP-inference problem for Markov random fields. Although combinatorial methods, which return a provably optimal integral solution of the problem, made a big progress in the past decade, they are still typically unable to cope with large-scale datasets. On the other hand, large scale datasets are typically defined on sparse graphs, and convex relaxation methods, such as linear programming relaxations often provide good approximations to integral solutions. We propose a novel method of combining combinatorial and convex programming techniques to obtain a global solution of the initial combinatorial problem. Based on the information obtained from the solution of the convex relaxation, our method confines application of the combinatorial solver to a small fraction of the initial graphical model, which allows to optimally solve big problems. We demonstrate the power of our approach on a computer vision energy minimization benchmark.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable configuration of an undirected graphical model can be expressed as an energy minimization problem. Combinatorial solvers can return provably optimal discrete solutions, but large problems often exceed their practical reach. Convex relaxations can handle large sparse graphs and often produce good approximations, creating an opportunity to combine the two approaches.

The paper uses information from a solved convex relaxation to shrink the portion of the graphical model that needs combinatorial search. The exact solver is then applied to only a small fraction of the original problem. This reduction is designed to retain a global solution of the original discrete problem while limiting the expensive search.

The authors demonstrate the method on a computer vision energy minimization benchmark. Its significance lies in using a tractable relaxation to guide exact optimization: the approximate formulation helps determine where combinatorial effort is needed. The reported approach thereby enables optimal solutions for large problems through coordination between convex and combinatorial techniques.
summary.tldr: Convex relaxation narrows the region requiring combinatorial search, enabling globally optimal solutions to large graphical-model problems.

title: Global MAP-Optimality by Shrinking the Combinatorial Search Area with Convex Relaxation

abstract: Recent work on molecular programming has explored new possibilities for computational abstractions with biomolecules, including logic gates, neural networks, and linear systems. In the future such abstractions might enable nanoscale devices that can sense and control the world at a molecular scale. Just as in macroscale robotics, it is critical that such devices can learn about their environment and reason under uncertainty. At this small scale, systems are typically modeled as chemical reaction networks. In this work, we develop a procedure that can take arbitrary probabilistic graphical models, represented as factor graphs over discrete random variables, and compile them into chemical reaction networks that implement inference. In particular, we show that marginalization based on sum-product message passing can be implemented in terms of reactions between chemical species whose concentrations represent probabilities. We show algebraically that the steady state concentration of these species correspond to the marginal distributions of the random variables in the graph and validate the results in simulations. As with standard sum-product inference, this procedure yields exact results for tree-structured graphs, and approximate solutions for loopy graphs.

paragraphs: Molecular devices that sense their surroundings would need ways to reason with uncertain information. This paper investigates how chemical reaction networks could perform that computation. It connects a familiar probabilistic inference procedure with a physical description in which chemical species interact through reactions.

The authors develop a procedure for translating arbitrary factor graphs over discrete random variables into reaction networks implementing sum-product message passing. Concentrations of chemical species represent probabilities, and reactions carry out the operations needed to compute marginal distributions. This provides a systematic connection between a graphical model and a chemical system intended to perform its inference.

The paper gives an algebraic analysis of the relationship between steady-state concentrations and the inferred distributions, and validates the construction in simulations. Its accuracy follows the distinction in standard sum-product inference: tree-structured graphs yield exact results, while graphs containing loops yield approximate solutions. The work therefore supplies a computational construction and supporting analysis for chemical probabilistic inference, with the graph's structure determining whether the resulting marginals are exact or approximate.
summary.tldr: Discrete graphical models can be compiled into chemical reactions that perform sum-product inference, exactly on trees and approximately on loopy graphs.

title: Message Passing Inference with Chemical Reaction Networks

abstract: We consider an infinite-armed bandit problem with Bernoulli rewards. The mean rewards are independent, uniformly distributed over $[0,1]$. Rewards 0 and 1 are referred to as a success and a failure, respectively. We propose a novel algorithm where the decision to exploit any arm is based on two successive targets, namely, the total number of successes until the first failure and the first $m$ failures, respectively, where $m$ is a fixed parameter. This two-target algorithm achieves a long-term average regret in $\sqrt{2n}$ for a large parameter $m$ and a known time horizon $n$. This regret is optimal and strictly less than the regret achieved by the best known algorithms, which is in $2\sqrt{n}$. The results are extended to any mean-reward distribution whose support contains 1 and to unknown time horizons. Numerical experiments show the performance of the algorithm for finite time horizons.

paragraphs: An infinite-armed bandit offers an unlimited collection of choices, each producing a binary outcome with an unknown mean. The initial setting in this paper assumes that these means are independent and uniformly distributed on [0,1]. The learner must decide when observations justify continuing with an arm instead of exploring another.

The proposed algorithm makes that decision using two successive targets. It considers the number of successes before the first failure and before the first m failures, where m is a fixed parameter. These two stages use an arm's observed outcome history to decide whether to exploit it. The abstract labels outcome 0 a success and outcome 1 a failure.

For a known horizon n and large m, the stated long-term regret is sqrt(2n), which is optimal and improves on the previous 2sqrt(n) result. The authors extend their results to unknown horizons and to other mean distributions whose support contains 1. Numerical experiments examine finite-horizon performance, complementing the long-term theoretical result.
summary.tldr: A two-target rule for infinite-armed Bernoulli bandits achieves the stated optimal sqrt(2n) long-term regret for large m and a known horizon.

title: Two-Target Algorithms for Infinite-Armed Bandits with Bernoulli Rewards

abstract: Analysis of estimation error and associated structured statistical recovery based on norm regularized regression, e.g., Lasso, needs to consider four aspects: the norm, the loss function, the design matrix, and the noise vector. This paper presents generalizations of such estimation error analysis on all four aspects, compared to the existing literature. We characterize the restricted error set, establish relations between error sets for the constrained and regularized problems, and present an estimation error bound applicable to {\em any} norm. Precise characterizations of the bound are presented for a variety of noise vectors, design matrices, including sub-Gaussian, anisotropic, and dependent samples, and loss functions, including least squares and generalized linear models. Gaussian widths, as a measure of size of suitable sets, and associated tools play a key role in our generalized analysis.

paragraphs: Norm-regularized regression balances fitting observations with a penalty that encourages structure in the estimated parameters. This paper develops a broader analysis of the resulting estimation error. It considers four interacting ingredients: the penalty norm, the loss used to measure fit, the design matrix containing the explanatory variables, and the noise affecting observations.

The authors characterize the restricted error set, which describes the estimation errors relevant to their analysis. They also relate the error sets of constrained formulations to those of regularized formulations. Their general estimation bound applies to any norm, providing a common framework for penalties beyond an individual example such as the Lasso.

The paper makes the bound more precise for several noise and design settings, including sub-Gaussian, anisotropic, and dependent samples, and for least-squares and generalized linear-model losses. Gaussian width supplies a geometric measure of the size of sets that enter the analysis. The contribution is a unified way to connect structural penalties and data properties to recovery accuracy, while retaining the distinctions between the particular settings being analyzed.
summary.tldr: A general error-analysis framework connects arbitrary norm penalties, loss functions, design properties, and noise to statistical recovery accuracy.

title: Estimation with Norm Regularization

abstract: Spectral inference provides fast algorithms and provable optimality for latent topic analysis. But for real data these algorithms require additional ad-hoc heuristics, and even then often produce unusable results. We explain this poor performance by casting the problem of topic inference in the framework of Joint Stochastic Matrix Factorization (JSMF) and showing that previous methods violate the theoretical conditions necessary for a good solution to exist. We then propose a novel rectification method that learns high quality topics and their interactions even on small, noisy data. This method achieves results comparable to probabilistic techniques in several domains while maintaining scalability and provable optimality.

This method achieves results comparable to probabilistic techniques in several domains while maintaining scalability and provable optimality.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why spectral methods for latent topic analysis can perform poorly on real data despite offering fast computation and theoretical optimality. In practice, the abstract reports that such methods often require ad hoc fixes and can still yield unusable results. The authors seek an explanation for this mismatch between theory and observed behavior.

They reformulate topic inference as joint stochastic matrix factorization. Within this framework, they show that previous methods violate theoretical conditions needed for a good solution to exist. This diagnosis points to a problem with satisfying the mathematical requirements of the inference task, rather than treating poor outputs only as something to repair through miscellaneous heuristics.

The proposed rectification method learns useful topics and their interactions, including from small, noisy datasets. Across several domains, its results are comparable to probabilistic techniques while retaining scalability and provable optimality. The contribution combines a structural explanation for earlier failures with a correction that makes the benefits of spectral inference more usable in the reported real-data settings.
summary.tldr: A matrix-factorization diagnosis and rectification method improve spectral topic inference while retaining scalability and theoretical optimality.

title: Robust Spectral Inference for Joint Stochastic Matrix Factorization

abstract: Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a popular model for blind signal separation. The ICA model assumes that a number of independent source signals are linearly mixed to form the observed signals. We propose a new algorithm, PEGI (for pseudo-Euclidean Gradient Iteration), for provable model recovery for ICA with Gaussian noise. The main technical innovation of the algorithm is to use a fixed point iteration in a pseudo-Euclidean (indefinite “inner product”) space. The use of this indefinite “inner product” resolves technical issues common to several existing algorithms for noisy ICA. This leads to an algorithm which is conceptually simple, efficient and accurate in testing.Our second contribution is combining PEGI with the analysis of objectives for optimal recovery in the noisy ICA model. It has been observed that the direct approach of demixing with the inverse of the mixing matrix is suboptimal for signal recovery in terms of the natural Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio (SINR) criterion. There have been several partial solutions proposed in the ICA literature. It turns out that any solution to the mixing matrix reconstruction problem can be used to construct an SINR-optimal ICA demixing, despite the fact that SINR itself cannot be computed from data. That allows us to obtain a practical and provably SINR-optimal recovery method for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise.

The main technical innovation of the algorithm is to use a fixed point iteration in a pseudo-Euclidean (indefinite “inner product”) space. The use of this indefinite “inner product” resolves technical issues common to several existing algorithms for noisy ICA. This leads to an algorithm which is conceptually simple, efficient and accurate in testing.Our second contribution is combining PEGI with the analysis of objectives for optimal recovery in the noisy ICA model. It has been observed that the direct approach of demixing with the inverse of the mixing matrix is suboptimal for signal recovery in terms of the natural Signal to Interference plus Noise Ratio (SINR) criterion. There have been several partial solutions proposed in the ICA literature. It turns out that any solution to the mixing matrix reconstruction problem can be used to construct an SINR-optimal ICA demixing, despite the fact that SINR itself cannot be computed from data. That allows us to obtain a practical and provably SINR-optimal recovery method for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Independent component analysis seeks to recover independent source signals from observations that mix them linearly. Gaussian noise complicates both learning how the signals were mixed and separating them effectively. This paper addresses these two tasks together, while distinguishing recovery of the mixing model from recovery of the underlying signals.

The proposed algorithm, PEGI, uses a fixed-point iteration in a pseudo-Euclidean space, where the inner-product-like operation is indefinite. This geometric choice resolves technical difficulties shared by several existing noisy ICA algorithms. The authors provide provable model recovery and report that the method is efficient and accurate in testing.

The second contribution concerns signal quality. Simply applying the inverse mixing matrix can be suboptimal under the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio criterion. The authors show how any solution to mixing-matrix reconstruction can instead produce an SINR-optimal demixing, even though SINR cannot itself be computed from the observed data. Combining this result with PEGI yields a practical recovery method with an optimality guarantee for ICA with arbitrary Gaussian noise.
summary.tldr: PEGI combines a new geometric iteration for noisy ICA with a construction that makes reconstructed mixing models yield SINR-optimal signal recovery.

title: A Pseudo-Euclidean Iteration for Optimal Recovery in Noisy ICA

abstract: Principal components analysis~(PCA) is the optimal linear encoder of data. Sparse linear encoders (e.g., sparse PCA) produce more interpretable features that can promote better generalization. (\rn{1}) Given a level of sparsity, what is the best approximation to PCA? (\rn{2}) Are there efficient algorithms which can achieve this optimal combinatorial tradeoff? We answer both questions by providing the first polynomial-time algorithms to construct \emph{optimal} sparse linear auto-encoders; additionally, we demonstrate the performance of our algorithms on real data.

(\rn{2}) Are there efficient algorithms which can achieve this optimal combinatorial tradeoff? We answer both questions by providing the first polynomial-time algorithms to construct \emph{optimal} sparse linear auto-encoders; additionally, we demonstrate the performance of our algorithms on real data.

paragraphs: Principal components analysis provides an optimal linear encoding of data, but sparse encoders offer a different advantage: features that depend on fewer inputs can be easier to interpret and may generalize better. This paper asks how much approximation quality must be traded away when the encoder is required to have a specified level of sparsity.

The authors formulate two linked questions. First, what is the best approximation to PCA available at that sparsity level? Second, can an efficient algorithm attain the optimal combinatorial tradeoff? These questions connect the quality of a sparse representation with the difficulty of finding it, rather than evaluating sparsity only as a descriptive property of a learned model.

The paper answers them by providing what it identifies as the first polynomial-time algorithms for constructing optimal sparse linear autoencoders. It also demonstrates the algorithms on real data. The contribution establishes efficient access to the stated optimal sparsity–approximation tradeoff, while the motivation of improved generalization remains a potential benefit of sparse features.
summary.tldr: The paper provides polynomial-time algorithms that attain the optimal tradeoff between sparse linear encoding and approximation to PCA.

title: Optimal Sparse Linear Encoders and Sparse PCA

abstract: In this work we analyze the class prediction of parallel randomized ensembles by majority voting as an urn model. For a given test instance, the ensemble can be viewed as an urn of marbles of different colors. A marble represents an individual classifier. Its color represents the class label prediction of the corresponding classifier. The sequential querying of classifiers in the ensemble can be seen as draws without replacement from the urn. An analysis of this classical urn model based on the hypergeometric distribution makes it possible to estimate the confidence on the outcome of majority voting when only a fraction of the individual predictions is known. These estimates can be used to speed up the prediction by the ensemble. Specifically, the aggregation of votes can be halted when the confidence in the final prediction is sufficiently high. If one assumes a uniform prior for the distribution of possible votes the analysis is shown to be equivalent to a previous one based on Dirichlet distributions. The advantage of the current approach is that prior knowledge on the possible vote outcomes can be readily incorporated in a Bayesian framework. We show how incorporating this type of problem-specific knowledge into the statistical analysis of majority voting leads to faster classification by the ensemble and allows us to estimate the expected average speed-up beforehand.

paragraphs: A classification ensemble combines predictions from multiple classifiers through voting. Computing every vote can be unnecessary when the eventual result is already sufficiently clear. This paper studies how to estimate confidence in the final vote while observing only part of a parallel randomized ensemble.

For a particular test example, the authors represent classifiers as marbles in an urn, with each marble’s color indicating its predicted class. Querying successive classifiers corresponds to drawing marbles without replacement. Analysis using the hypergeometric distribution estimates confidence in the full ensemble’s decision from the votes observed so far. Prediction can stop once that confidence reaches a sufficiently high level.

The framework also accommodates prior knowledge about possible voting outcomes. With a uniform prior, its analysis is equivalent to an earlier approach using Dirichlet distributions. Its advantage is the ease of incorporating problem-specific knowledge through Bayesian reasoning. The authors show that this knowledge can accelerate classification and support advance estimates of the expected average speed-up.
summary.tldr: An urn-based analysis lets ensembles stop querying classifiers once confidence in the final vote is sufficiently high.

title: An urn model for majority voting in classification ensembles

abstract: We introduce a new sample complexity measure, which we refer to as split-sample growth rate. For any hypothesis $H$ and for any sample $S$ of size $m$, the split-sample growth rate $\hat{\tau}_H(m)$ counts how many different hypotheses can empirical risk minimization output on any sub-sample of $S$ of size $m/2$. We show that the expected generalization error is upper bounded by $O\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(\hat{\tau}_H(2m))}{m}}\right)$. Our result is enabled by a strengthening of the Rademacher complexity analysis of the expected generalization error. We show that this sample complexity measure, greatly simplifies the analysis of the sample complexity of optimal auction design, for many auction classes studied in the literature. Their sample complexity can be derived solely by noticing that in these auction classes, ERM on any sample or sub-sample will pick parameters that are equal to one of the points in the sample.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a way to assess how much training data a learning procedure needs by counting the different answers it can produce from parts of a sample. Its split-sample growth rate counts the distinct hypotheses that empirical risk minimization can select when given every possible half-sized subset of that sample.

This count connects the behavior of the learning procedure to its expected generalization error. The authors prove an upper bound proportional to the square root of log(split-sample growth rate at size 2m) divided by m. They obtain the result by strengthening an analysis based on Rademacher complexity. A smaller count therefore gives a tighter bound through this expression.

The application is learning revenue-optimal auctions from data. For many auction classes studied previously, empirical risk minimization chooses parameters from the observed sample points. That property makes the possible outputs easier to count, simplifying sample-complexity arguments. The contribution is a measure that turns this concrete property of auction learning into a generalization guarantee.
summary.tldr: A new count of what empirical risk minimization can learn from subsamples simplifies generalization bounds for several auction classes.

title: A Sample Complexity Measure with Applications to Learning Optimal Auctions

abstract: Dynamic neural networks toolkits such as PyTorch, DyNet, and Chainer offer more flexibility for implementing models that cope with data of varying dimensions and structure, relative to toolkits that operate on statically declared computations (e.g., TensorFlow, CNTK, and Theano). However, existing toolkits - both static and dynamic - require that the developer organize the computations into the batches necessary for exploiting high-performance data-parallel algorithms and hardware. This batching task is generally difficult, but it becomes a major hurdle as architectures become complex. In this paper, we present an algorithm, and its implementation in the DyNet toolkit, for automatically batching operations. Developers simply write minibatch computations as aggregations of single instance computations, and the batching algorithm seamlessly executes them, on the fly, in computationally efficient batches. On a variety of tasks, we obtain throughput similar to manual batches, as well as comparable speedups over single-instance learning on architectures that are impractical to batch manually.

paragraphs: Dynamic neural network toolkits make it easier to express models whose inputs vary in size or structure. Efficient execution, however, often requires organizing operations into batches that can exploit parallel hardware. Manually arranging those batches becomes difficult as model architectures grow more complex, limiting the practical benefit of flexible computation graphs.

The paper introduces an algorithm for automatically batching operations and implements it in DyNet. Developers express a minibatch as a collection of computations for individual examples. The system then organizes operations into computationally efficient batches during execution, taking over scheduling work that would otherwise need to appear in the model implementation.

Across a variety of tasks, the authors obtain throughput similar to manually constructed batches. They also report comparable speedups over single-instance learning for architectures that are impractical to batch by hand. The findings show that a convenient, example-by-example programming style can coexist with efficient batched execution in the evaluated settings. The contribution makes batching part of the toolkit's execution machinery rather than an additional model-development burden.
summary.tldr: Automatic operation batching in DyNet brings efficient parallel execution to models written as individual-example computations.

title: On-the-fly Operation Batching in Dynamic Computation Graphs

abstract: A generative recurrent neural network is quickly trained in an unsupervised manner to model popular reinforcement learning environments through compressed spatio-temporal representations. The world model's extracted features are fed into compact and simple policies trained by evolution, achieving state of the art results in various environments. We also train our agent entirely inside of an environment generated by its own internal world model, and transfer this policy back into the actual environment. Interactive version of this paper is available at https://worldmodels.github.io
