The world model's extracted features are fed into compact and simple policies trained by evolution, achieving state of the art results in various environments. We also train our agent entirely inside of an environment generated by its own internal world model, and transfer this policy back into the actual environment. Interactive version of this paper is available at https://worldmodels.github.io

paragraphs: An agent can use a learned representation of its environment to simplify action selection. This paper trains a generative recurrent neural network to model reinforcement learning environments through compressed representations of space and time. The world model is trained quickly in an unsupervised manner, producing features that summarize the environment's observations and temporal structure.

Those features become inputs to compact, simple policies trained through evolution. The approach separates learning a rich representation of the environment from optimizing the policy that acts on it. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across various environments, showing that a small policy can be effective when supplied with features extracted by the recurrent world model.

The paper also demonstrates training an agent entirely inside an environment generated by its own internal model, then transferring the resulting policy back to the actual environment. This gives the learned model a second role beyond feature extraction: it can provide an environment for policy training. The transfer demonstration supports that possibility in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: A recurrent world model supplies features for evolved policies and can generate an environment in which a policy is trained before transfer.

title: Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution

abstract: Modern large-scale machine learning applications require stochastic optimization algorithms to be implemented on distributed computational architectures. A key bottleneck is the communication overhead for exchanging information such as stochastic gradients among different workers. In this paper, to reduce the communication cost, we propose a convex optimization formulation to minimize the coding length of stochastic gradients. The key idea is to randomly drop out coordinates of the stochastic gradient vectors and amplify the remaining coordinates appropriately to ensure the sparsified gradient to be unbiased. To solve the optimal sparsification efficiently, several simple and fast algorithms are proposed for an approximate solution, with a theoretical guarantee for sparseness. Experiments on $\ell_2$ regularized logistic regression, support vector machines, and convolutional neural networks validate our sparsification approaches.

paragraphs: When multiple workers train a model together, exchanging stochastic gradients can become a major communication cost. This paper treats reducing that cost as an optimization problem. It proposes a convex formulation aimed at minimizing the coding length of the gradients sent between workers.

The compression method randomly removes gradient coordinates and increases the retained values appropriately. This adjustment makes the sparse gradient unbiased: averaging over the random choices recovers the original gradient. Individual messages contain fewer coordinates, but the random compression does not systematically change the expected update. That property is central to the proposed way of communicating less information.

To make the formulation practical, the authors develop several simple, fast algorithms that approximately solve the sparsification problem. They provide a theoretical guarantee on sparseness and evaluate the approaches on regularized logistic regression, support vector machines, and convolutional neural networks. The experiments validate the methods across these different learning problems, connecting the communication-focused formulation to implementations that can be used during distributed optimization.
summary.tldr: A convex formulation compresses distributed gradients by randomly dropping coordinates while preserving their expected values.

title: Gradient Sparsification for Communication-Efficient Distributed Optimization

abstract: We present MubyNet -- a feed-forward, multitask, bottom up system for the integrated localization, as well as 3d pose and shape estimation, of multiple people in monocular images. The challenge is the formal modeling of the problem that intrinsically requires discrete and continuous computation, e.g. grouping people vs. predicting 3d pose. The model identifies human body structures (joints and limbs) in images, groups them based on 2d and 3d information fused using learned scoring functions, and optimally aggregates such responses into partial or complete 3d human skeleton hypotheses under kinematic tree constraints, but without knowing in advance the number of people in the scene and their visibility relations. We design a multi-task deep neural network with differentiable stages where the person grouping problem is formulated as an integer program based on learned body part scores parameterized by both 2d and 3d information. This avoids suboptimality resulting from separate 2d and 3d reasoning, with grouping performed based on the combined representation. The final stage of 3d pose and shape prediction is based on a learned attention process where information from different human body parts is optimally integrated. State-of-the-art results are obtained in large scale datasets like Human3.6M and Panoptic, and qualitatively by reconstructing the 3d shape and pose of multiple people, under occlusion, in difficult monocular images.

paragraphs: MubyNet estimates the locations, three-dimensional poses, and body shapes of multiple people from a single image. It works from detected body parts upward, rather than requiring the number of people or their visibility relationships in advance. A central challenge is combining discrete decisions about which parts belong together with continuous predictions of three-dimensional structure.

The network identifies joints and limbs, then scores possible groupings using learned combinations of two-dimensional and three-dimensional information. An integer-program formulation assembles partial or complete skeleton hypotheses subject to constraints from the body's kinematic tree. Joint reasoning avoids the suboptimality the authors associate with separating grouping in the image from reasoning about three-dimensional pose.

A final learned attention process integrates information from different body parts to predict pose and shape. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on Human3.6M and Panoptic, alongside qualitative reconstructions of multiple people under occlusion in difficult images. These findings support treating grouping and three-dimensional estimation as connected parts of one system.
summary.tldr: MubyNet combines two-dimensional and three-dimensional body-part evidence to group people and estimate their poses and shapes from one image.

title: Deep Network for the Integrated 3D Sensing of Multiple People in Natural Images

abstract: This paper studies the problem of distributed stochastic optimization in an adversarial setting where, out of $m$ machines which allegedly compute stochastic gradients every iteration, an $\alpha$-fraction are Byzantine, and may behave adversarially. Our main result is a variant of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) which finds $\varepsilon$-approximate minimizers of convex functions in $T = \tilde{O}\big( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 m} + \frac{\alpha^2}{\varepsilon^2} \big)$ iterations. In contrast, traditional mini-batch SGD needs $T = O\big( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 m} \big)$ iterations, but cannot tolerate Byzantine failures. Further, we provide a lower bound showing that, up to logarithmic factors, our algorithm is information-theoretically optimal both in terms of sample complexity and time complexity.

Our main result is a variant of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) which finds $\varepsilon$-approximate minimizers of convex functions in $T = \tilde{O}\big( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 m} + \frac{\alpha^2}{\varepsilon^2} \big)$ iterations. In contrast, traditional mini-batch SGD needs $T = O\big( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 m} \big)$ iterations, but cannot tolerate Byzantine failures. paragraphs: Distributed optimization speeds up learning by asking several machines to estimate gradients at each iteration. This paper considers an adversarial version of that arrangement: an alpha fraction of the m machines can behave arbitrarily instead of providing trustworthy estimates. Ordinary mini-batch stochastic gradient descent benefits from more machines, but does not tolerate these Byzantine failures.

The authors develop an SGD variant for convex objectives that reaches an epsilon-approximate minimum in roughly 1/(epsilon² m) + alpha²/epsilon² iterations, ignoring logarithmic factors. The first term captures the familiar benefit of distributing work. The second expresses the additional cost associated with the adversarial fraction. Consequently, increasing the number of machines reduces one component of the bound while leaving the corruption-related component.

A matching lower bound shows that, up to logarithmic factors, the method is information-theoretically optimal in sample and time complexity. This makes the result more than a robustness construction: it characterizes how much optimization efficiency must be sacrificed to tolerate adversarial workers in the studied convex setting.
summary.tldr: A Byzantine-tolerant SGD variant achieves near-optimal sample and time complexity for distributed convex optimization.

title: Byzantine Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Negative sampling approaches are prevalent in implicit collaborative ﬁltering for obtaining negative labels from massive unlabeled data. As two major concerns in negative sampling, efﬁciency and effectiveness are still not fully achieved by recent works that use complicate structures and overlook risk of false negative instances. In this paper, we ﬁrst provide a novel understanding of negative instances by empirically observing that only a few instances are potentially important for model learning, and false negatives tend to have stable predictions over many training iterations. Above ﬁndings motivate us to simplify the model by sampling from designed memory that only stores a few important candidates and, more importantly, tackle the untouched false negative problem by favouring high-variance samples stored in memory, which achieves efﬁcient sampling of true negatives with high-quality. Empirical results on two synthetic datasets and three real-world datasets demonstrate both robustness and superiorities of our negative sampling method. The implementation is available at https://github.com/dingjingtao/SRNS.

paragraphs: Implicit collaborative filtering must learn from large amounts of unlabeled data, so negative sampling selects examples to treat as negative feedback. This creates both a computational challenge and a labeling risk: some selected examples may be false negatives. The paper seeks a sampling procedure that is simpler, efficient, and less vulnerable to that risk.

Two empirical observations motivate the method. Only a small number of candidate negatives appear especially important for learning, and false negatives tend to receive stable predictions over many training iterations. The authors therefore maintain a small memory of important candidates and favor those whose predictions vary more during training. Prediction variability serves as a sampling signal based on the observed tendency, not as a certain test of an example's true label.

Experiments on two synthetic datasets and three real-world datasets demonstrate robustness and superior performance for the proposed sampling method. The approach links efficiency and sample quality through the same compact memory: it narrows the candidate pool while using training history to help select useful negatives. The paper also makes an implementation available.
summary.tldr: A small candidate memory and prediction-variance sampling improve negative selection while reducing sensitivity to false negatives in recommendation experiments.

title: Simplify and Robustify Negative Sampling for Implicit Collaborative Filtering

abstract: The Column Subset Selection Problem (CSSP) and the Nystrom method are among the leading tools for constructing small low-rank approximations of large datasets in machine learning and scientific computing. A fundamental question in this area is: how well can a data subset of size k compete with the best rank k approximation? We develop techniques which exploit spectral properties of the data matrix to obtain improved approximation guarantees which go beyond the standard worst-case analysis. Our approach leads to significantly better bounds for datasets with known rates of singular value decay, e.g., polynomial or exponential decay. Our analysis also reveals an intriguing phenomenon: the approximation factor as a function of k may exhibit multiple peaks and valleys, which we call a multiple-descent curve. A lower bound we establish shows that this behavior is not an artifact of our analysis, but rather it is an inherent property of the CSSP and Nystrom tasks. Finally, using the example of a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, we show that both our improved bounds and the multiple-descent curve can be observed on real datasets simply by varying the RBF parameter.

paragraphs: Column subset selection and the Nystrom method compress large datasets by constructing approximations from selected data. A central question is how an approximation using k selected elements compares with the best rank-k approximation. This paper sharpens that comparison by taking account of the matrix's spectral structure instead of relying only on general worst-case guarantees.

The authors derive improved bounds when the rate of singular-value decay is known, including polynomial and exponential decay. Their analysis also reveals that the approximation factor can have several peaks and valleys as k changes. This multiple-descent behavior concerns performance relative to the best rank-k approximation, so it describes how that comparison changes with subset size.

A lower bound establishes that multiple descent can be inherent to these approximation problems, rather than merely an artifact of the proof technique. Using an RBF kernel on real datasets, the authors show that changing its parameter can expose both the improved guarantees and multiple-descent curves. Spectral structure thus helps explain behavior hidden by a single worst-case bound.
summary.tldr: Spectral information sharpens subset-approximation guarantees and reveals an inherent possibility of multiple peaks and valleys in relative approximation quality.

title: Improved guarantees and a multiple-descent curve for Column Subset Selection and the Nystrom method

abstract: We study the problem of learning from aggregate observations where supervision signals are given to sets of instances instead of individual instances, while the goal is still to predict labels of unseen individuals. A well-known example is multiple instance learning (MIL). In this paper, we extend MIL beyond binary classification to other problems such as multiclass classification and regression. We present a general probabilistic framework that accommodates a variety of aggregate observations, e.g., pairwise similarity/triplet comparison for classification and mean/difference/rank observation for regression. Simple maximum likelihood solutions can be applied to various differentiable models such as deep neural networks and gradient boosting machines. Moreover, we develop the concept of consistency up to an equivalence relation to characterize our estimator and show that it has nice convergence properties under mild assumptions. Experiments on three problem settings --- classification via triplet comparison and regression via mean/rank observation indicate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

We present a general probabilistic framework that accommodates a variety of aggregate observations, e.g., pairwise similarity/triplet comparison for classification and mean/difference/rank observation for regression. Simple maximum likelihood solutions can be applied to various differentiable models such as deep neural networks and gradient boosting machines. Moreover, we develop the concept of consistency up to an equivalence relation to characterize our estimator and show that it has nice convergence properties under mild assumptions. Experiments on three problem settings --- classification via triplet comparison and regression via mean/rank observation indicate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when supervision describes groups of examples, but predictions are needed for individual examples. Multiple instance learning is one familiar version of this problem. The authors broaden the setting beyond binary classification to include multiclass classification and regression, bringing several kinds of indirect supervision into one framework.

The probabilistic formulation accommodates classification information such as pairwise similarity and triplet comparisons, as well as regression information such as group means, differences, and ranks. It enables maximum likelihood learning with models including deep neural networks and gradient boosting machines. The central idea is to connect individual predictions to the aggregate observations that are actually available during training.

The authors characterize their estimator using consistency up to an equivalence relation, allowing the convergence statement to account for solutions treated as equivalent. They establish favorable convergence properties under mild assumptions. Experiments on classification from triplet comparisons and regression from means or ranks support the approach's effectiveness, showing how several forms of group-level supervision can inform individual-level prediction.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework learns individual predictions from aggregate supervision such as comparisons, group means, and ranks.

title: Learning from Aggregate Observations

abstract: Domain generalization aims to learn from multiple source domains a predictive model that can generalize to unseen target domains. One essential problem in domain generalization is to learn discriminative domain-invariant features. To arrive at this, some methods introduce a domain discriminator through adversarial learning to match the feature distributions in multiple source domains. However, adversarial training can only guarantee that the learned features have invariant marginal distributions, while the invariance of conditional distributions is more important for prediction in new domains. To ensure the conditional invariance of learned features, we propose an entropy regularization term that measures the dependency between the learned features and the class labels. Combined with the typical task-related loss, e.g., cross-entropy loss for classification, and adversarial loss for domain discrimination, our overall objective is guaranteed to learn conditional-invariant features across all source domains and thus can learn classifiers with better generalization capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comparison with state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real-world datasets. Code is available at: https://github.com/sshan-zhao/DG_via_ER.
originalAbstract: Domain generalization aims to learn from multiple source domains a predictive model that can generalize to unseen target domains. One essential problem in domain generalization is to learn discriminative domain-invariant features. To arrive at this, some methods introduce a domain discriminator through adversarial learning to match the feature distributions in multiple source domains. However, adversarial training can only guarantee that the learned features have invariant marginal distributions, while the invariance of conditional distributions is more important for prediction in new domains. To ensure the conditional invariance of learned features, we propose an entropy regularization term that measures the dependency between the learned features and the class labels. Combined with the typical task-related loss, e.g., cross-entropy loss for classification, and adversarial loss for domain discrimination, our overall objective is guaranteed to learn conditional-invariant features across all source domains and thus can learn classifiers with better generalization capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comparison with state-of-the-art methods on both simulated and real-world datasets. Code is available at: https://github.com/sshan-zhao/DG_via_ER.

paragraphs: Domain generalization seeks a predictor that learns from several source domains and works in an unseen target domain. A common strategy makes feature distributions look alike across sources using an adversarial domain discriminator. The paper argues that this addresses only marginal distributions, leaving unresolved whether the features' relationship with class labels is consistent.

The authors add an entropy regularizer that measures dependence between learned features and labels. They combine it with the prediction loss and the adversarial domain-discrimination loss. This joins the goal of hiding domain differences with the need to retain a stable connection between features and the classes being predicted.

The paper gives a guarantee that its overall objective learns conditionally invariant features across the source domains. This is the property the authors identify as more relevant to prediction in new domains. Comparisons with leading methods on simulated and real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The findings support strengthening domain alignment with label-related structure to improve generalization.
summary.tldr: An entropy regularizer strengthens domain alignment by enforcing conditional feature invariance across source domains.

title: Domain Generalization via Entropy Regularization

abstract: Multivariate time-series forecasting plays a crucial role in many real-world applications. It is a challenging problem as one needs to consider both intra-series temporal correlations and inter-series correlations simultaneously. Recently, there have been multiple works trying to capture both correlations, but most, if not all of them only capture temporal correlations in the time domain and resort to pre-defined priors as inter-series relationships. In this paper, we propose Spectral Temporal Graph Neural Network (StemGNN) to further improve the accuracy of multivariate time-series forecasting. StemGNN captures inter-series correlations and temporal dependencies jointly in the spectral domain. It combines Graph Fourier Transform (GFT) which models inter-series correlations and Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) which models temporal dependencies in an end-to-end framework. After passing through GFT and DFT, the spectral representations hold clear patterns and can be predicted effectively by convolution and sequential learning modules. Moreover, StemGNN learns inter-series correlations automatically from the data without using pre-defined priors. We conduct extensive experiments on ten real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of StemGNN.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series together requires modeling both each series' temporal behavior and relationships among series. Existing approaches often analyze time directly while relying on predefined relationships between the series. StemGNN instead learns those relationships and processes both kinds of dependence in the spectral domain.

The model combines a Graph Fourier Transform for relationships among series with a Discrete Fourier Transform for temporal dependencies. These transformations form part of an end-to-end learning framework. The authors describe the resulting spectral representations as exposing clear patterns that convolutional and sequential learning modules can predict effectively.

The reported evidence supports this combination for the evaluated multivariate forecasting problems.
summary.tldr: StemGNN jointly models learned relationships between time series and temporal dependencies through graph and temporal Fourier transforms.

title: Spectral Temporal Graph Neural Network for Multivariate Time-series Forecasting

abstract: Distributed multi-task learning provides significant advantages in multi-agent networks with heterogeneous data sources where agents aim to learn distinct but correlated models simultaneously. However, distributed algorithms for learning relatedness among tasks are not resilient in the presence of Byzantine agents. In this paper, we present an approach for Byzantine resilient distributed multi-task learning. We propose an efficient online weight assignment rule by measuring the accumulated loss using an agent’s data and its neighbors’ models. A small accumulated loss indicates a large similarity between the two tasks. In order to ensure the Byzantine resilience of the aggregation at a normal agent, we introduce a step for filtering out larger losses. We analyze the approach for convex models and show that normal agents converge resiliently towards the global minimum. Further, aggregation with the proposed weight assignment rule always results in an improved expected regret than the non-cooperative case. Finally, we demonstrate the approach using three case studies, including regression and classification problems, and show that our method exhibits good empirical performance for non-convex models, such as convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: Distributed multi-task learning lets networked agents learn different but related models from heterogeneous data. Cooperation can help, but methods that learn relationships between tasks can be vulnerable to Byzantine agents. This paper develops a way for normal agents to cooperate while making their model aggregation resilient to such agents.

Each agent evaluates neighboring models using its own data and tracks their accumulated losses. A smaller loss indicates greater similarity between the agent’s task and the neighboring task. These measurements guide an online weighting rule, while a filtering step removes larger losses to protect aggregation at normal agents.

For convex models, the authors analyze resilient convergence of normal agents toward the global minimum. They also show that aggregation under the proposed weighting rule improves expected regret relative to learning without cooperation. Three case studies cover regression and classification, with good empirical performance also reported for nonconvex models such as convolutional neural networks. The theoretical convex results and the nonconvex experiments provide distinct kinds of support for the approach.
summary.tldr: Loss-based weighting and filtering enable resilient cooperation among agents learning related models, with convex guarantees and supporting nonconvex experiments.

title: Byzantine Resilient Distributed Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Variable Importance (VI) has traditionally been cast as the process of estimating each variables contribution to a predictive model's overall performance. Analysis of a single model instance, however, guarantees no insight into a variables relevance to underlying generative processes. Recent research has sought to address this concern via analysis of Rashomon sets - sets of alternative model instances that exhibit equivalent predictive performance to some reference model, but which take different functional forms. Measures such as Model Class Reliance (MCR) have been proposed, that are computed against Rashomon sets, in order to ascertain how much a variable must be relied on to make robust predictions, or whether alternatives exist. If MCR range is tight, we have no choice but to use a variable; if range is high then there exists competing, perhaps fairer models, that provide alternative explanations of the phenomena being examined. Applications are wide, from enabling construction of `fairer' models in areas such as recidivism, health analytics and ethical marketing. Tractable estimation of MCR for non-linear models is currently restricted to Kernel Regression under squared loss \cite{fisher2019all}. In this paper we introduce a new technique that extends computation of Model Class Reliance (MCR) to Random Forest classifiers and regressors. The proposed approach addresses a number of open research questions, and in contrast to prior Kernel SVM MCR estimation, runs in linearithmic rather than polynomial time. Taking a fundamentally different approach to previous work, we provide a solution for this important model class, identifying situations where irrelevant covariates do not improve predictions.

paragraphs: A variable can appear important to one predictive model even when equally accurate alternatives use it differently. This perspective helps distinguish a particular model's choices from reliance shared across competing models.

Model Class Reliance summarizes the range of dependence on a variable within such a set. The paper develops a way to compute this quantity for random forest classifiers and regressors, extending its tractable use to another nonlinear model family.

The proposed approach has linearithmic runtime, compared with the polynomial runtime of the prior kernel-based estimation discussed in the abstract. It also identifies situations where irrelevant covariates do not improve predictions. The contribution makes comparisons across predictive alternatives more computationally accessible for random forests, while preserving the distinction between predictive reliance and insight into the underlying data-generating process.
summary.tldr: The paper makes Model Class Reliance tractable for random forests, measuring how variable dependence differs across equally predictive alternatives.

title: Model Class Reliance for Random Forests

abstract: While agents trained by Reinforcement Learning (RL) can solve increasingly challenging tasks directly from visual observations, generalizing learned skills to novel environments remains very challenging. Extensive use of data augmentation is a promising technique for improving generalization in RL, but it is often found to decrease sample efficiency and can even lead to divergence. In this paper, we investigate causes of instability when using data augmentation in common off-policy RL algorithms. We identify two problems, both rooted in high-variance Q-targets. Based on our findings, we propose a simple yet effective technique for stabilizing this class of algorithms under augmentation. We perform extensive empirical evaluation of image-based RL using both ConvNets and Vision Transformers (ViT) on a family of benchmarks based on DeepMind Control Suite, as well as in robotic manipulation tasks. Our method greatly improves stability and sample efficiency of ConvNets under augmentation, and achieves generalization results competitive with state-of-the-art methods for image-based RL in environments with unseen visuals. We further show that our method scales to RL with ViT-based architectures, and that data augmentation may be especially important in this setting.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can help reinforcement learning agents handle unfamiliar visual environments, but it can also make training less sample-efficient or cause it to diverge. This paper investigates that tension in common off-policy algorithms. The authors identify two instability problems that both originate in high-variance Q-targets, the targets used to train value estimates.

Based on this diagnosis, they propose a simple stabilization technique for learning under augmentation. They evaluate image-based reinforcement learning with convolutional networks and Vision Transformers on benchmarks based on the DeepMind Control Suite and on robotic manipulation tasks. This tests the approach across both visual architectures and task settings.

For convolutional networks, the method substantially improves stability and sample efficiency under augmentation. It also achieves generalization competitive with state-of-the-art image-based reinforcement learning methods in environments with unseen visuals. The authors show that the technique extends to Vision Transformer architectures and suggest that augmentation may be especially important there. The findings connect more stable value-learning targets with the ability to benefit from visually varied training inputs.
summary.tldr: Addressing high-variance Q-targets stabilizes augmented visual reinforcement learning and improves reported sample efficiency and generalization.

title: Stabilizing Deep Q-Learning with ConvNets and Vision Transformers under Data Augmentation

abstract: As major progress is made in open-ended text generation, measuring how close machine-generated text is to human language remains a critical open problem. We introduce Mauve, a comparison measure for open-ended text generation, which directly compares the learnt distribution from a text generation model to the distribution of human-written text using divergence frontiers. Mauve scales up to modern text generation models by computing information divergences in a quantized embedding space. Through an extensive empirical study on three open-ended generation tasks, we find that Mauve identifies known properties of generated text, scales naturally with model size, and correlates with human judgments, with fewer restrictions than existing distributional evaluation metrics.

Mauve scales up to modern text generation models by computing information divergences in a quantized embedding space. paragraphs: Open-ended text generation raises a distributional evaluation question: how closely does a model's language resemble the range of human-written language? This paper introduces MAUVE to measure that gap. It compares the model's learned text distribution with a human-text distribution using divergence frontiers, making the relationship between those distributions the central object of evaluation.

To make the comparison scalable, MAUVE computes information divergences in a quantized embedding space. Text is represented through embeddings and grouped into discrete regions before the distributional calculations. This provides a practical way to apply the measure to modern text-generation models while retaining a comparison of generated and human text at the distribution level.

Across three open-ended generation tasks, the authors find that MAUVE reflects known properties of generated text, scales naturally with model size, and correlates with human judgments. They also report fewer restrictions than existing distributional metrics. These empirical findings support its usefulness as an evaluation measure; correlation with human judgment remains the stated evidence.
summary.tldr: MAUVE compares generated and human text distributions in a quantized embedding space and empirically correlates with human judgments.

title: MAUVE: Measuring the Gap Between Neural Text and Human Text using Divergence Frontiers

abstract: Several out-of-distribution (OOD) detection scores have been recently proposed for deep generative models because the direct use of the likelihood threshold for OOD detection has been shown to be problematic. In this paper, we propose a new OOD score based on a Bayesian hypothesis test called the locally most powerful Bayesian test (LMPBT). The LMPBT is locally most powerful in that the alternative hypothesis (the representative parameter for the OOD sample) is specified to maximize the probability that the Bayes factor exceeds the evidence threshold in favor of the alternative hypothesis provided that the parameter specified under the alternative hypothesis is in the neighborhood of the parameter specified under the null hypothesis. That is, under this neighborhood parameter condition, the test with the proposed alternative hypothesis maximizes the probability of correct detection of OOD samples. We also propose numerical strategies for more efficient and reliable computation of the LMPBT for practical application to deep generative models. Evaluations conducted of the OOD detection performance of the LMPBT on various benchmark datasets demonstrate its superior performance over existing OOD detection methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops an out-of-distribution detection score for deep generative models. It starts from the problem that simply thresholding a model's likelihood can be unreliable for detecting unfamiliar samples. The proposed score instead uses a Bayesian hypothesis test, called the locally most powerful Bayesian test, to compare evidence for an out-of-distribution alternative.

The alternative hypothesis is chosen to maximize the probability that the Bayes factor exceeds a threshold favoring that alternative. The optimality claim has an essential local condition: the alternative's parameter must lie in a neighborhood of the null hypothesis's parameter. Within this condition, the proposed choice maximizes the probability of correctly detecting out-of-distribution samples.

The authors also introduce numerical strategies to make the test's computation more efficient and reliable in deep generative models. Evaluations on several benchmark datasets show superior detection performance over existing methods. The paper thus combines a locally qualified statistical optimality result with computational methods and empirical evidence for using the resulting score in practice.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian detection score optimizes local out-of-distribution detection power under a neighborhood condition and performs strongly on benchmark evaluations.

title: Locally Most Powerful Bayesian Test for Out-of-Distribution Detection using Deep Generative Models

abstract: Dubbing is a post-production process of re-recording actors’ dialogues, which is extensively used in filmmaking and video production. It is usually performed manually by professional voice actors who read lines with proper prosody, and in synchronization with the pre-recorded videos. In this work, we propose Neural Dubber, the first neural network model to solve a novel automatic video dubbing (AVD) task: synthesizing human speech synchronized with the given video from the text. Neural Dubber is a multi-modal text-to-speech (TTS) model that utilizes the lip movement in the video to control the prosody of the generated speech. Furthermore, an image-based speaker embedding (ISE) module is developed for the multi-speaker setting, which enables Neural Dubber to generate speech with a reasonable timbre according to the speaker’s face. Experiments on the chemistry lecture single-speaker dataset and LRS2 multi-speaker dataset show that Neural Dubber can generate speech audios on par with state-of-the-art TTS models in terms of speech quality. Most importantly, both qualitative and quantitative evaluations show that Neural Dubber can control the prosody of synthesized speech by the video, and generate high-fidelity speech temporally synchronized with the video.

paragraphs: Automatic dubbing must do more than read a script clearly: the generated speech must fit the timing of an existing video. Neural Dubber frames this as a multimodal text-to-speech task, combining the words to be spoken with visual evidence about how the speaker is moving. This brings synchronization into the speech-generation process itself.

The model uses lip movements to control speech prosody, connecting the delivery of the script to the recorded video. For videos containing different speakers, an image-based speaker embedding module uses the speaker’s face to generate a reasonable vocal timbre. The stated aim is a suitable voice characteristic, rather than a claim of recovering the speaker’s exact voice.

Experiments use a single-speaker chemistry lecture dataset and the multi-speaker LRS2 dataset. Reported speech quality is on par with state-of-the-art text-to-speech systems. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations also show video-guided prosody and high-fidelity speech synchronized with the footage. Together, these findings support generating convincing audio while using visual timing to meet the additional requirements of dubbing.
summary.tldr: Neural Dubber uses scripts and visible lip movements to generate high-quality speech synchronized with video.

title: Neural Dubber: Dubbing for Videos According to Scripts

abstract: We formulate the continual learning (CL) problem via dynamic programming and model the trade-off between catastrophic forgetting and generalization as a two-player sequential game. In this approach, player 1 maximizes the cost due to lack of generalization whereas player 2 minimizes the cost due to catastrophic forgetting. We show theoretically that a balance point between the two players exists for each task and that this point is stable (once the balance is achieved, the two players stay at the balance point). Next, we introduce balanced continual learning (BCL), which is designed to attain balance between generalization and forgetting and empirically demonstrate that BCL is comparable to or better than the state of the art.

paragraphs: Continual learning must handle successive tasks while balancing generalization against catastrophic forgetting. This paper gives that tension a formal structure using dynamic programming and a two-player sequential game. The formulation makes the competing costs explicit, providing a mathematical way to reason about how they can be balanced during learning.

The first player maximizes the cost associated with a lack of generalization, while the second minimizes the cost associated with forgetting. Within this formulation, the authors prove that a balance point exists for each task. They also establish stability: once the players reach that point, they remain there. This is a statement about the balance in the proposed game.

The paper then introduces balanced continual learning, or BCL, an algorithm designed to attain that balance. Empirical comparisons show BCL matching or exceeding the performance of leading methods. The theoretical and experimental contributions play complementary roles: the game establishes a stable balancing target, while the experiments support the usefulness of an algorithm designed around it.
summary.tldr: A two-player formulation establishes a stable balance between generalization and forgetting and motivates the empirically competitive BCL algorithm.

title: Formalizing the Generalization-Forgetting Trade-off in Continual Learning

abstract: Domain generalization (DG) aims to transfer the learning task from a single or multiple source domains to unseen target domains. To extract and leverage the information which exhibits sufficient generalization ability, we propose a simple yet effective approach of Adversarial Teacher-Student Representation Learning, with the goal of deriving the domain generalizable representations via generating and exploring out-of-source data distributions. Our proposed framework advances Teacher-Student learning in an adversarial learning manner, which alternates between knowledge-distillation based representation learning and novel-domain data augmentation. The former progressively updates the teacher network for deriving domain-generalizable representations, while the latter synthesizes data out-of-source yet plausible distributions. Extensive image classification experiments on benchmark datasets in multiple and single source DG settings confirm that, our model exhibits sufficient generalization ability and performs favorably against state-of-the-art DG methods.

The former progressively updates the teacher network for deriving domain-generalizable representations, while the latter synthesizes data out-of-source yet plausible distributions. paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether a model trained on available source domains can work on a target domain it has never seen. This paper addresses that problem by learning representations while generating plausible data distributions beyond the sources. The goal is to expose training to variation that can support transfer to unfamiliar domains.

The framework combines teacher-student learning with an adversarial training process. It alternates between representation learning through knowledge distillation and data augmentation that creates novel domains. The representation-learning stage progressively updates the teacher network, while the augmentation stage synthesizes data from plausible distributions outside the source domains. These stages jointly support the search for representations that generalize.

The authors evaluate the approach on image classification benchmarks with both multiple source domains and a single source domain. They report favorable performance against state-of-the-art domain-generalization methods. The findings support the usefulness of combining representation transfer with generated domain variation in these settings. The stated result concerns generalization demonstrated in the experiments, rather than a guarantee of successful transfer to every unseen distribution.
summary.tldr: An adversarial teacher-student framework alternates knowledge distillation with plausible novel-domain generation to improve generalization to unseen domains.

title: Adversarial Teacher-Student Representation Learning for Domain Generalization

abstract: The sparse generalized eigenvalue problem (SGEP) aims to find the leading eigenvector with sparsity structure. SGEP plays an important role in statistical learning and has wide applications including, but not limited to, sparse principal component analysis, sparse canonical correlation analysis and sparse Fisher discriminant analysis, etc. Due to the sparsity constraint, the solution of SGEP entails interesting properties from both numerical and statistical perspectives. In this paper, we provide a detailed sensitivity analysis for SGEP and establish the rate-optimal perturbation bound under the sparse setting. Specifically, we show that the bound is related to the perturbation/noise level and the recovery of the true support of the leading eigenvector as well. We also investigate the estimator of SGEP via imposing a non-convex regularization. Such estimator can achieve the optimal error rate and can recover the sparsity structure as well. Extensive numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings via using alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM)-based computational method.

paragraphs: The sparse generalized eigenvalue problem seeks a leading eigenvector whose nonzero entries have a sparse structure. This connects a numerical problem about eigenvectors with a statistical problem about identifying relevant variables. The paper studies this combination, which appears in sparse principal component analysis, sparse canonical correlation analysis, and sparse Fisher discriminant analysis.

Its first contribution is a sensitivity analysis: how much can the estimated eigenvector change when the underlying quantities are perturbed or noisy? The resulting perturbation bound is rate-optimal in the sparse setting. Crucially, the bound reflects both the size of the disturbance and recovery of the true support, meaning the positions of the eigenvector's nonzero entries.

The paper also investigates an estimator based on nonconvex regularization. It shows that this estimator can attain the optimal error rate and recover the sparsity structure. Numerical experiments using an ADMM-based computational method support the theoretical findings. Together, the results connect estimation accuracy with identifying the correct sparse structure, rather than treating these as unrelated goals.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal sensitivity bounds for sparse generalized eigenvectors and studies a regularized estimator that can recover their sparse structure.

title: A Note on Sparse Generalized Eigenvalue Problem

abstract: Several recent works in machine learning have focused on evaluating the test-time robustness of a classifier: how well the classifier performs not just on the target domain it was trained upon, but upon perturbed examples. In these settings, the focus has largely been on two extremes of robustness: the robustness to perturbations drawn _at random_ from within some distribution (i.e., robustness to random perturbations), and the robustness to the _worst case_ perturbation in some set (i.e., adversarial robustness). In this paper, we argue that a sliding scale between these two extremes provides a valuable additional metric by which to gauge robustness. Specifically, we illustrate that each of these two extremes is naturally characterized by a (functional) q-norm over perturbation space, with q=1 corresponding to robustness to random perturbations and q=\infty corresponding to adversarial perturbations. We then present the main technical contribution of our paper: a method for efficiently estimating the value of these norms by interpreting them as the partition function of a particular distribution, then using path sampling with MCMC methods to estimate this partition function (either traditional Metropolis-Hastings for non-differentiable perturbations, or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for differentiable perturbations). We show that our approach provides substantially better estimates than simple random sampling of the actual “intermediate-q” robustness of both standard, data-augmented, and adversarially-trained classifiers, illustrating a clear tradeoff between classifiers that optimize different metrics. Code for reproducing experiments can be found at https://github.com/locuslab/intermediate_robustness.

In these settings, the focus has largely been on two extremes of robustness: the robustness to perturbations drawn _at random_ from within some distribution (i.e., robustness to random perturbations), and the robustness to the _worst case_ perturbation in some set (i.e., adversarial robustness). In this paper, we argue that a sliding scale between these two extremes provides a valuable additional metric by which to gauge robustness. Specifically, we illustrate that each of these two extremes is naturally characterized by a (functional) q-norm over perturbation space, with q=1 corresponding to robustness to random perturbations and q=\infty corresponding to adversarial perturbations. We then present the main technical contribution of our paper: a method for efficiently estimating the value of these norms by interpreting them as the partition function of a particular distribution, then using path sampling with MCMC methods to estimate this partition function (either traditional Metropolis-Hastings for non-differentiable perturbations, or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for differentiable perturbations). We show that our approach provides substantially better estimates than simple random sampling of the actual “intermediate-q” robustness of both standard, data-augmented, and adversarially-trained classifiers, illustrating a clear tradeoff between classifiers that optimize different metrics. Code for reproducing experiments can be found at https://github.com/locuslab/intermediate_robustness.

paragraphs: Classifier robustness is often evaluated at two extremes: performance under randomly drawn perturbations and performance under the worst allowed perturbation. This paper argues that intermediate evaluations provide useful additional information. It expresses the extremes through functional q-norms over perturbations, with q equal to one for random perturbations and infinity for adversarial robustness.

The main contribution is a method for efficiently estimating these norms between the extremes. The authors interpret the required quantity as a distribution's partition function and estimate it using path sampling with Markov chain Monte Carlo. They use Metropolis-Hastings for nondifferentiable perturbations and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo when perturbations are differentiable.

Experiments examine standard classifiers as well as models trained with data augmentation or adversarial training. The proposed method gives substantially better estimates of intermediate-q robustness than simple random sampling. The evaluations also reveal trade-offs between classifiers optimized for different robustness metrics. This makes the sliding scale useful for understanding how robustness changes as the evaluation places increasing emphasis on difficult perturbations.
summary.tldr: The paper measures robustness between random and worst-case perturbations and estimates these intermediate metrics efficiently using MCMC.

title: Robustness between the worst and average case

abstract: Large pre-trained language models have shown promise for few-shot learning, completing text-based tasks given only a few task-specific examples. Will models soon solve classification tasks that have so far been reserved for human research assistants? Existing benchmarks are not designed to measure progress in applied settings, and so don't directly answer this question. The RAFT benchmark (Real-world Annotated Few-shot Tasks) focuses on naturally occurring tasks and uses an evaluation setup that mirrors deployment. Baseline evaluations on RAFT reveal areas current techniques struggle with: reasoning over long texts and tasks with many classes. Human baselines show that some classification tasks are difficult for non-expert humans, reflecting that real-world value sometimes depends on domain expertise. Yet even non-expert human baseline F1 scores exceed GPT-3 by an average of 0.11. The RAFT datasets and leaderboard will track which model improvements translate into real-world benefits at https://raft.elicit.org/.

paragraphs: Few-shot text classification asks a model to learn a categorization task from only a small number of examples. Its motivation is practical: existing benchmarks do not directly establish how well models can handle classification work previously performed by human research assistants.

These challenges help distinguish practical task demands from a broad impression that a model can learn effectively whenever a few labeled examples are available.

summary.tldr: RAFT tests practical few-shot text classification and finds persistent gaps involving long texts, many classes, and human performance.

title: RAFT: A Real-World Few-Shot Text Classification Benchmark

abstract: Learning the underlying equation from data is a fundamental problem in many disciplines. Recent advances rely on Neural Networks (NNs) but do not provide theoretical guarantees in obtaining the exact equations owing to the non-convexity of NNs. In this paper, we propose Convex Neural Symbolic Learning (CoNSoLe) to seek convexity under mild conditions. The main idea is to decompose the recovering process into two steps and convexify each step. In the first step of searching for right symbols, we convexify the deep Q-learning. The key is to maintain double convexity for both the negative Q-function and the negative reward function in each iteration, leading to provable convexity of the negative optimal Q function to learn the true symbol connections. Conditioned on the exact searching result, we construct a Locally Convex equation Learning (LoCaL) neural network to convexify the estimation of symbol coefficients. With such a design, we quantify a large region with strict convexity in the loss surface of LoCaL for commonly used physical functions. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of the CoNSoLe framework over the state-of-the-art on a diverse set of datasets.

paragraphs: Recovering an equation from data requires finding both its symbolic structure and its numerical coefficients. Neural approaches can tackle this task, but their nonconvex optimization complicates guarantees about recovering the exact equation. CoNSoLe separates recovery into two stages and seeks convexity in each under the paper’s stated mild conditions.

The first stage searches for the right symbols using a modified deep Q-learning procedure. It maintains convexity of both the negative Q-function and the negative reward function at each iteration. This yields a provably convex negative optimal Q-function for learning the true connections between symbols.

Given an exact symbolic search result, the second stage uses a Locally Convex equation Learning network to estimate coefficients. For commonly used physical functions, the authors characterize a large region where its loss is strictly convex. This is a conditional, local guarantee rather than unrestricted global convexity of the entire recovery problem. Experiments on diverse datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches.
summary.tldr: CoNSoLe separates equation discovery into symbol search and coefficient fitting, establishing convexity properties under stated conditions.

title: CoNSoLe: Convex Neural Symbolic Learning

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Graph Kernels (GKs) are two fundamental tools used to analyze graph-structured data. Efforts have been recently made in developing a composite graph learning architecture combining the expressive power of GNNs and the transparent trainability of GKs. However, learning efficiency on these models should be carefully considered as the huge computation overhead. Besides, their convolutional methods are often straightforward and introduce severe loss of graph structure information. In this paper, we design a novel quantum graph learning model to characterize the structural information while using quantum parallelism to improve computing efficiency. Specifically, a quantum algorithm is proposed to approximately estimate the neural tangent kernel of the underlying graph neural network where a multi-head quantum attention mechanism is introduced to properly incorporate semantic similarity information of nodes into the model. We empirically show that our method achieves competitive performance on several graph classification benchmarks, and theoretical analysis is provided to demonstrate the superiority of our quantum algorithm. Source code is available at \url{https://github.com/abel1231/graphQNTK}.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks and graph kernels offer different ways to learn from connected data. Combining them promises expressive representations together with the trainability of kernel methods, but the resulting computation can be expensive. This paper also identifies loss of graph structure in straightforward convolution methods as a concern for such models.

GraphQNTK introduces a quantum algorithm that approximately estimates the neural tangent kernel of an underlying graph neural network. The approach uses quantum parallelism with the aim of improving computational efficiency. A multi-head quantum attention mechanism incorporates semantic similarities between nodes, helping the model account for information beyond a straightforward convolutional treatment of the graph.

The authors report competitive results on several graph classification benchmarks and provide theoretical analysis supporting the quantum algorithm’s advantages. These are complementary claims: the experiments address predictive performance, while the theory addresses the proposed algorithm. The contribution is a quantum approach to constructing a graph-learning kernel that considers both structural information and computational cost.
summary.tldr: GraphQNTK uses a quantum algorithm and quantum attention to approximate a graph neural tangent kernel with competitive classification performance.

title: GraphQNTK: Quantum Neural Tangent Kernel for Graph Data

abstract: Learning structures between groups of variables from data with missing values is an important task in the real world, yet difficult to solve. One typical scenario is discovering the structure among topics in the education domain to identify learning pathways. Here, the observations are student performances for questions under each topic which contain missing values. However, most existing methods focus on learning structures between a few individual variables from the complete data. In this work, we propose VISL, a novel scalable structure learning approach that can simultaneously infer structures between groups of variables under missing data and perform missing value imputations with deep learning. Particularly, we propose a generative model with a structured latent space and a graph neural network-based architecture, scaling to a large number of variables. Empirically, we conduct extensive experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world education data sets. We show improved performances on both imputation and structure learning accuracy compared to popular and recent approaches.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain groups of related variables as well as missing observations. In education, for example, questions belong to topics, but students may not answer every question. Discovering relationships among topics and estimating missing responses are connected challenges. This paper addresses both within one learning approach.

The proposed VISL model jointly infers structure between variable groups and fills missing values. It uses a generative model with a structured latent space and a graph-neural-network architecture, designed to scale to many variables. This makes the grouping of observations part of the representation rather than restricting structure learning to a small set of individual variables with complete data.

The authors evaluate VISL on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real educational datasets. They report improved accuracy in both missing-value imputation and structure learning compared with popular and recent approaches. The findings support joint modeling as a way to recover useful relationships even when observations are incomplete, with education providing a setting where group-level structure can help identify learning pathways.
summary.tldr: VISL jointly learns relationships between variable groups and imputes missing values, improving both tasks in reported experiments.

title: Simultaneous Missing Value Imputation and Structure Learning with Groups

abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) solves statistical inverse problems by repeatedly running a stochastic simulator and inferring posterior distributions from model-simulations. To improve simulation efficiency, several inference methods take a sequential approach and iteratively adapt the proposal distributions from which model simulations are generated. However, many of these sequential methods are difficult to use in practice, both because the resulting optimisation problems can be challenging and efficient diagnostic tools are lacking. To overcome these issues, we present Truncated Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation (TSNPE). TSNPE performs sequential inference with truncated proposals, sidestepping the optimisation issues of alternative approaches. In addition, TSNPE allows to efficiently perform coverage tests that can scale to complex models with many parameters. We demonstrate that TSNPE performs on par with previous methods on established benchmark tasks. We then apply TSNPE to two challenging problems from neuroscience and show that TSNPE can successfully obtain the posterior distributions, whereas previous methods fail. Overall, our results demonstrate that TSNPE is an efficient, accurate, and robust inference method that can scale to challenging scientific models.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates plausible model parameters by comparing observations with outputs from a stochastic simulator. Sequential methods improve simulation efficiency by repeatedly adapting the distribution used to generate new simulations. In practice, however, those adaptations can introduce difficult optimisation problems, and checking the resulting inference can itself be challenging.

The paper proposes Truncated Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation, or TSNPE. It uses truncated proposal distributions during sequential inference to sidestep optimisation difficulties encountered by alternative approaches. It also supports efficient coverage tests that scale to models with many parameters. This makes diagnostic assessment part of the method's contribution alongside the posterior estimation procedure.

On established benchmarks, TSNPE performs comparably to previous methods. The authors then apply it to two challenging neuroscience problems, obtaining posterior distributions where earlier methods fail. These findings support the method's stated efficiency, accuracy, and robustness in the evaluated settings. Its significance is the combination of sequential simulation efficiency with a more manageable optimisation procedure and scalable tools for checking inference quality.
summary.tldr: TSNPE uses truncated proposals to simplify sequential simulation-based inference and enable scalable coverage testing.

title: Truncated proposals for scalable and hassle-free simulation-based inference

abstract: Optimal scaling has been well studied for Metropolis-Hastings (M-H) algorithms in continuous spaces, but a similar understanding has been lacking in discrete spaces.Recently, a family of locally balanced proposals (LBP) for discrete spaces has been proved to be asymptotically optimal, but the question of optimal scaling has remained open.In this paper, we establish, for the first time, that the efficiency of M-H in discrete spaces can also be characterized by an asymptotic acceptance rate that is independent of the target distribution. Moreover, we verify, both theoretically and empirically, that the optimal acceptance rates for LBP and random walk Metropolis (RWM) are $0.574$ and $0.234$ respectively. These results also help establish that LBP is asymptotically $O(N^\frac{2}{3})$ more efficient than RWM with respect to model dimension $N$. Knowledge of the optimal acceptance rate allows one to automatically tune the neighborhood size of a proposal distribution in a discrete space, directly analogous to step-size control in continuous spaces.We demonstrate empirically that such adaptive M-H sampling can robustly improve sampling in a variety of target distributions in discrete spaces, including training deep energy based models.

paragraphs: Metropolis–Hastings sampling proposes moves and then accepts or rejects them. Choosing the scale of those moves matters for efficiency, but the corresponding theory has been less developed for discrete spaces than for continuous ones. This paper studies how proposal neighborhood size should be tuned for locally balanced proposals and random walk Metropolis.

The authors establish an asymptotic characterization of efficiency through acceptance rates that do not depend on the target distribution. Their theoretical and empirical results identify optimal rates of 0.574 for locally balanced proposals and 0.234 for random walk Metropolis. The analysis also establishes an asymptotic O(N^(2/3)) efficiency advantage for locally balanced proposals as model dimension N grows.

These acceptance-rate targets provide a practical signal for automatically adjusting discrete proposal neighborhoods, analogous to tuning step sizes in continuous sampling. Experiments show that adaptive sampling improves performance across varied discrete target distributions, including in training deep energy-based models. The optimality claims are asymptotic, while the experiments supply evidence that the resulting tuning principle is useful in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: The paper derives asymptotically optimal acceptance rates that enable automatic tuning of discrete Metropolis–Hastings proposals.

title: Optimal Scaling for Locally Balanced Proposals in Discrete Spaces

abstract: Data continuously emitted from industrial ecosystems such as social or e-commerce platforms are commonly represented as heterogeneous graphs (HG) composed of multiple node/edge types. State-of-the-art graph learning methods for HGs known as heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs) are applied to learn deep context-informed node representations. However, many HG datasets from industrial applications suffer from label imbalance between node types. As there is no direct way to learn using labels rooted at different node types, HGNNs have been applied to only a few node types with abundant labels. We propose a zero-shot transfer learning module for HGNNs called a Knowledge Transfer Network (KTN) that transfers knowledge from label-abundant node types to zero-labeled node types through rich relational information given in the HG. KTN is derived from the theoretical relationship, which we introduce in this work, between distinct feature extractors for each node type given in an HGNN model. KTN improves the performance of 6 different types of HGNN models by up to 960% for inference on zero-labeled node types and outperforms state-of-the-art transfer learning baselines by up to 73% across 18 different transfer learning tasks on HGs.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous graphs contain multiple types of nodes and relationships, as in social and e-commerce systems. Labels may be abundant for one node type and absent for another. This creates a problem for heterogeneous graph neural networks: useful supervision exists inside the same graph, but it is attached to a different kind of node than the prediction target.

The proposed Knowledge Transfer Network moves knowledge from a labeled source node type to an unlabeled target type using the graph's relational information. Its construction follows a theoretical relationship between the distinct feature extractors used for different node types within a heterogeneous graph neural network. The module therefore connects representations that would otherwise lack a direct route for sharing supervision.

Across 18 transfer tasks, KTN improves six types of heterogeneous graph neural networks, with gains reaching 960% for inference on unlabeled node types. It also exceeds transfer-learning baselines by up to 73%. These are reported maximum improvements across the evaluations, supporting the module's usefulness across several architectures and transfer settings.
summary.tldr: Knowledge Transfer Networks use heterogeneous-graph relationships to transfer supervision from labeled node types to types with no labels.

title: Zero-shot Transfer Learning within a Heterogeneous Graph via Knowledge Transfer Networks

abstract: Consider the task of learning an unknown concept from a given concept class; to what extent does interacting with a domain expert accelerate the learning process? It is common to measure the effectiveness of learning algorithms by plotting the "learning curve", that is, the decay of the error rate as a function of the algorithm's resources (examples, queries, etc). Thus, the overarching question in this work is whether (and which kind of) interaction accelerates the learning curve. Previous work in interactive learning focused on uniform bounds on the learning rates which only capture the upper envelope of the learning curves over families of data distributions. We thus formalize our overarching question within the distribution dependent framework of universal learning, which aims to understand the performance of learning algorithms on every data distribution, but without requiring a single upper bound which applies uniformly to all distributions. Our main result reveals a fundamental trichotomy of interactive learning rates, thus providing a complete characterization of universal interactive learning. As a corollary we deduce a strong affirmative answer to our overarching question, showing that interaction is beneficial. Remarkably, we show that in important cases such benefits are realized with label queries, that is, by active learning algorithms. On the other hand, our lower bounds apply to arbitrary binary queries and, hence, they hold in any interactive learning setting.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much interaction with a domain expert can accelerate learning an unknown concept. It studies the learning curve: how prediction error falls as an algorithm receives more examples or asks more questions. The issue is whether interaction changes the rate of improvement.

Earlier uniform bounds describe an upper envelope across families of data distributions. The authors instead use universal learning, which studies behavior on every distribution without demanding one common bound for all of them. This distribution-dependent viewpoint allows a more detailed characterization of learning rates than a single shared worst-case envelope provides.

summary.tldr: A distribution-dependent theory classifies interactive learning rates and shows when expert interaction, including label queries, accelerates learning.

title: Universal Rates for Interactive Learning

abstract: We consider optimization problems in which the goal is to find a $k$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$, $k<<n$, which minimizes a convex and smooth loss. Such problems generalize the fundamental task of principal component analysis (PCA) to include robust and sparse counterparts, and logistic PCA for binary data, among others. This problem could be approached either via nonconvex gradient methods with highly-efficient iterations, but for which arguing about fast convergence to a global minimizer is difficult or, via a convex relaxation for which arguing about convergence to a global minimizer is straightforward, but the corresponding methods are often inefficient. In this work we bridge these two approaches under a strict complementarity assumption, which in particular implies that the optimal solution to the convex relaxation is unique and is also the optimal solution to the original nonconvex problem. Our main result is a proof that a natural nonconvex gradient method which is \textit{SVD-free} and requires only a single QR-factorization of an $n\times k$ matrix per iteration, converges locally with a linear rate. We also establish linear convergence results for the nonconvex projected gradient method, and the Frank-Wolfe method when applied to the convex relaxation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find a low-dimensional subspace that minimizes a smooth convex loss. This covers extensions of principal component analysis, including robust, sparse, and binary-data variants. Although the loss is convex, the subspace search is nonconvex, creating a trade-off between inexpensive iterations and straightforward guarantees about reaching a global solution.

The authors connect nonconvex methods with a convex relaxation under a strict complementarity assumption. In this setting, the relaxation has a unique optimum that also solves the original problem. That connection lets the analysis use the convex formulation to justify fast behavior of methods operating directly on the subspace.

The paper also establishes linear convergence results for nonconvex projected gradient and for Frank-Wolfe applied to the relaxation.
summary.tldr: Under strict complementarity, an SVD-free subspace gradient method has provably local linear convergence with one small QR factorization per iteration.

title: Local Linear Convergence of Gradient Methods for Subspace Optimization via Strict Complementarity

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has been successfully used to design numerous high-performance neural networks. However, NAS is typically compute-intensive, so most existing approaches restrict the search to decide the operations and topological structure of a single block only, then the same block is stacked repeatedly to form an end-to-end model. Although such an approach reduces the size of search space, recent studies show that a macro search space, which allows blocks in a model to be different, can lead to better performance. To provide a systematic study of the performance of NAS algorithms on a macro search space, we release Blox – a benchmark that consists of 91k unique models trained on the CIFAR-100 dataset. The dataset also includes runtime measurements of all the models on a diverse set of hardware platforms. We perform extensive experiments to compare existing algorithms that are well studied on cell-based search spaces, with the emerging blockwise approaches that aim to make NAS scalable to much larger macro search spaces. The Blox benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/SamsungLabs/blox.
