The benchmark targets problems in existing evaluations: overly simple tasks, contaminated data, and flawed questions. Original content addresses contamination concerns, while systematic curation is used to remove defective items.

The problems elicit reasoning across multiple steps and conditions. Evaluations report greater token use and stronger differentiation among reasoning models than AIME 2024, OlympiadBench, and GPQA. The strongest evaluated model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 36.9% accuracy, compared with 61.9% for human experts. This gap indicates substantial remaining difficulty on the benchmark's curated physics tasks.

The paper also introduces an Expression Edit Distance score for assessing mathematical expressions. It reports a 204% improvement in sample efficiency over binary scoring, providing a more informative evaluation signal than a simple correct-or-incorrect outcome. Together, the problem set and scoring method support examination of reasoning robustness, preferences, and deficiencies in demanding physical reasoning.
summary.tldr: PHYBench uses 500 original physics problems and expression-based scoring to distinguish reasoning models and expose a substantial gap from human experts.

title: PHYBench: Holistic Evaluation of Physical Perception and Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has significantly improved the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) across various domains. However, this reasoning process has been confined exclusively to textual space, limiting its effectiveness in visually intensive tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of pixel-space reasoning. Within this novel framework, Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are equipped with a suite of visual reasoning operations, such as zoom-in and select-frame. These operations enable VLMs to directly inspect, interrogate, and infer from visual evidences, thereby enhancing reasoning fidelity for visual tasks. Cultivating such pixel-space reasoning capabilities in VLMs presents notable challenges, including the model’s initially imbalanced competence and its reluctance to adopt the newly introduced pixel-space operations. We address these challenges through a two-phase training approach. The first phase employs instruction tuning on synthesized reasoning traces to familiarize the model with the novel visual operations. Following this, a reinforcement learning (RL) phase leverages a curiosity-driven reward scheme to balance exploration between pixel-space reasoning and textual reasoning. With these visual operations, VLMs can interact with complex visual inputs, such as information-rich images or videos to proactively gather necessary information. We demonstrate that this approach significantly improves VLM performance across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks. Our 7B model, Pixel-Reasoner, achieves 84% on V* bench, 74% on TallyQA-Complex, and 84% on InfographicsVQA, marking the highest accuracy achieved by any open-source model to date. These results highlight the importance of pixel-space reasoning and the effectiveness of our framework.

title: Pixel Reasoner: Incentivizing Pixel Space Reasoning via Curiosity-Driven Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have proven effective in exploring the vast solution spaces typical of graph-structured combinatorial problems. However, traditional encoding schemes, such as binary or numerical representations, often fail to straightforwardly capture the intricate structural properties of networks. Through employing the image-based encoding to preserve topological context, this study utilizes multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as evolutionary operators to facilitate structure-aware optimization over graph data. To address the visual clutter inherent in large-scale network visualizations, we leverage graph sparsification techniques to simplify structures while maintaining essential structural features. To further improve robustness and mitigate bias from different sparsification views, we propose a cooperative evolutionary optimization framework that facilitates cross-domain knowledge transfer and unifies multiple sparsified variants of diverse structures. Additionally, recognizing the sensitivity of MLLMs to network layout, we introduce an ensemble strategy that aggregates outputs from various layout configurations through consensus voting. Finally, experiments on real-world networks through various tasks demonstrate that our approach improves both the quality and reliability of solutions in MLLM-driven evolutionary optimization.

paragraphs: This paper uses multimodal language models as evolutionary operators for graph-structured combinatorial optimization. It represents networks as images so that the models can work with visible topological context. The motivation is that conventional binary or numerical encodings do not straightforwardly express the structural relationships that matter in these problems.

Large graph visualizations can be cluttered, so the method applies sparsification to simplify them while preserving essential structural features. A cooperative optimization framework combines multiple sparsified variants and supports knowledge transfer across different structures. This is intended to improve robustness and reduce the bias introduced by any single simplified view.

The approach therefore addresses two representation choices that affect visual graph optimization: which structure remains visible after simplification and how that structure is arranged in the image presented to the model.
summary.tldr: Combining sparsified graph views and layout voting improves multimodal-language-model-driven evolutionary optimization on graph problems.

title: Structure-Aware Cooperative Ensemble Evolutionary Optimization on Combinatorial Problems with Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: With the rapid progress of large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models, there has been growing interest in personalized content generation. However, current conversational systems often present the same recommended content to all users, falling into the dilemma of "one-size-fits-all." To break this limitation and boost user engagement, in this paper, we introduce PCG (**P**ersonalized Visual **C**ontent **G**eneration), a unified framework for personalizing item images within conversational systems. We tackle two key bottlenecks: the depth of personalization and the fidelity of generated images. Specifically, an LLM-powered Inclinations Analyzer is adopted to capture user likes and dislikes from context to construct personalized prompts. Moreover, we design a dual-stage LoRA mechanism—Global LoRA for understanding task-specific visual style, and Local LoRA for capturing preferred visual elements from conversation history. During training, we introduce the visual content condition method to ensure LoRA learns both historical visual context and maintains fidelity to the original item images. Extensive experiments on benchmark conversational datasets—including objective metrics and GPT-based evaluations—demonstrate that our framework outperforms strong baselines, which highlight its potential to redefine personalization in visual content generation for conversational scenarios like e-commerce and real-world recommendation.

paragraphs: Conversational recommendation systems can personalize what they say while still showing every user the same item images. PCG addresses the visual side of personalization, generating item imagery informed by the user's conversation. The challenge is to reflect individual preferences while preserving fidelity to the original item rather than letting personalization overwhelm its appearance.

A visual-content conditioning method during training supports learning historical context while maintaining the original item's fidelity.

These findings support combining explicit preference analysis with visual adaptation at both task and individual levels. The proposed applications include e-commerce and recommendation conversations, where adapting an item's presentation to the user could make generated visual content more personally relevant.
summary.tldr: PCG combines conversational preference analysis with global and local LoRA adaptation to personalize item images while preserving fidelity.

title: Personalized Visual Content Generation in Conversational Systems

abstract: ``Caught in a landslide, no escape from reality" summarizes the state of the research in AI offense: an attack might work on paper but does not necessarily in practice. In the last 5 years, we have seen the rise of latency attacks against computer vision systems. Most of them targeted 2D object detection, especially its Non-Max-Suppression (NMS) block, via adversarial images. However, we uncovered that, when tested in realistic deployment settings, the NMS latency attacks, accepted to top conferences, have very limited negative effects. In this paper, we define an evaluation framework (EVADE) to assess the practicality of attacks, and apply it to state-of-the-art NMS latency attacks. Attacks were tested on different hardware platforms, and different model formats and quantization. Results show that these attacks are not able to generate the claimed latency increase, nor transfer to other models (from the same family or not). Moreover, the latency increases remain within the latency requirements of downstream tasks in our evaluation, suggesting limited practical impact under these conditions. We also tested three defenses, which were successful in mitigating the NMS latency attacks. Therefore, in their current form, NMS latency attacks are just fantasy.

The question is practical: do the reported slowdowns persist across deployed configurations, and do they interfere with the timing requirements of downstream tasks?

Their broader methodological point is that deployment configuration and task requirements are essential to interpreting a latency attack's significance.
summary.tldr: EVADE finds that tested NMS latency attacks have limited practical impact across the evaluated deployment settings.

title: Latency NMS Attacks: Is It Real Life or Is It Just Fantasy?

abstract: We introduce a new projection-free (Frank-Wolfe) method for optimizing structured nonconvex functions that are expressed as a difference of two convex functions. This problem class subsumes smooth nonconvex minimization, positioning our method as a promising alternative to the classical Frank-Wolfe algorithm. DC decompositions are not unique; by carefully selecting a decomposition, we can better exploit the problem structure, improve computational efficiency, and adapt to the underlying problem geometry to find better local solutions. We prove that the proposed method achieves a first-order stationary point in $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, matching the complexity of the standard Frank-Wolfe algorithm for smooth nonconvex minimization in general. Specific decompositions can, for instance, yield a gradient-efficient variant that requires only $\mathcal{O}(1/\epsilon)$ calls to the gradient oracle by reusing computed gradients over multiple iterations. Finally, we present numerical experiments demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to other projection-free algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a projection-free optimization method for objectives written as the difference of two convex functions. That class includes smooth nonconvex minimization. Its central opportunity is that the same objective can have multiple such decompositions, allowing the algorithm's formulation to reflect useful structure in the problem.

By choosing a decomposition carefully, the method can improve computational efficiency, adapt to the problem's geometry, and find better local solutions. The authors prove an O(1/epsilon²) iteration bound for reaching a first-order stationary point to the desired accuracy, matching the general complexity of standard Frank-Wolfe for smooth nonconvex minimization. This is a stationarity guarantee, with local solutions remaining central to the nonconvex setting.

Specific decompositions offer an additional benefit: a gradient-efficient variant needs only O(1/epsilon) gradient-oracle calls by reusing gradients across several iterations. This distinguishes the cost of obtaining gradients from the total iteration count. Numerical experiments support the method's effectiveness relative to other projection-free algorithms, showing why decomposition choice can matter even when the general iteration bound stays unchanged.
summary.tldr: A structured Frank-Wolfe method exploits convex-difference decompositions, matching standard stationarity complexity while enabling fewer gradient calls in specific cases.

title: Revisiting Frank-Wolfe for Structured Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is crucial for ensuring the reliability and safety of machine learning models in real-world applications, where they frequently face data distributions unseen during training. Despite progress, existing methods are often vulnerable to spurious correlations that mislead models and compromise robustness. To address this, we propose SPROD, a novel prototype-based OOD detection approach that explicitly addresses the challenge posed by unknown spurious correlations. Our post-hoc method refines class prototypes to mitigate bias from spurious features without additional data or hyperparameter tuning, and is broadly applicable across diverse backbones and OOD detection settings. We conduct a comprehensive spurious correlation OOD detection benchmarking, comparing our method against existing approaches and demonstrating its superior performance across challenging OOD datasets, such as CelebA, Waterbirds, UrbanCars, Spurious Imagenet, and the newly introduced Animals MetaCoCo. On average, SPROD improves AUROC by 4.8% and FPR@95 by 9.4% over the second best.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the kinds of data a model learned from. Spurious correlations can undermine that judgment by making unreliable features appear informative. SPROD addresses this problem by refining class prototypes, the representations used to summarize known classes.

The method operates after training and is designed to reduce prototype bias from unknown spurious features. It requires neither additional data nor hyperparameter tuning. The authors describe it as broadly applicable across model backbones and detection settings, making prototype refinement the main intervention rather than collecting new examples or adjusting a separate tuning process.

The evaluation compares methods on challenging datasets including CelebA, Waterbirds, UrbanCars, Spurious Imagenet, and the newly introduced Animals MetaCoCo. SPROD reports average improvements of 4.8% in AUROC and 9.4% in FPR@95 over the second-best method. These results support correcting the influence of misleading features in class summaries as a practical way to improve detection reliability under the benchmarked spurious correlations.
summary.tldr: SPROD refines class prototypes after training to improve out-of-distribution detection under unknown spurious correlations.

title: Spurious-Aware Prototype Refinement for Reliable Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: Class-imbalanced learning (CIL) on tabular data is important in many real-world applications where the minority class holds the critical but rare outcomes. In this paper, we present CLIMB, a comprehensive benchmark for class-imbalanced learning on tabular data. CLIMB includes 73 real-world datasets across diverse domains and imbalance levels, along with unified implementations of 29 representative CIL algorithms. Built on a high-quality open-source Python package with unified API designs, detailed documentation, and rigorous code quality controls, CLIMB supports easy implementation and comparison between different CIL algorithms. Through extensive experiments, we provide practical insights on method accuracy and efficiency, highlighting the limitations of naive rebalancing, the effectiveness of ensembles, and the importance of data quality. Our code, documentation, and examples are available at https://github.com/ZhiningLiu1998/imbalanced-ensemble.

paragraphs: In many tabular prediction problems, the outcomes that matter most occur much less often than other outcomes. Class-imbalanced learning addresses this uneven distribution. CLIMB provides a shared benchmark for studying these methods across different application domains and levels of imbalance, allowing comparisons beyond a single dataset or setting.

The benchmark brings together 73 real-world datasets and unified implementations of 29 representative algorithms. Its Python package supplies a common interface, documentation, and code quality controls. This shared implementation framework makes methods easier to apply and compare, while the dataset collection exposes them to a range of practical data conditions.

The experimental analysis considers both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. Its findings highlight weaknesses of naive rebalancing, the effectiveness of ensembles, and the importance of data quality. These are practical observations from the benchmark rather than a claim that one approach always wins. The paper’s main contribution is an evaluation resource that connects method comparisons with guidance about the factors influencing their performance.
summary.tldr: CLIMB compares 29 class-imbalanced learning algorithms across 73 tabular datasets and identifies practical lessons about ensembles, rebalancing, and data quality.

title: CLIMB: Class-imbalanced Learning Benchmark on Tabular Data

abstract: Egocentric hand-object motion generation is crucial for immersive AR/VR and robotic imitation but remains challenging due to unstable viewpoints, self-occlusions, perspective distortion, and noisy ego-motion. Existing methods rely on predefined 3D object priors, limiting generalization to novel objects, which restricts their generalizability to novel objects. Meanwhile, recent multimodal approaches suffer from ambiguous generation from abstract textual cues, intricate pipelines for modeling 3D hand-object correlation, and compounding errors in open-loop prediction. We propose **MEgoHand**, a multimodal framework that synthesizes physically plausible hand-object interactions from egocentric RGB, text, and initial hand pose. MEgoHand introduces a bi-level architecture: a high-level “cerebrum” leverages a vision language model (VLM) to infer motion priors from visual-textual context and a monocular depth estimator for object-agnostic spatial reasoning, while a low-level DiT-based flow-matching policy generates fine-grained trajectories with temporal orthogonal filtering to enhance stability. To address dataset inconsistency, we design a dataset curation paradigm with an Inverse MANO Retargeting Network and Virtual RGB-D Renderer, curating a unified dataset of **3.35M** RGB-D frames, **24K** interactions, and **1.2K** objects. Extensive experiments across **five** in-domain and **two** cross-domain datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MEgoHand, achieving substantial reductions in wrist translation error (**86.9%**) and joint rotation error (**34.1%**), highlighting its capacity to accurately model fine-grained hand joint structures and generalize robustly across diverse scenarios.

paragraphs: MEgoHand generates hand-object interaction motions from first-person RGB images, text, and an initial hand pose. This setting is difficult because the viewpoint moves, hands obscure themselves, and perspective and camera motion complicate spatial interpretation. The framework aims to produce physically plausible interactions without relying on predefined three-dimensional object priors.

Its architecture separates contextual interpretation from detailed movement generation. A high-level component uses a vision-language model to infer motion guidance and a monocular depth estimator for spatial reasoning about objects. A lower-level flow-matching policy generates detailed trajectories, with temporal orthogonal filtering to improve stability. This division connects visual and textual intent to fine-grained hand motion.

The paper also unifies inconsistent datasets through an Inverse MANO Retargeting Network and a Virtual RGB-D Renderer. The resulting collection contains 3.35 million RGB-D frames, 24,000 interactions, and 1,200 objects. Evaluations across five in-domain and two cross-domain datasets report reductions of 86.9% in wrist translation error and 34.1% in joint rotation error, supporting accurate motion generation and transfer across the tested scenarios.
summary.tldr: MEgoHand combines visual-language interpretation, depth estimation, and trajectory generation to produce accurate first-person hand-object motions across diverse evaluated settings.

title: MEgoHand: Multimodal Egocentric Hand-Object Interaction Motion Generation

abstract: Understanding how humans move their eyes to gather visual information is a central question in neuroscience, cognitive science, and vision research. While recent deep learning (DL) models achieve state-of-the-art performance in predicting human scanpaths, their underlying decision processes remain opaque. At an opposite end of the modeling spectrum, cognitively inspired mechanistic models aim to explain scanpath behavior through interpretable cognitive mechanisms but lag far behind in predictive accuracy. In this work, we bridge this gap by using a high-performing deep model—DeepGaze III—to discover and test mechanisms that improve a leading mechanistic model, SceneWalk. By identifying individual fixations where DeepGaze III succeeds and SceneWalk fails, we isolate behaviorally meaningful discrepancies and use them to motivate targeted extensions of the mechanistic framework. These include time-dependent temperature scaling, saccadic momentum and an adaptive cardinal attention bias: Simple, interpretable additions that substantially boost predictive performance. With these extensions, SceneWalk’s explained variance on the MIT1003 dataset doubles from 35% to 70%, setting a new state of the art in mechanistic scanpath prediction. Our findings show how performance-optimized neural networks can serve as tools for cognitive model discovery, offering a new path toward interpretable and high-performing models of visual behavior. Our code is available at https://github.com/bethgelab/what-moves-the-eyes

Mechanistic models describe behavior through explicit cognitive mechanisms yet tend to predict less accurately. This paper uses the stronger predictions of DeepGaze III to discover targeted improvements to SceneWalk, an interpretable model of how people look around scenes.

The authors identify individual fixations that DeepGaze III predicts successfully and SceneWalk misses. These discrepancies motivate specific additions to SceneWalk: time-dependent temperature scaling, saccadic momentum, and an adaptive cardinal attention bias. The approach uses disagreements between models to guide the development and testing of interpretable mechanisms for visual behavior.

The improvement concerns explained variance on this dataset, giving a precise meaning to the reported doubling. More broadly, the results demonstrate how a high-performing neural model can help develop a more accurate mechanistic account of human behavior.
summary.tldr: DeepGaze III guides interpretable extensions to SceneWalk that double its explained variance on MIT1003 from 35% to 70%.

title: What Moves the Eyes: Doubling Mechanistic Model Performance Using Deep Networks to Discover and Test Cognitive Hypotheses

abstract: Model editing offers a promising paradigm for efficiently and precisely updating knowledge in pre-trained transformers without costly retraining. While extensively studied in language models (LMs), model editing for vision transformers (ViTs) remains underexplored. Existing methods typically adapt LM-based techniques by modifying the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules, overlooking the unique characteristics of ViTs. In this work, we show that ViT predictions are more strongly influenced by the multi-head self-attention (MSA) modules than by the MLPs. Building on this observation, we propose a two-stage framework for editing ViTs. First, we identify which attention heads are most responsible for incorrect predictions. Next, we selectively remove the corresponding features to correct the model’s prediction. To further balance error correction with predictive stability on unrelated data, we learn a projection matrix that refines the image representations. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets and model editing benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing model editing methods for ViTs, achieving superior generalization and locality. Our code is available at https://github.com/shanghxy/Model-editing-for-vision-transformers.

Existing methods typically adapt LM-based techniques by modifying the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) modules, overlooking the unique characteristics of ViTs. In this work, we show that ViT predictions are more strongly influenced by the multi-head self-attention (MSA) modules than by the MLPs. Building on this observation, we propose a two-stage framework for editing ViTs. First, we identify which attention heads are most responsible for incorrect predictions. Next, we selectively remove the corresponding features to correct the model’s prediction. To further balance error correction with predictive stability on unrelated data, we learn a projection matrix that refines the image representations. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets and model editing benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing model editing methods for ViTs, achieving superior generalization and locality. Our code is available at https://github.com/shanghxy/Model-editing-for-vision-transformers.

paragraphs: Model editing seeks to correct a pretrained model efficiently without retraining it extensively. For vision transformers, existing approaches often borrow language-model editing techniques that modify multilayer perceptrons. This paper reports that vision-transformer predictions are more strongly influenced by multi-head self-attention modules, motivating a different location for targeted corrections.

The proposed framework first identifies the attention heads most responsible for an incorrect prediction. It then selectively removes the associated features to change that prediction. A learned projection matrix further refines image representations, helping balance the desired correction against stable predictions on unrelated data. The procedure therefore treats identifying the source of an error and limiting collateral changes as connected objectives.

Experiments across real-world datasets and model-editing benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing vision-transformer editing methods. The reported gains include generalization and locality: edits transfer better while preserving behavior outside the intended correction. The contribution highlights the value of designing editing methods around the architectural components that most influence the model being edited.
summary.tldr: This vision-transformer editing method targets error-associated attention features while learning a projection to preserve unrelated predictions.

title: Model Editing for Vision Transformers

abstract: Demonstrations and instructions are two primary approaches for prompting language models to perform in-context learning (ICL) tasks. Do identical tasks elicited in different ways result in similar representations of the task? An improved understanding of task representation mechanisms would offer interpretability insights and may aid in steering models. We study this through function vectors (FVs), recently proposed as a mechanism to extract few-shot ICL task representations. We generalize FVs to alternative task presentations, focusing on short textual instruction prompts, and successfully extract instruction function vectors that promote zero-shot task accuracy. We find evidence that demonstration- and instruction-based function vectors leverage different model components, and offer several controls to dissociate their contributions to task performance. Our results suggest that different task prompting forms do not induce a common task representation through FVs but elicit different, partly overlapping mechanisms. Our findings offer principled support to the practice of combining instructions and task demonstrations, imply challenges in universally monitoring task inference across presentation forms, and encourage further examinations of LLM task inference mechanisms.

paragraphs: A language model can learn what to do from examples or from a written instruction. This paper asks whether those different presentations of the same task produce a shared internal task representation. Understanding that relationship could help explain model behavior and inform methods for steering it.

The researchers study function vectors, a mechanism previously used to extract task representations from prompts containing demonstrations. They extend this approach to short textual instructions and extract instruction-based vectors that improve zero-shot task accuracy. Controls examining the contributions of each prompting form provide evidence that instruction and demonstration vectors use different model components.

The findings suggest that the two forms of prompting recruit partly overlapping mechanisms rather than a common representation through function vectors. This supplies principled support for combining instructions with demonstrations, because they can contribute through different components. It also suggests difficulties for a universal monitoring method that assumes task inference looks the same across presentation styles. The conclusion concerns the function-vector mechanism studied here.
summary.tldr: Instructions and demonstrations appear to elicit different, partly overlapping task mechanisms when examined through function vectors.

title: Do different prompting methods yield a common task representation in language models?

abstract: Zeroth-order optimization (ZOO) is an important framework for stochastic optimization when gradients are unavailable or expensive to compute. A potential limitation of existing ZOO methods is the bias inherent in most gradient estimators unless the perturbation stepsize vanishes. In this paper, we overcome this biasedness issue by proposing a novel family of *unbiased* gradient estimators based solely on function evaluations. By reformulating directional derivatives as a telescoping series and sampling from carefully designed distributions, we construct estimators that eliminate bias while maintaining favorable variance. We analyze their theoretical properties, derive optimal scaling distributions and perturbation stepsizes of four specific constructions, and prove that SGD using the proposed estimators achieves optimal complexity for smooth non-convex objectives. Experiments on synthetic tasks and language model fine-tuning confirm the superior accuracy and convergence of our approach compared to standard methods.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization uses function evaluations when gradients are unavailable or costly. Many gradient estimates used in this setting are biased unless the perturbation step size tends to zero. This paper proposes a family of estimators whose average equals the desired gradient, addressing that bias while relying solely on function values.

The construction rewrites directional derivatives as a telescoping series and samples from carefully chosen distributions. This randomized treatment removes bias while retaining favorable variance. The authors analyze four specific constructions, deriving optimal scaling distributions and perturbation step sizes. The central design problem is therefore how to randomize the series in a way that combines unbiasedness with useful statistical behavior.

For smooth non-convex objectives, the paper proves optimal complexity for stochastic gradient descent using the proposed estimators. That guarantee applies within the stated objective setting. Experiments on synthetic problems and language-model fine-tuning report better accuracy and convergence than standard methods. Together, the results connect a mathematical correction to gradient-estimation bias with improvements in the optimization tasks examined.
summary.tldr: Randomized telescoping-series constructions yield unbiased gradient estimates from function values, with optimal SGD complexity for smooth non-convex objectives.

title: On the Optimal Construction of Unbiased Gradient Estimators for Zeroth-Order Optimization

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used method for parameter-efficient finetuning. However, existing LoRA variants lack mechanisms to explicitly disambiguate task-relevant information within the learned low-rank subspace, potentially limiting downstream performance. We propose Factorized Variational Autoencoder LoRA (FVAE-LoRA), which leverages a VAE to learn two distinct latent spaces. Our novel Evidence Lower Bound formulation explicitly promotes factorization between the latent spaces, dedicating one latent space to task-salient features and the other to residual information. Extensive experiments on text, audio, and image tasks demonstrate that FVAE-LoRA consistently outperforms standard LoRA. Moreover, spurious correlation evaluations confirm that FVAE-LoRA better isolates task-relevant signals, leading to improved robustness under distribution shifts. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/idiap/FVAE-LoRA

paragraphs: LoRA adapts a model through a low-rank representation, but the information learned inside that representation can remain mixed together. This paper argues that existing variants lack an explicit mechanism for distinguishing features useful to the task from other information. That mixing may limit downstream performance and motivate a more structured adaptation space.

Factorized Variational Autoencoder LoRA, or FVAE-LoRA, uses a variational autoencoder to learn two latent spaces. One is dedicated to task-salient features, while the other holds residual information. A new evidence-lower-bound objective explicitly encourages the two spaces to factorize. The key change is therefore in how adaptation information is organized, giving the training objective a direct role in separating its different components.

Across text, audio, and image tasks, the authors report consistent improvements over standard LoRA. Evaluations involving spurious correlations also indicate better isolation of task-relevant signals and greater robustness under distribution shifts. These findings support the practical value of separating useful signals from residual information within low-rank adaptation, across the modalities and shifts examined.
summary.tldr: FVAE-LoRA separates task-relevant and residual information into two latent spaces, improving reported performance and robustness over standard LoRA.

title: Latent Space Factorization in LoRA

abstract: Photorealistic Codec Avatars (PCA), which generate high-fidelity human face renderings, are increasingly being used in Virtual Reality (VR) environments to enable immersive communication and interaction through deep learning–based generative models. However, these models impose significant computational demands, making real-time inference challenging on resource-constrained VR devices such as head-mounted displays (HMDs), where latency and power efficiency are critical. To address this challenge, we propose an efficient post-training quantization (PTQ) method tailored for Codec Avatar models, enabling low-precision execution without compromising output quality. In addition, we design a custom hardware accelerator that can be integrated into the system-on-chip (SoC) of VR devices to further enhance processing efficiency. Building on these components, we introduce ESCA, a full-stack optimization framework that accelerates PCA inference on edge VR platforms. Experimental results demonstrate that ESCA boosts FovVideoVDP quality scores by up to +0.39 over the best 4-bit baseline, delivers up to 3.36× latency reduction, and sustains a rendering rate of 100 frames per second in end-to-end tests, satisfying real-time VR requirements. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying high-fidelity codec avatars on resource-constrained devices, opening the door to more immersive and portable VR experiences.

ESCA addresses this deployment problem by coordinating changes to model execution with a purpose-built hardware design.

title: ESCA: Enabling Seamless Codec Avatar Execution through Algorithm and Hardware Co-Optimization for Virtual Reality

abstract: *Can algebraic geometry enhance the sharpness, robustness, and interpretability of modern neural reasoning models by equipping them with a mathematically grounded inductive bias?* To answer this, we introduce Tropical Attention, an attention mechanism grounded in tropical geometry that lifts the attention kernel into tropical projective space, where reasoning is piecewise-linear and 1-Lipschitz, thus preserving the polyhedral decision structure inherent to combinatorial reasoning. We prove that multi-head Tropical Attention (MHTA) stacks universally approximate tropical circuits and realize tropical transitive closure through composition, achieving polynomial resource bounds without invoking recurrent mechanisms. These guarantees explain why the induced polyhedral decision boundaries remain sharp and scale-invariant, rather than smoothed by Softmax. Empirically, we show that Tropical Attention delivers stronger out-of-distribution generalization in both length and value, with high robustness against perturbative noise, and substantially faster inference with fewer parameters compared to Softmax-based and recurrent attention baselines, respectively. For the first time, we push the domain of neural algorithmic reasoning beyond **PTIME** problems to **NP-hard/complete** problems, paving the way toward sharper and more expressive Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) capable of tackling complex combinatorial challenges in Phylogenetics, Cryptography, Particle Physics, and Mathematical Discovery. The code is available at https://github.com/Baran-phys/Tropical-Attention/.

paragraphs: Tropical Attention introduces a mathematical structure intended to suit combinatorial reasoning. It moves the attention kernel into tropical projective space, where computation is piecewise linear and has a 1-Lipschitz property that controls sensitivity. This preserves sharp, polyhedral decision regions associated with combinatorial problems, providing an architectural bias toward their structure.

The authors prove that stacks of multi-head Tropical Attention can universally approximate tropical circuits and implement tropical transitive closure through composition. These constructions have polynomial resource bounds and do not require recurrent mechanisms. The guarantees explain properties of the represented computations, including sharp and scale-invariant decision boundaries.

Experiments report stronger generalization to unfamiliar lengths and values, robustness to perturbative noise, and substantially faster inference with fewer parameters relative to the stated Softmax and recurrent baselines. The work also extends its neural algorithmic reasoning study to NP-hard and NP-complete problems. That empirical scope is distinct from the polynomial resource guarantees for the specific tropical constructions proved in the paper.
summary.tldr: Tropical Attention uses piecewise-linear geometry to support combinatorial reasoning, with theoretical representation guarantees and improved empirical generalization and robustness.

title: Tropical Attention: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning for Combinatorial Algorithms

abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as close collaborators for humans, it is crucial that they express their reasoning in ways that humans can understand and learn from. However, this capability remains relatively less understood and under-evaluated. To address this, we introduce a conceptual framework for such Human-AI knowledge transfer capabilities and conduct the first large-scale user study (N=118) explicitly designed to measure it. In our two-phase setup, humans first ideate with an LLM on problem-solving strategies, then independently implement solutions, isolating the influence of model reasoning on human understanding. Our findings reveal that while model benchmark performance correlates with collaborative outcomes, this relationship is notably inconsistent with significant outliers, highlighting that knowledge transfer is a distinct capability requiring dedicated optimization. Our analysis uncovers behavioral and strategic factors that mediate successful knowledge transfer, and we release our code, dataset, and evaluation framework to support future work on communicatively aligned models.

paragraphs: A language model can solve a problem successfully without necessarily helping a person understand how to solve it. This paper treats the transfer of knowledge from an AI collaborator to a human as a capability requiring its own evaluation. It introduces a conceptual framework and a user study involving 118 participants to measure that capability.

The study separates collaboration from implementation. Participants first discuss problem-solving strategies with a language model, then implement solutions independently. This two-phase setup is designed to isolate how the model’s reasoning influences human understanding, using the person’s subsequent independent work as evidence of what the interaction enabled them to learn.

Model benchmark performance correlates with collaborative outcomes, but the relationship is inconsistent and includes substantial outliers. The authors interpret this as evidence that knowledge transfer needs dedicated optimization. Their analysis also identifies behavioral and strategic factors mediating successful transfer. By releasing the study’s code, data, and evaluation framework, they provide a basis for assessing how well models communicate usable reasoning to human collaborators.
summary.tldr: A 118-person study shows that model benchmark strength inconsistently predicts how effectively humans learn from collaborating with it.

title: When Models Know More Than They Can Explain: Quantifying Knowledge Transfer in Human-AI Collaboration

abstract: Air pollution was responsible for 2.6 million deaths across South Asia in 2021 alone, with brick manufacturing contributing significantly to this burden. In particular, the Indo-Gangetic Plain; a densely populated and highly polluted region spanning northern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and parts of Afghanistan sees brick kilns contributing 8–14% of ambient air pollution. Traditional monitoring approaches, such as field surveys and manual annotation using tools like Google Earth Pro, are time and labor-intensive. Prior ML-based efforts for automated detection have relied on costly high-resolution commercial imagery and non-public datasets, limiting reproducibility and scalability. In this work, we introduce SENTINELKILNDB, a publicly available, hand-validated benchmark of 62,671 brick kilns spanning threekiln types Fixed Chimney Bull’s Trench Kiln (FCBK), Circular FCBK (CFCBK), and Zigzag kilns - annotated with oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) across 2.8 million km2 using free and globally accessible Sentinel-2 imagery. We benchmark state-of-the-art oriented object detection models and evaluate generalization across in-region, out-of-region, and super-resolution settings. SENTINELKILNDB enables rigorous evaluation of geospatial generalization and robustness for low-resolution object detection, and provides a new testbed for ML models addressing real-world environmental and remote sensing challenges at a continental scale. Datasets and code are available in SentinelKilnDB Dataset and SentinelKilnDB Bench-mark, under the Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International License.

summary.tldr: SentinelKilnDB provides public, validated satellite annotations and benchmarks for detecting South Asian brick kilns across geographic regions.

title: SentinelKilnDB: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for OBB Brick Kiln Detection in South Asia Using Satellite Imagery

abstract: Inference scaling empowers LLMs with unprecedented reasoning ability, with reinforcement learning as the core technique to elicit complex reasoning. However, key technical details of state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs are concealed (such as in OpenAI o1 blog and DeepSeek R1 technical report), thus the community still struggles to reproduce their RL training results. We propose the **D**ecoupled Clip and **D**ynamic s**A**mpling **P**olicy **O**ptimization (**DAPO**) algorithm, and fully open-source a state-of-the-art large-scale RL system that achieves 50 points on AIME 2024 using Qwen2.5-32B base model. Unlike previous works that withhold training details, we introduce four key techniques of our algorithm that make large-scale LLM RL a success. In addition, we open-source our training code, which is built on the verl framework, along with a carefully curated and processed dataset. These components of our open-source system enhance reproducibility and support future research in large-scale LLM RL.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning is a central technique for eliciting complex reasoning from language models, but reproducing leading results can be difficult when training details remain hidden. This paper addresses that reproducibility problem by presenting an openly released algorithm, training system, and processed dataset for reinforcement learning at large scale.

The algorithm is called Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization, or DAPO. The authors describe four key techniques that make their large-scale training successful and release an implementation built on the verl framework. Sharing the implementation alongside a curated dataset makes both the training procedure and its data available for subsequent research.

Using the Qwen2.5-32B base model, the system achieves 50 points on AIME 2024. That result provides a concrete demonstration of the released system's mathematical-reasoning performance in the reported setting. The contribution combines an algorithmic proposal with the practical components needed to investigate and reproduce this kind of training, giving researchers an accessible foundation for further large-scale LLM reinforcement-learning work.
summary.tldr: DAPO releases a large-scale LLM reinforcement-learning algorithm, system, and dataset, reporting 50 points on AIME 2024 with Qwen2.5-32B.

title: DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale

abstract: Poisoning attacks compromise the training phase of federated learning (FL) such that the learned global model misclassifies attacker-chosen inputs called target inputs. Existing defenses mainly focus on protecting the training phase of FL such that the learnt global model is poison free. However, these defenses often achieve limited effectiveness when the clients' local training data is highly non-iid or the number of malicious clients is large, as confirmed in our experiments. In this work, we propose FLForensics, the first poison-forensics method for FL. FLForensics complements existing training-phase defenses. In particular, when training-phase defenses fail and a poisoned global model is deployed, FLForensics aims to trace back the malicious clients that performed the poisoning attack after a misclassified target input is identified. We theoretically show that FLForensics can accurately distinguish between benign and malicious clients under a formal definition of poisoning attack. Moreover, we empirically show the effectiveness of FLForensics at tracing back both existing and adaptive poisoning attacks on five benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Poisoning attacks in federated learning manipulate training so the shared model misclassifies attacker-chosen inputs. Training-time defenses aim to prevent this outcome, but the paper reports limited effectiveness when client data distributions differ greatly or many clients are malicious. FLForensics addresses what happens after such defenses fail and a poisoned model has been deployed.

The method starts when a misclassified target input is identified and aims to trace the attack back to the responsible clients. Its role is therefore forensic and complementary to prevention. It asks which participants caused the poisoning, using the discovered target failure as the starting point for attributing the attack.

The authors theoretically show that FLForensics can distinguish benign from malicious clients under their formal definition of a poisoning attack. They also evaluate existing and adaptive attacks across five benchmark datasets and report effective tracing. Together, these results support post-attack attribution as an additional defense capability, with the theoretical claim tied to the paper's specified attack definition.
summary.tldr: FLForensics traces federated-learning poisoning attacks back to malicious clients after a target misclassification has been discovered.

title: Tracing Back the Malicious Clients in Poisoning Attacks to Federated Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their extensive parameter scales pose significant challenges for practical deployment. Unstructured pruning has emerged as an effective model compression strategy with minimal performance loss, which introduces fine-grained sparsity for weight parameters. While existing methods employ a layer-wise pruning strategy to avoid the complexity of global pruning for billion-scale LLMs, they require appropriate sparsity allocation for the layer-wise pruning objectives and often lead to suboptimal solutions for the overall model. In this paper, we propose Lua-LLM ($\textbf{L}$earning $\textbf{u}$nstructured-sparsity $\textbf{a}$llocation in LLMs), a learning-based global pruning framework that explores the optimal unstructured sparsity allocation. Unlike existing pruning methods, which primarily focus on allocating per-layer sparsity, Lua-LLM achieves flexible allocation for both layer-wise and intra-layer sparsity. Furthermore, Lua-LLM leverages a soft Top-K operator to approximate the importance-based mask selection mechanism, enabling efficient binary mask learning. Experimental results on LLaMA and OPT families demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing methods.

paragraphs: Unstructured pruning compresses a language model by removing individual weight parameters. A central challenge is deciding where those removals should occur. Existing methods often prune one layer at a time to manage the scale of the problem, but their layer-level sparsity choices can produce a suboptimal allocation for the model as a whole.

Lua-LLM treats sparsity allocation as a learning problem across the model. It allows flexible decisions both between layers and within each layer. A soft Top-K operator approximates the process of choosing weights by importance, enabling efficient learning of binary masks that determine which parameters remain active.

Experiments on the LLaMA and OPT model families report significant performance improvements over existing methods. The contribution is therefore broader than choosing a pruning amount for each layer: it learns a more detailed distribution of retained weights. This addresses the mismatch between convenient layer-by-layer compression decisions and the objective of preserving performance across the entire model.
summary.tldr: Lua-LLM learns where to prune weights across and within layers, improving reported performance over existing pruning methods.

title: Lua-LLM: Learning Unstructured-Sparsity Allocation for Large Language Models

abstract: Training multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) that align with human intentions is a long-term challenge. Traditional score-only reward models for alignment suffer from low accuracy, weak generalization, and poor interpretability, blocking the progress of alignment methods, \textit{e.g.,} reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). Generative reward models (GRMs) leverage MLLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities to discriminate pair-wise responses, but their pair-wise paradigm makes it hard to generalize to learnable rewards. We introduce Generative RLHF-V, a novel alignment framework that integrates GRMs with multi-modal RLHF. We propose a two-stage pipeline: \textbf{multi-modal generative reward modeling from RL}, where RL guides GRMs to actively capture human intention, then predict the correct pair-wise scores; and \textbf{RL optimization from grouped comparison}, which enhances multi-modal RL scoring precision by grouped responses comparison. Experimental results demonstrate that, besides out-of-distribution generalization of RM discrimination, our framework improves 4 MLLMs' performance across 7 benchmarks by 18.1\%, while the baseline RLHF is only 5.3\%. We further validate that Generative RLHF-V achieves a near-linear improvement with an increasing number of candidate responses.

paragraphs: Aligning multimodal language models with human preferences depends on feedback that reliably distinguishes better responses. Score-only reward models can struggle with accuracy, generalization, and interpretability. Generative reward models use reasoning to compare responses, but translating pairwise judgments into useful rewards for reinforcement learning introduces another challenge.

Generative RLHF-V connects these components through a two-stage pipeline. First, reinforcement learning trains the generative reward model to capture human intentions and predict correct pairwise scores. Second, policy optimization uses comparisons among grouped candidate responses to improve scoring precision. This makes response comparison part of the alignment procedure, rather than leaving a pairwise judge disconnected from policy training.

The authors report improved reward discrimination outside the training distribution and an 18.1% performance improvement across four multimodal models and seven benchmarks, compared with 5.3% for baseline RLHF. They also observe near-linear improvement as the number of candidate responses increases. These findings suggest that reasoning-based reward modeling and grouped comparisons can make human-preference feedback more effective in the evaluated multimodal settings.
summary.tldr: Generative RLHF-V combines reasoning-based preference judgments with grouped response comparisons to improve multimodal reinforcement learning from human feedback.

title: Generative RLHF-V: Learning Principles from Multi-modal Human Preference

abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train a lightweight student model by transferring knowledge from a large, high-capacity teacher. Recent studies have shown that leveraging diverse teacher perspectives can significantly improve distillation performance; however, achieving such diversity typically requires multiple teacher networks, leading to high computational costs. In this work, we propose a novel cost-efficient knowledge augmentation method for KD that generates diverse multi-views by attaching multiple branches to a single teacher. To ensure meaningful semantic variation across multi-views, we introduce two angular diversity objectives: 1) $\textit{constrained inter-angle diversify loss}$, which maximizes angles between augmented views while preserving proximity to the original teacher output, and 2) $\textit{intra-angle diversify loss}$, which encourages an even distribution of views around the original output. The ensembled knowledge from these angularly diverse views, along with the original teacher, is distilled into the student. We further theoretically demonstrate that our objectives increase the diversity among ensemble members and thereby reduce the upper bound of the ensemble's expected loss, leading to more effective distillation. Experimental results show that our method surpasses an existing knowledge augmentation method across diverse configurations. Moreover, the proposed method is compatible with other KD frameworks in a plug-and-play fashion, providing consistent improvements in generalization performance.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model using information from a larger teacher. Diverse teacher perspectives can improve the transfer, but maintaining several teachers adds computational cost. This paper creates multiple perspectives by attaching branches to one teacher, aiming to obtain useful diversity with a more economical source of supervision.

Two objectives shape the branch outputs through their angular relationships. One increases the angles between augmented views while keeping them close to the original teacher output. The other encourages an even arrangement of views around that output. The combined knowledge from the original teacher and these augmented views is then distilled into the student.

The theoretical analysis shows that the objectives increase ensemble diversity and reduce an upper bound on expected ensemble loss. Experiments show improvements over an existing knowledge-augmentation method across varied configurations. The approach also works with other distillation frameworks and produces consistent generalization gains in the reported evaluations. Its contribution is a controlled way to diversify supervision without requiring multiple separate teacher networks.
summary.tldr: Multiple angularly diversified branches on one teacher improve knowledge distillation while avoiding the cost of separate teacher networks.

title: Single-Teacher View Augmentation: Boosting Knowledge Distillation via Angular Diversity

abstract: Deployment of neural networks on resource-constrained devices demands models that are both compact and robust to adversarial inputs. However, compression and adversarial robustness often conflict. In this work, we introduce a dynamical low-rank training scheme enhanced with a novel spectral regularizer that controls the condition number of the low-rank core in each layer. This approach mitigates the sensitivity of compressed models to adversarial perturbations without sacrificing clean accuracy. The method is model- and data-agnostic, computationally efficient, and supports rank adaptivity to automatically compress the network at hand. Extensive experiments across standard architectures, datasets, and adversarial attacks show the regularized networks can achieve over 94 compression while recovering or improving adversarial accuracy relative to uncompressed baselines.

paragraphs: This paper tackles the tension between making neural networks smaller and keeping them resistant to adversarial inputs. Resource-constrained deployment benefits from compression, but the abstract identifies a recurring conflict with robustness. The proposed method aims to reduce model size while retaining accuracy on ordinary inputs and improving behavior under adversarial perturbations.

The approach uses dynamical low-rank training, enhanced by a spectral regularizer. That regularizer controls the condition number of each layer's low-rank core, targeting sensitivity within the compressed representation. The method also adapts ranks automatically, allowing the amount of compression to change with the network. The authors describe it as computationally efficient and applicable across models and data.

Experiments span standard architectures, datasets, and attacks. The reported networks achieve substantial compression while recovering or improving adversarial accuracy relative to uncompressed baselines, without sacrificing clean accuracy. The findings support incorporating robustness considerations directly into low-rank training. The important result is the observed combination of compactness and resistance to perturbations within the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Dynamical low-rank training with spectral regularization compresses networks while retaining clean accuracy and recovering or improving adversarial accuracy.

title: Dynamical Low-Rank Compression of Neural Networks with Robustness under Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Benefiting from the availability of extensive navigation trajectories, both manually and automatically annotated, current graphical user interface (GUI) agents have achieved remarkable advancements in performance. However, these annotated datasets often contain substantial noise, which impedes effective agent training and underscores the necessity for rigorous trajectory quality assessment. In contrast to existing prompting-based evaluators that rely on proprietary multimodal large language models (MLLMs), we propose an Uncertainty-aware Reinforced Self-Training (URST) framework to train lightweight MLLMs for efficient and reliable trajectory evaluation. URST iteratively fine-tunes MLLMs using their own generated thoughts and judgments to enable self-improvement, while its uncertainty-aware sampling strategy ensures the selection of the most informative training examples. To further enhance reasoning and judgment capabilities, we propose a simplified group policy optimization approach that effectively leverages diverse positive and negative samples for evaluator learning. Our evaluator demonstrates superior judgment performance across both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets. When used to filter navigation datasets, it consistently leads to performance improvements in training GUI agents.

paragraphs: GUI agents learn from records of navigation through graphical interfaces, but those records can contain substantial annotation noise. The authors also introduce a simplified group policy optimization method that uses varied positive and negative samples to improve the evaluator’s reasoning and decision-making.

The resulting evaluator achieves superior judgment performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets. When it filters navigation data, GUI agents trained on that data consistently improve in the reported evaluations. The findings connect evaluator learning to a downstream benefit: assessing trajectory quality more effectively can improve the agents that consume those trajectories. The framework’s contribution lies in combining iterative self-training, informative sample selection, and learning from contrasting examples.
summary.tldr: URST trains lightweight trajectory evaluators whose data filtering consistently improves GUI-agent training in the reported evaluations.

title: Enhancing GUI Agent with Uncertainty-Aware Self-Trained Evaluator

abstract: We study the problem of posterior sampling in discrete-state spaces using discrete diffusion models. While posterior sampling methods for continuous diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress, analogous methods for discrete diffusion models remain challenging. In this work, we introduce a principled plug-and-play discrete diffusion posterior sampling algorithm based on split Gibbs sampling, which we call SGDD. Our algorithm enables reward-guided generation and solving inverse problems in discrete-state spaces. We demonstrate the convergence of SGDD to the target posterior distribution and verify this through controlled experiments on synthetic benchmarks. Our method enjoys state-of-the-art posterior sampling performance on a range of benchmarks for discrete data, including DNA sequence design, discrete image inverse problems, and music infilling, achieving more than 30% improved performance compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: SGDD addresses posterior sampling for data whose states are discrete, such as sequences or discrete images. The task is to generate samples that reflect both a diffusion model's learned distribution and additional information or objectives. Although analogous methods for continuous diffusion have advanced substantially, transferring that capability to discrete spaces remains challenging.

The proposed algorithm uses split Gibbs sampling to create a principled, plug-and-play discrete diffusion sampler. It supports both reward-guided generation and inverse problems, allowing the same sampling framework to address different forms of conditioning. The authors prove convergence to the intended posterior distribution and use controlled synthetic experiments to verify that behavior, connecting the algorithm's design to a specific sampling target.

Applications include DNA sequence design, discrete image inverse problems, and filling missing sections of music. Across the evaluated discrete-data benchmarks, the paper reports state-of-the-art posterior sampling performance and improvements exceeding 30% relative to existing baselines. These findings indicate that the framework can combine a theoretical convergence result with effective generation across several distinct kinds of discrete structures.
summary.tldr: SGDD uses split Gibbs sampling to guide discrete diffusion models toward target posteriors for design, reconstruction, and infilling tasks.

title: Split Gibbs Discrete Diffusion Posterior Sampling

abstract: Low-rank gradient-based optimization methods have significantly improved memory efficiency during the training of large language models (LLMs), enabling operations within constrained hardware without sacrificing performance. However, these methods primarily emphasize memory savings, often overlooking potential acceleration in convergence due to their reliance on standard isotropic steepest descent techniques, which can perform suboptimally in the highly anisotropic landscapes typical of deep networks, particularly LLMs. In this paper, we propose SUMO (Subspace-Aware Moment-Orthogonalization), an optimizer that employs exact singular value decomposition (SVD) for moment orthogonalization within a dynamically adapted low-dimensional subspace, enabling norm-inducing steepest descent optimization steps. By explicitly aligning optimization steps with the spectral characteristics of the loss landscape, SUMO effectively mitigates approximation errors associated with commonly used methods like Newton-Schulz orthogonalization approximation. We theoretically establish an upper bound on these approximation errors, proving their dependence on the condition numbers of moments, conditions we analytically demonstrate are encountered during LLM training. Furthermore, we both theoretically and empirically illustrate that exact orthogonalization via SVD substantially improves convergence rates while reducing overall complexity. Empirical evaluations confirm that SUMO accelerates convergence, enhances stability, improves performance, and reduces memory requirements by up to 20\% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Low-rank optimization reduces the memory needed to train language models, but memory savings alone do not ensure fast convergence. This paper focuses on optimization landscapes whose behavior differs sharply across directions. Standard isotropic steepest-descent methods can perform poorly in these settings, motivating update rules that account more explicitly for the landscape’s spectral structure.

SUMO performs exact singular value decomposition to orthogonalize optimization moments inside a low-dimensional subspace that adapts during training. This enables norm-inducing steepest-descent updates while avoiding approximation errors associated with methods such as Newton–Schulz orthogonalization. Evaluations also report better stability and performance, with memory reductions of up to 20% relative to state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is the combination of exact orthogonalization and an adaptive low-dimensional working space to improve both optimization and memory use.
summary.tldr: SUMO uses exact moment orthogonalization in an adaptive low-dimensional subspace to accelerate language-model training and reduce memory use.

title: SUMO: Subspace-Aware Moment-Orthogonalization for Accelerating Memory-Efficient LLM Training

abstract: Current text-to-image (T2I) models often fail to account for diverse human experiences, leading to misaligned systems. We advocate for pluralism in AI alignment, where an AI understands and is steerable towards diverse, and often conflicting, human values. Our work provides three core contributions to achieve this in T2I models. First, we introduce a novel dataset for Diverse Intersectional Visual Evaluation (DIVE) -- the first multimodal dataset for pluralistic alignment. It enables deep alignment to diverse safety perspectives through a large pool of demographically intersectional human raters who provided extensive feedback across 1000 prompts, with high replication, capturing nuanced safety perceptions. Second, we empirically confirm demographics as a crucial proxy for diverse viewpoints in this domain, revealing significant, context-dependent differences in harm perception that diverge from conventional evaluations. Finally, we discuss implications for building aligned T2I models, including efficient data collection strategies, LLM judgment capabilities, and model steerability towards diverse perspectives. This research offers foundational tools for more equitable and aligned T2I systems.Content Warning: The paper includes sensitive content that may be harmful.

paragraphs: DIVE studies how safety judgments about text-to-image systems vary across human perspectives. The paper advocates pluralistic alignment: systems should understand and be steerable toward diverse values, including values that conflict. Its central concern is that evaluations which overlook this diversity can miss important differences in how people experience generated content.

The dataset collects extensive feedback across 1,000 prompts from a large pool of human raters with intersecting demographic characteristics. High replication provides multiple judgments, allowing the analysis to capture nuanced differences in perceived safety. The authors empirically find significant, context-dependent differences in harm perception and identify demographics as an important proxy for viewpoints in this domain.

These patterns diverge from conventional evaluations, supporting the need to examine whose judgments an evaluation represents. The paper also discusses implications for efficient feedback collection, language-model judging, and steering models toward different perspectives. Its contribution is foundational data and analysis for pluralistic evaluation and alignment; the stated findings concern variation in human judgments and tools for incorporating that variation.
summary.tldr: DIVE collects diverse human safety judgments for text-to-image systems and reveals context-dependent differences that conventional evaluations can overlook.

title: Whose View of Safety? A Deep DIVE Dataset for Pluralistic Alignment of Text-to-Image Models

abstract: Transformers have demonstrated effectiveness in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, extending them to solve PDEs on complex geometries remains a challenge. In this work, we propose SpiderSolver, a geometry-aware transformer that introduces spiderweb tokenization for handling complex domain geometry and irregularly discretized points. Our method partitions the irregular spatial domain into spiderweb-like patches, guided by the domain boundary geometry. SpiderSolver leverages a coarse-grained attention mechanism to capture global interactions across spiderweb tokens and a fine-grained attention mechanism to refine feature interactions between the domain boundary and its neighboring interior points. We evaluate SpiderSolver on PDEs with diverse domain geometries across seven datasets, including cars, airfoils, blood flow in the human thoracic aorta, as well as canonical cases governed by the Navier-Stokes, Darcy flow, elasticity, and plasticity equations. Experimental results demonstrate that SpiderSolver consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across different datasets and metrics, with better generalization ability in the OOD setting. The code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Qi/SpiderSolver.

paragraphs: SpiderSolver is a transformer designed to solve partial differential equations on domains with complicated shapes and irregularly distributed points. The paper addresses the difficulty of extending transformer-based PDE methods to such geometries. Its central idea is to organize the spatial representation around the domain boundary, making geometry part of how the model groups and processes its inputs.

The method divides the domain into spiderweb-like patches guided by boundary geometry. These patches become tokens for a coarse attention mechanism that captures interactions across the whole domain. A separate fine attention mechanism refines interactions between the boundary and nearby interior points. The two levels combine global spatial relationships with detailed treatment of the boundary region.

Evaluation spans seven datasets, including cars, airfoils, and blood flow in the human thoracic aorta, together with cases involving Navier-Stokes, Darcy flow, elasticity, and plasticity equations. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated datasets and metrics, as well as better out-of-distribution generalization. These findings support geometry-aware tokenization and multiscale attention for the tested PDE problems.
summary.tldr: SpiderSolver uses boundary-guided spatial patches and two levels of attention to solve PDEs on complex geometries.

title: SpiderSolver: A Geometry-Aware Transformer for Solving PDEs on Complex Geometries

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have revolutionized the field of graph learning by learning expressive graph representations from massive graph data. As a common pattern to train powerful GNNs, the "pre-training, adaptation" scheme first pre-trains GNNs over unlabeled graph data and subsequently adapts them to specific downstream tasks. In the adaptation phase, graph prompting is an effective strategy that modifies input graph data with learnable prompts while keeping pre-trained GNN models frozen. Typically, existing graph prompting studies mainly focus on *feature-oriented* methods that apply graph prompts to node features or hidden representations. However, these studies often achieve suboptimal performance, as they consistently overlook the potential of *topology-oriented* prompting, which adapts pre-trained GNNs by modifying the graph topology. In this study, we conduct a pioneering investigation of graph prompting in terms of graph topology. We propose the first **Graph** **T**opology-**O**riented **P**rompting (GraphTOP) framework to effectively adapt pre-trained GNN models for downstream tasks. More specifically, we reformulate topology-oriented prompting as an edge rewiring problem within multi-hop local subgraphs and relax it into the continuous probability space through reparameterization while ensuring tight relaxation and preserving graph sparsity. Extensive experiments on five graph datasets under four pre-training strategies demonstrate that our proposed GraphTOP outshines six baselines on multiple node classification datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/xbfu/GraphTOP.

paragraphs: Graph prompting adapts a pretrained graph neural network by changing its input while keeping the network frozen. Many existing methods modify node features or hidden representations. GraphTOP instead focuses on the graph’s connectivity, asking whether changing which nodes are connected can make a pretrained model more useful for a downstream task.

The framework expresses this adaptation as edge rewiring within local subgraphs spanning multiple hops. Because edge choices are discrete, it uses reparameterization to move the optimization into a continuous probability space. The proposed relaxation is designed to remain tight while preserving graph sparsity, allowing topology changes to be learned without turning the graph into a densely connected structure.

Experiments cover five graph datasets and four pretraining strategies. The authors report that GraphTOP outperforms six baselines on multiple node-classification datasets. These results support connectivity as a useful target for graph prompting: a frozen network can be adapted through the relationships presented to it, extending the range of input changes available during downstream adaptation.
summary.tldr: GraphTOP adapts frozen graph neural networks by learning sparse local edge rewiring, outperforming six baselines in reported node-classification experiments.

title: GraphTOP: Graph Topology-Oriented Prompting for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Understanding when learning is possible is a fundamental task in the theory of machine learning. However, many characterizations known from the literature deal with abstract learning as a mathematical object and ignore the crucial question: when can learning be implemented as a computer program? We address this question for universal online learning, a generalist theoretical model of online binary classification, recently characterized by Bousquet et al. (STOC 2021). In this model, there is no hypothesis fixed in advance; instead, Adversary—playing the role of Nature—can change their mind as long as local consistency with the given class of hypotheses is maintained. We require Learner to achieve a finite number of mistakes while using a strategy that can be implemented as a computer program. We show that universal online learning does not imply computable universal online learning, even if the class of hypotheses is relatively easy from a computability-theoretic perspective. We then study the agnostic variant of computable universal online learning and provide an exact characterization of classes that are learnable in this sense. We also consider a variant of proper universal online learning and show exactly when it is possible. Together, our results give a more realistic perspective on the existing theory of online binary classification and the related problem of inductive inference.
