paragraphs: This paper develops a way to generate samples from a target density whose normalization constant need not be known. The method begins with samples from a reference density and moves them toward the target. Its interacting particle systems require target-to-reference density ratios but do not require gradients of the target density.

The construction follows a geometric mixture connecting the reference and target densities. The authors obtain a velocity field by solving a Poisson equation, using a reproducing-kernel Hilbert-space representation to make the problem tractable. This yields a mean-field differential equation that can be discretized using finitely many particles. They also derive the equation from successive linearizations within sample-driven optimal transport.

A stochastic variant broadens the proposed approach. Empirical evaluations show high-quality samples across varied target distributions, with results exceeding comparable gradient-free particle systems and competing with gradient-based alternatives. The practical attraction is a sampling procedure based on accessible density ratios and reference samples, supported by a connection between Fisher-Rao flow, kernel representations, and transport.
summary.tldr: Kernel Fisher-Rao flow produces gradient-free particle samplers using reference samples and unnormalized density ratios.

title: Sampling in Unit Time with Kernel Fisher-Rao Flow

abstract: Scaling up deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods presents a significant challenge. Following developments in generative modelling, model-based RL positions itself as a strong contender. Recent advances in sequence modelling have led to effective transformer-based world models, albeit at the price of heavy computations due to the long sequences of tokens required to accurately simulate environments. In this work, we propose $\Delta$-IRIS, a new agent with a world model architecture composed of a discrete autoencoder that encodes stochastic deltas between time steps and an autoregressive transformer that predicts future deltas by summarizing the current state of the world with continuous tokens. In the Crafter benchmark, $\Delta$-IRIS sets a new state of the art at multiple frame budgets, while being an order of magnitude faster to train than previous attention-based approaches. We release our code and models at https://github.com/vmicheli/delta-iris.

In this work, we propose $\Delta$-IRIS, a new agent with a world model architecture composed of a discrete autoencoder that encodes stochastic deltas between time steps and an autoregressive transformer that predicts future deltas by summarizing the current state of the world with continuous tokens. paragraphs: A world model lets a reinforcement-learning agent predict how its environment evolves. Transformer-based world models can simulate environments effectively, but accurate simulation may require long token sequences and substantial computation. This paper introduces Δ-IRIS, an agent whose world model changes what is encoded and predicted to make that process more efficient.

The architecture has two complementary parts. A discrete autoencoder encodes stochastic changes between consecutive time steps. An autoregressive transformer predicts future changes while using continuous tokens to summarize the current world state. This separates the representation of the present from the representation of what changes next, making temporal context part of the tokenization and prediction design.

On the Crafter benchmark, Δ-IRIS achieves the best reported performance at several frame budgets. It also trains an order of magnitude faster than previous attention-based approaches. The findings therefore connect the architectural change to both learning performance and training efficiency in the evaluated environment. The contribution is a concrete example of improving a transformer world model by rethinking its representation of environmental change.
summary.tldr: Δ-IRIS models changes between world states, achieving leading Crafter results while training an order of magnitude faster than previous attention-based approaches.

title: Efficient World Models with Context-Aware Tokenization

abstract: Exploration is a crucial phase in reinforcement learning (RL). The reward-free RL paradigm, as explored by (Jin et al., 2020), offers an efficient method to design exploration algorithms for risk-neutral RL across various reward functions with a single exploration phase. However, as RL applications in safety critical settings grow, there’s an increasing need for risk-sensitive RL, which considers potential risks in decision-making. Yet, efficient exploration strategies for risk-sensitive RL remain underdeveloped. This study presents a novel risk-sensitive reward-free framework based on Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR), designed to effectively address CVaR RL for any given reward function through a single exploration phase. We introduce the CVaR-RF-UCRL algorithm, which is shown to be $(\epsilon,p)$-PAC, with a sample complexity upper bounded by $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{S^2AH^4}{\epsilon^2\tau^2}\right)$ with $\tau$ being the risk tolerance parameter. We also prove a $\Omega\left(\frac{S^2AH^2}{\epsilon^2\tau}\right)$ lower bound for any CVaR-RF exploration algorithm, demonstrating the near-optimality of our algorithm. Additionally, we propose the planning algorithms: CVaR-VI and its more practical variant, CVaR-VI-DISC. The effectiveness and practicality of our CVaR reward-free approach are further validated through numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates exploration from the eventual choice of reward function, so one exploration phase can support multiple objectives. This paper extends that idea to risk-sensitive learning using Conditional Value-at-Risk. The aim is to collect information once and then address CVaR-based decision-making for any given reward function within the proposed framework.

The authors introduce CVaR-RF-UCRL and prove an accuracy-and-confidence guarantee with a sample-complexity upper bound. They also establish a lower bound for any exploration algorithm in this framework. The bounds support a near-optimality claim while retaining different dependencies on the horizon and risk-tolerance parameter; the upper and lower bounds are not identical.

For the planning stage, the paper supplies CVaR-VI and a more practical variant, CVaR-VI-DISC. Numerical experiments support the approach's effectiveness and practicality. The overall contribution brings risk sensitivity into reusable exploration: the learner gathers data before a reward is specified, then uses dedicated planning procedures to address a risk-sensitive objective once the reward becomes available.
summary.tldr: A CVaR-based framework enables one reward-free exploration phase to support later risk-sensitive planning, with sample-complexity guarantees.

title: Risk-Sensitive Reward-Free Reinforcement Learning with CVaR

abstract: In light of recent advancements in AI capabilities and the increasingly widespread integration of AI systems into society, governments worldwide are actively seeking to mitigate the potential harms and risks associated with these technologies through regulation and other governance tools. However, there exist significant gaps between governance aspirations and the current state of the technical tooling necessary for their realisation. In this position paper, we survey policy documents published by public-sector institutions in the EU, US, and China to highlight specific areas of disconnect between the technical requirements necessary for enacting proposed policy actions, and the current technical state of the art. Our analysis motivates a call for tighter integration of the AI/ML research community within AI governance in order to i) catalyse technical research aimed at bridging the gap between current and supposed technical underpinnings of regulatory action, as well as ii) increase the level of technical expertise within governing institutions so as to inform and guide effective governance of AI.

paragraphs: AI governance proposals depend on technical capabilities to make their goals achievable. This position paper argues that there are significant gaps between what governance seeks to accomplish and what current technical tools can support. As governments pursue regulation and other interventions, those gaps affect the practical foundations of proposed policy actions.

The authors survey policy documents from public-sector institutions in the EU, the US, and China. Their analysis identifies disconnects between the technical requirements of proposed actions and the current state of the art. This makes the relationship between policy ambitions and technical readiness the central object of study, linking governance proposals to the capabilities needed to enact them.

The paper calls for closer integration of AI and machine-learning researchers into governance in two ways. Researchers should help develop tools that address gaps in the technical basis of regulatory action, and governing institutions should gain more technical expertise to inform their decisions. The argument treats research capacity and institutional talent as complementary ingredients of effective AI governance.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that effective AI governance needs technical research and institutional expertise to bridge gaps between policy ambitions and available tools.

title: Position: Technical Research and Talent is Needed for Effective AI Governance

abstract: Topological Neural Networks (TNNs) incorporate higher-order relational information beyond pairwise interactions, enabling richer representations than Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Concurrently, topological descriptors based on persistent homology (PH) are being increasingly employed to augment the GNNs. We investigate the benefits of integrating these two paradigms. Specifically, we introduce TopNets as a broad framework that subsumes and unifies various methods in the intersection of GNNs/TNNs and PH such as (generalizations of) RePHINE and TOGL. TopNets can also be readily adapted to handle (symmetries in) geometric complexes, extending the scope of TNNs and PH to spatial settings. Theoretically, we show that PH descriptors can provably enhance the expressivity of simplicial message-passing networks. Empirically, (continuous and $E(n)$-equivariant extensions of) TopNets achieve strong performance across diverse tasks, including antibody design, molecular dynamics simulation, and drug property prediction.

paragraphs: Topological neural networks represent relationships involving more than pairs of objects, extending the relational information available to graph neural networks. Persistent homology supplies another kind of topological description used to enrich graph models. This paper brings these two approaches together in a broad framework called TopNets.

TopNets unifies several methods at the intersection of graph or topological neural networks and persistent homology, including generalizations of RePHINE and TOGL. It can also be adapted to geometric complexes and their symmetries, bringing the framework into spatial settings. This connects richer relational structures with topological descriptors within a common modeling approach.

The authors prove that persistent-homology descriptors can increase the expressivity of simplicial message-passing networks. That is a representational result about what the networks can distinguish or express, complemented by empirical evaluations. Continuous and E(n)-equivariant extensions achieve strong performance on antibody design, molecular dynamics simulation, and drug property prediction. The paper thus combines a unifying framework, a theoretical expressivity benefit, and evidence across several scientific tasks.
summary.tldr: TopNets combines topological neural networks with persistent homology, proving an expressivity benefit and demonstrating strong performance on scientific tasks.

title: Topological Neural Networks go Persistent, Equivariant, and Continuous

abstract: Efficiently and effectively estimating counterfactuals over time is crucial for optimizing treatment strategies. We present the Adversarial Counterfactual Temporal Inference Network (ACTIN), a novel framework with dual modules to enhance counterfactual estimation. The balancing module employs a distribution-based adversarial method to learn balanced representations, extending beyond the limitations of current classification-based methods to mitigate confounding bias across various treatment types. The integrating module adopts a novel Temporal Integration Predicting (TIP) strategy, which has a wider receptive field of treatments and balanced representations from the beginning to the current time for a more profound level of analysis. TIP goes beyond the established Direct Predicting (DP) strategy, which only relies on current treatments and representations, by empowering the integrating module to effectively capture long-range dependencies and temporal treatment interactions. ACTIN exceeds the confines of specific base models, and when implemented with simple base models, consistently delivers state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across both synthetic and real-world datasets.

ACTIN exceeds the confines of specific base models, and when implemented with simple base models, consistently delivers state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Estimating counterfactuals over time means asking how outcomes might have changed under different treatment histories. ACTIN addresses this problem with two cooperating modules: one learns representations that reduce confounding bias, and the other combines information across time. This division connects two challenges that matter for treatment planning: making treatment comparisons more balanced and accounting for how earlier treatments affect later outcomes.

The balancing module uses an adversarial method based on distributions. Its purpose is to learn balanced representations across different treatment types, extending beyond the classification-based approaches discussed in the paper. The integrating module then applies Temporal Integration Predicting, which considers treatments and balanced representations from the start of the sequence through the current time.

That broader history distinguishes the method from Direct Predicting, which uses only current treatments and representations. It allows ACTIN to capture long-range dependencies and interactions between treatments over time. Across synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and efficiency even with simple underlying models, supporting the usefulness of the framework beyond a particular base architecture.
summary.tldr: ACTIN combines distribution-based balancing with treatment-history integration to improve counterfactual estimation over time.

title: A Dual-module Framework for Counterfactual Estimation over Time

abstract: Distributed data analysis is a large and growing field driven by a massive proliferation of user devices, and by privacy concerns surrounding the centralised storage of data. We consider two adaptive algorithms for estimating one quantile (e.g. the median) when each user holds a single data point lying in a domain $[B]$ that can be queried once through a private mechanism; one under local differential privacy (LDP) and another for shuffle differential privacy (shuffle-DP). In the adaptive setting we present an $\varepsilon$-LDP algorithm which can estimate any quantile within error $\alpha$ only requiring $O(\frac{\log B}{\varepsilon^2\alpha^2})$ users, and an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-shuffle DP algorithm requiring only $\widetilde{O}((\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}+\frac{1}{\alpha^2})\log B)$ users. Prior (nonadaptive) algorithms require more users by several logarithmic factors in $B$. We further provide a matching lower bound for adaptive protocols, showing that our LDP algorithm is optimal in the low-$\varepsilon$ regime. Additionally, we establish lower bounds against non-adaptive protocols which paired with our understanding of the adaptive case, proves a fundamental separation between these models.

Each user holds one value in a domain of size B and can be queried once through a private mechanism. The central question is whether adaptively choosing queries can reduce how many users are needed compared with fixing the queries in advance.

The authors propose one protocol under local differential privacy and another under shuffle differential privacy. For target error alpha, the local protocol requires O(log B divided by epsilon squared alpha squared) users. The shuffle protocol requires approximately (1/epsilon squared + 1/alpha squared) log B users, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Both improve on prior nonadaptive requirements by several logarithmic factors in B.

Additional lower bounds for nonadaptive protocols prove a fundamental separation between adaptive and nonadaptive approaches. The contribution therefore goes beyond proposing lighter protocols: it identifies a setting where adapting queries provides a provable statistical advantage, even though each participant is contacted only once.
summary.tldr: Adaptive private quantile protocols reduce user requirements and establish a provable advantage over nonadaptive approaches.

title: Lightweight Protocols for Distributed Private Quantile Estimation

abstract: Conformal prediction is a powerful distribution-free framework for constructing prediction sets with coverage guarantees. Classical methods, such as split conformal prediction, provide marginal coverage, ensuring that the prediction set contains the label of a random test point with a target probability. However, these guarantees may not hold uniformly across different subpopulations, leading to disparities in coverage. Prior work has explored coverage guarantees conditioned on events related to the covariates and label of the test point. We present Kandinsky conformal prediction, a framework that significantly expands the scope of conditional coverage guarantees. In contrast to Mondrian conformal prediction, which restricts its coverage guarantees to disjoint groups—reminiscent of the rigid, structured grids of Piet Mondrian’s art—our framework flexibly handles overlapping and fractional group memberships defined jointly on covariates and labels, reflecting the layered, intersecting forms in Wassily Kandinsky’s compositions. Our algorithm unifies and extends existing methods, encompassing covariate-based group conditional, class conditional, and Mondrian conformal prediction as special cases, while achieving a minimax-optimal high-probability conditional coverage bound. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of our approach through empirical evaluation on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs sets of possible labels with coverage guarantees. A marginal guarantee describes coverage for a randomly selected test point, but it can conceal differences across subpopulations. Kandinsky conformal prediction addresses how to provide more flexible conditional coverage guarantees for groups defined using both input features and labels.

The framework allows groups to overlap and permits fractional membership, so a point need not belong entirely to just one disjoint category. This expands beyond the disjoint grouping used by Mondrian conformal prediction. It also brings covariate-based group coverage, class-conditional coverage, and Mondrian methods together as special cases.

The paper establishes a minimax-optimal conditional coverage bound that holds with high probability and evaluates the approach on real-world datasets. Its theoretical contribution is a coverage bound for this richer grouping structure. Its practical significance is the ability to represent intersecting or partial memberships when assessing reliability, making the grouping scheme more expressive than a partition into separate categories.
summary.tldr: Kandinsky conformal prediction extends conditional coverage guarantees to overlapping and fractional groups defined jointly by features and labels.

title: Kandinsky Conformal Prediction: Beyond Class- and Covariate-Conditional Coverage

abstract: Softmax distributions are widely used in machine learning, including Large Language Models (LLMs), where the attention unit uses softmax distributions. We abstract the attention unit as the softmax model, where given a vector input, the model produces an output drawn from the softmax distribution (which depends on the vector input). We consider the fundamental problem of binary hypothesis testing in the setting of softmax models. That is, given an unknown softmax model, which is known to be one of the two given softmax models, how many queries are needed to determine which one is the truth? We show that the sample complexity is asymptotically $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ where $\epsilon$ is a certain distance between the parameters of the models. Furthermore, we draw an analogy between the softmax model and the leverage score model, an important tool for algorithm design in linear algebra and graph theory. The leverage score model, on a high level, is a model which, given a vector input, produces an output drawn from a distribution dependent on the input. We obtain similar results for the binary hypothesis testing problem for leverage score models.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations are needed to distinguish between two possible probabilistic models. Its main setting is a softmax model: a vector goes in, and an output is sampled from a distribution determined by that input. This abstracts a distributional component used in language-model attention into a mathematical testing problem.

The unknown model is assumed to be one of two specified candidates. The authors show an asymptotic query-complexity upper bound of O(ε⁻²), where ε measures a particular distance between their parameters. The inverse-square dependence describes how the bound grows as candidate models become closer under that distance. It is an upper bound on the required observations, rather than a stated exact count for every pair.

The authors then connect this setup to leverage-score models, which also return samples from input-dependent distributions and are useful in linear algebra and graph algorithms. They obtain similar testing results there. The contribution provides a shared perspective on identifying two kinds of probabilistic models through queries, under the explicit two-candidate assumption.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the queries needed to distinguish two candidate softmax models and obtains analogous results for leverage-score models.

title: Binary Hypothesis Testing for Softmax Models and Leverage Score Models

abstract: Off-policy deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents typically leverage replay buffers for reusing past experiences during learning. This can help sample efficiency when the collected data is informative and aligned with the learning objectives; when that is not the case, it has the effect of “polluting” the replay buffer with data that can exacerbate optimization challenges in addition to wasting environment interactions due to redundant sampling. We argue that sampling these uninformative and wasteful transitions can be avoided by addressing the sunk cost fallacy which, in the context of deep RL, is the tendency towards continuing an episode until termination. To address this, we propose the learn to stop (LEAST) mechanism which uses statistics based on $Q$-values and gradient to guide early episode termination which helps agents recognize when to terminate unproductive episodes early. We demonstrate that our method improves learning efficiency on a variety of RL algorithms, evaluated on both the MuJoCo and DeepMind Control Suite benchmarks.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning agents reuse stored experience through replay buffers. This improves sample efficiency when the data is informative and relevant to learning. Unproductive experience can instead complicate optimization and consume environment interactions, especially when an agent continues collecting redundant transitions during an episode that is no longer useful.

The paper frames the tendency to continue until an episode naturally ends as a form of sunk cost fallacy. Its learn-to-stop mechanism, LEAST, uses statistics derived from Q-values and gradients to guide early termination. These signals help the agent recognize when an episode is unproductive and stop collecting experience from it.

Evaluations across several reinforcement learning algorithms on MuJoCo and the DeepMind Control Suite show improved learning efficiency. The result supports making episode continuation part of the learning process rather than always waiting for natural termination. The proposed benefit depends on avoiding uninformative transitions: replay remains useful when stored experience supports the objective, while selective early stopping reduces the collection of data that can hinder progress.
summary.tldr: LEAST uses Q-value and gradient statistics to stop unproductive episodes early and improve reinforcement-learning efficiency.

title: The Courage to Stop: Overcoming Sunk Cost Fallacy in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative learning among clients via a coordinating server while avoiding direct data sharing, offering a perceived solution to preserve privacy. However, recent studies on Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) have challenged this notion, showing high success rates against unprotected training data. While local differential privacy (LDP) is widely regarded as a gold standard for privacy protection in data analysis, most studies on MIAs either neglect LDP or fail to provide theoretical guarantees for attack success against LDP-protected data. To address this gap, we derive theoretical lower bounds for the success rates of low-polynomial-time MIAs that exploit vulnerabilities in fully connected or self-attention layers, regardless of the LDP mechanism used. We establish that even when data are protected by LDP, privacy risks persist, depending on the privacy budget. Practical evaluations on models like ResNet and Vision Transformer confirm considerable privacy risks, revealing that the noise required to mitigate these attacks significantly degrades models’ utility.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps clients’ raw data from being directly shared with a coordinating server, but this alone does not settle privacy questions. Membership inference attacks seek to determine whether particular data participated in training. This paper examines such attacks when clients also use local differential privacy, explicitly incorporating that protection into the analysis.

The authors derive lower bounds on the success rates of low-polynomial-time attacks exploiting fully connected or self-attention layers. Their bounds apply regardless of which local differential privacy mechanism is used. The resulting privacy risk depends on the privacy budget, so the analysis characterizes residual exposure under protection rather than treating privacy as simply present or absent.

Evaluations with models including ResNet and Vision Transformer confirm considerable risks in the studied settings. They also show that increasing noise enough to mitigate these attacks significantly harms model utility. The contribution connects theoretical attack-success guarantees with a practical privacy–utility tradeoff, clarifying why protected federated training can still permit meaningful membership inference.
summary.tldr: Theoretical bounds and vision-model experiments show privacy-budget-dependent membership risks even with local differential privacy.

title: Theoretically Unmasking Inference Attacks Against LDP-Protected Clients in Federated Vision Models

abstract: Although numerous complex algorithms for treatment effect estimation have been developed in recent years, their effectiveness remains limited when handling insufficiently labeled training sets due to the high cost of labeling the post-treatment effect, e.g., the expensive tumor imaging or biopsy procedures needed to evaluate treatment effects. Therefore, it becomes essential to actively incorporate more high-quality labeled data, all while adhering to a constrained labeling budget. To enable data-efficient treatment effect estimation, we formalize the problem through rigorous theoretical analysis within the active learning context, where the derived key measures – factual and counterfactual covering radii determine the risk upper bound. To reduce the bound, we propose a greedy radius reduction algorithm, which excels under an idealized, balanced data distribution. To generalize to more realistic data distributions, we further propose FCCM, which transforms the optimization objective into the Factual and Counterfactual Coverage Maximization to ensure effective radius reduction during data acquisition. Furthermore, benchmarking FCCM against other baselines demonstrates its superiority across both fully synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets. Code: https://github.com/uqhwen2/FCCM.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects becomes difficult when collecting post-treatment outcomes is expensive. The paper gives imaging and biopsy procedures as examples of costly labeling. It asks how active learning can choose useful additional observations within a limited budget, improving estimation through targeted data acquisition rather than relying only on a more complex estimator.

The theoretical analysis identifies factual and counterfactual covering radii as quantities determining an upper bound on risk. These describe coverage relevant to observed treatment outcomes and alternative-treatment comparisons. The authors first propose a greedy algorithm that reduces these radii. Its strength is established under an idealized, balanced data distribution, making that condition important to the method’s stated effectiveness.

To handle more realistic distributions, they introduce FCCM, which reformulates acquisition as maximizing factual and counterfactual coverage. This objective is designed to achieve effective radius reduction as new labels are acquired. Comparisons against other methods on fully synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets favor FCCM. The results connect a theoretically motivated coverage objective to empirical improvements in budget-constrained treatment-effect estimation.
summary.tldr: FCCM selects treatment-outcome labels by improving factual and counterfactual coverage, outperforming compared methods on synthetic and semi-synthetic data.

title: Enhancing Treatment Effect Estimation via Active Learning: A Counterfactual Covering Perspective

abstract: Recent advances have highlighted the benefits of scaling language models to enhance performance across a wide range of NLP tasks. However, these approaches still face limitations in effectiveness and efficiency when applied to domain-specific tasks, particularly for small edge-side models. We propose the LoRA-Gen framework, which utilizes a large cloud-side model to generate LoRA parameters for edge-side models based on task descriptions. By employing the reparameterization technique, we merge the LoRA parameters into the edge-side model to achieve flexible specialization. Our method facilitates knowledge transfer between models while significantly improving the inference efficiency of the specialized model by reducing the input context length. Without specialized training, LoRA-Gen outperforms conventional LoRA fine-tuning, which achieves competitive accuracy and a 2.1x speedup with TinyLLaMA-1.1B in reasoning tasks. Besides, our method delivers a compress ratio of 10.1x with Gemma-2B on intelligent agent tasks.

paragraphs: LoRA-Gen aims to specialize small language models running at the edge by using a larger model in the cloud. Its starting point is that increasing model scale does not fully resolve the efficiency and effectiveness challenges of domain-specific tasks, particularly when the deployed model must remain small.

Given a task description, the cloud model generates low-rank adaptation parameters for the edge model. A reparameterization step merges these parameters into the smaller model, enabling flexible specialization. The approach transfers knowledge between models and reduces the input context length needed by the specialized model, improving its inference efficiency.

The paper reports that specialization without specialized training outperforms conventional LoRA fine-tuning. Its results include competitive reasoning accuracy and a 2.1-fold speedup with TinyLLaMA-1.1B, plus a reported compression ratio of 10.1 with Gemma-2B on intelligent-agent tasks. These findings support generating adaptations from task descriptions as a practical way to connect cloud-model capabilities with smaller deployed models.
summary.tldr: LoRA-Gen uses a cloud language model to generate task-specific adapters for smaller edge models, reducing context needs and improving inference efficiency.

title: LoRA-Gen: Specializing Large Language Model via Online LoRA Generation

abstract: Code repair is an important capability for language models (LMs): given a buggy program and unit tests, an LM must produce a fixed program that passes the tests. We aim to scale supervision for code repair by having an LM generate bug–fix tasks with unconstrained edits, using unit tests as the only verifier. We propose generator-fixer self-play, in which a single model is trained with reinforcement learning to alternate between generating bugs and fixing them. As the fixer improves, the generator adapts to produce increasingly difficult bugs, yielding an automatic curriculum. However, because unit tests certify correctness but not realism, we find that the generator can drift from bugs encountered in practice, improving repair on self-generated bugs while degrading on real-world bugs. We propose Anchored Self Play (ASP), which anchors self-play with a small reference set by (i) adding a code-embedding similarity reward to guide generation and (ii) mixing reference bugs into fixer training to prevent drift. To reflect LM-assisted programming, where bugs come from humans, LMs, and human edits of LM code, we introduce BugSourceBench, a code repair benchmark spanning human-authored bugs, human-edited buggy LM code, and errors in LM-generated code. Across bug sources, ASP achieves the best fix rates, improving average fix rate by $+25$% (relative) / $+7.2$ pp (absolute) over standard self-play, with gains on both LM-error bugs ($+100$% relative / $+11$ pp absolute) and human-authored bugs ($+7.1$% relative / $+3.4$ pp absolute).

title: Anchored Self-Play for Code Repair

abstract: We study the active learning problem of fixed-confidence top-$k$ identification from noisy pairwise comparisons. In this problem, an algorithm sequentially chooses pairs of items to compare, observes the outcomes, and stops when it can return the set of top-$k$ items with error probability at most $\delta$. The objective is to design such a $\delta$-correct procedure that minimizes the expected number of comparisons (the sample complexity). This problem falls within the broader literature on fixed-confidence pure exploration in bandit models, where a common target is asymptotic optimality: the algorithm’s expected sample complexity matches the information theoretic lower bound as $\delta \to 0$. Asymptotically optimal procedures have been developed for a range of fixed-confidence pure-exploration problems, however to the best of our knowledge, for top-$1$, or more generally top-$k$ identification from pairwise comparisons under latent utility models an asymptotically optimal algorithm has not been established. In this setting, we develop such an algorithm. We characterize the structure of the lower bound and formulate it as a saddle-point problem. This structure enables a computationally efficient primal–dual procedure that learns the asymptotically optimal comparison allocation online. We then construct an adaptive comparison-allocation algorithm that tracks the allocation learned by the primal–dual procedure and prove it is asymptotically optimal.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify the best k items using noisy comparisons between pairs. An algorithm chooses comparisons sequentially and stops when it can return a set with error probability at most a chosen threshold, delta. The goal is to achieve that confidence while minimizing the expected number of comparisons.

Under latent utility models, the authors characterize the information-theoretic lower bound on the required comparisons and express it as a saddle-point problem. This structure supports an efficient primal-dual procedure that learns how comparisons should be allocated. A second, adaptive component tracks that learned allocation when selecting which pairs to compare.

The authors prove that the resulting procedure is asymptotically optimal: as the allowed error probability approaches zero, its expected comparison count matches the lower bound. This covers both finding the single best item and identifying a larger top-k set. The guarantee concerns this high-confidence limit, making precise the sense in which the allocation uses comparisons optimally.
summary.tldr: An adaptive pairwise-comparison algorithm identifies top-k items with asymptotically optimal sample complexity under latent utility models.

title: Optimal Top-$k$ Identification from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: While the rapid adoption of multimodal generative models offers immense potential, it has also increased the risks of harmful content synthesis, deepfakes, and copyright infringements. To address these challenges, concept erasure has emerged as a prospective safeguard. However, as the field gradually transitions from U-Net-based diffusion models to Rectified Flow Transformers, erasure research has struggled to keep pace. In this work, we introduce GEM, a simple but highly effective erasure framework for Rectified Flow models. As part of our contribution, we establish a principled bridge between trajectory-based unlearning grounded in Generative Flow Networks and classic teacher-guided erasure: we translate trajectory-based signals into a teacher-guided flow-matching setup that unifies the strengths of both paradigms. Concretely, a teacher provides complementary attraction and repulsion signals that we combine into a single geometric guidance objective, yielding targeted suppression of unwanted concepts while preserving benign generation.

paragraphs: Concept erasure aims to suppress unwanted content in a generative model while retaining its useful capabilities. The paper focuses on Rectified Flow models, which are becoming more prominent as generative systems move beyond U-Net-based diffusion architectures. Its motivation is that erasure methods need to match the generation framework in which they will operate.

GEM connects two approaches to modifying generative behavior: trajectory-based unlearning grounded in Generative Flow Networks and teacher-guided erasure. The authors translate signals about generation trajectories into a teacher-guided flow-matching formulation. This provides a common objective through which trajectory information can guide changes to a Rectified Flow model.

The teacher supplies complementary attraction and repulsion signals, which GEM combines into one geometric guidance objective. Together, these signals support targeted suppression of unwanted concepts while preserving benign generation. The stated contribution is this principled connection and unified training formulation, described as simple and highly effective. Its significance is to give concept erasure a method tailored to Rectified Flow generation, with preservation of benign outputs built into the same guidance objective as suppression.
summary.tldr: GEM combines teacher-provided attraction and repulsion signals to erase unwanted concepts from Rectified Flow models while preserving benign generation.

title: GEM: Geometric Erasure by Contrastive Velocity Matching in Rectified Flows

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) learns policies from fixed datasets, thereby avoiding costly or unsafe environment interactions. However, its reliance on finite static datasets inherently restricts the ability to generalize beyond the training distribution. Prior solutions based on synthetic data augmentation often fail to generalize to unseen scenarios in the (augmented) dataset. To address these challenges, we propose Retrieval High-quAlity Demonstrations (RAD) for decision-making, which innovatively introduces a retrieval mechanism into offline RL. Specifically, RAD retrieves high-return and reachable states from the offline dataset as target states, and leverages a generative model to generate sub-trajectories conditioned on these targets for planning. Since the targets are high-return states, once the agent reaches such a target, it can continue to obtain high returns by following the associated high-return actions, thereby improving policy generalization. Extensive experiments confirm that RAD achieves competitive or superior performance compared to baselines across diverse benchmarks, validating its effectiveness. Our code is available at https://github.com/LeahGL/RAD.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns decisions from a fixed dataset, avoiding additional costly or unsafe interactions. That same fixed collection can limit generalization, and synthetic augmentation may still leave unseen situations unsupported. RAD introduces retrieval into planning so that useful recorded experience can guide the construction of new action sequences.

The method retrieves target states that are both reachable and associated with high returns. A generative model then produces sub-trajectories conditioned on those targets. This links generated plans to desirable states already represented in the dataset. Once such a target is reached, the associated high-return actions provide a way to continue obtaining strong returns.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks show competitive or superior performance relative to the evaluated baselines. The results support combining retrieval and generation for offline decision-making: retrieval supplies promising destinations, while generation supplies sub-trajectories toward them. Reachability is central to the proposed mechanism, because a high-return state is useful as a planning target only if the agent can get there in the relevant setting.
summary.tldr: RAD guides offline reinforcement-learning plans toward retrieved, reachable high-return states using target-conditioned generated sub-trajectories.

title: RAD: Retrieval High-quality Demonstrations to Enhance Decision-making

abstract: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models predominantly rely on explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to bridge perception and action. While effective, this paradigm suffers from high computational costs and error propagation in multi-step tasks. In this paper, we propose Adaptive Variable Alignment VLA (AVA-VLA), a novel Latent Reasoning VLA framework that models reasoning as a sequence of unobservable latent variables, bypassing the need for explicit text generation. However, latent trajectories are inherently susceptible to noise interference and misalignment with downstream objectives. To address this, we introduce a Reinforcement Learning-based Denoising mechanism that treats latent state generation as a sequential decision process, optimizing reasoning trajectories via task-level rewards. Furthermore, we incorporate an Early-Exit Strategy that adaptively terminates reasoning based on state confidence, enabling a dynamic trade-off between depth and efficiency. Extensive experiments on embodied decision benchmarks demonstrate that AVA-VLA significantly reduces inference latency while achieving superior stability and success rates compared to full-reasoning baselines.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models often produce explicit chains of reasoning before acting. That process can be costly and allow errors to propagate across multi-step tasks. AVA-VLA instead represents reasoning as a sequence of internal latent variables, avoiding the need to generate reasoning text while still providing a sequence of intermediate states between perception and action.

Internal reasoning has its own difficulties: latent trajectories can be disrupted by noise or become misaligned with the task. The proposed reinforcement-learning denoising mechanism treats latent-state generation as sequential decision-making and optimizes it with task-level rewards. This connects the quality of an internal reasoning trajectory to its contribution to the eventual task outcome.

AVA-VLA also uses an early-exit strategy that ends reasoning adaptively according to state confidence. This allows reasoning depth and computational effort to vary instead of always completing the full trajectory. Experiments on embodied decision benchmarks report significantly lower inference latency alongside better stability and success rates than full-reasoning baselines, supporting the combination of reward-guided latent reasoning and adaptive stopping.
summary.tldr: AVA-VLA combines reward-guided latent reasoning with confidence-based early exit to reduce action latency and improve benchmark success.

title: Think Less, Act Early: Reinforced Latent Reasoning with Early Exit in Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Differentiating through the solution of a quadratic program (QP) is a central problem in differentiable optimization. Most existing approaches differentiate through the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system, but their computational cost and numerical robustness can degrade at scale. To address these limitations, we propose dXPP, a penalty-based differentiation framework that decouples QP solving from differentiation. In the solving step (forward pass), dXPP is solver-agnostic and can leverage any black-box QP solver. In the differentiation step (backward pass), we map the solution to a smooth approximate penalty problem and implicitly differentiate through it, requiring only the solution of a much smaller linear system in the primal variables. This approach bypasses the difficulties inherent in explicit KKT differentiation and significantly improves computational efficiency and robustness. We evaluate dXPP on various tasks, including randomly generated QPs, large-scale sparse projection problems, and a real-world multi-period portfolio optimization task. Empirical results demonstrate that dXPP is competitive with KKT-based differentiation methods and achieves substantial speedups on large-scale problems. Our implementation is open source and available at https://github.com/mmmmmmlinghu/dXPP.

paragraphs: A quadratic program can serve as a component inside a learning system, but training that system requires understanding how the program’s solution changes when its inputs change. Common methods obtain these derivatives through the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker system. The paper addresses the computational and numerical difficulties that this approach can encounter at large scales.

The proposed framework, dXPP, separates finding a solution from differentiating through it. The forward pass can use any black-box quadratic-programming solver. For the backward pass, dXPP maps the returned solution to a smooth approximate problem built with penalties. It then uses implicit differentiation, solving a smaller linear system involving only the primal variables.

This separation allows the solver and derivative calculation to use different machinery. Tests cover random quadratic programs, large sparse projection problems, and multi-period portfolio optimization. The authors report competitive performance against KKT-based differentiation and substantial speedups on large problems. The central contribution is a more efficient differentiation route built around a smooth approximation while retaining freedom in solver choice.
summary.tldr: dXPP differentiates through black-box quadratic-programming solutions using a smooth penalty approximation and a smaller backward-pass linear system.

title: A Penalty Approach For Differentiation Through Black-box Quadratic Programming Solvers

abstract: Tool-calling is a central component of modern large language model (LLM) agents, equipping them with skills beyond their parametric knowledge. This paper studies tool-calling along two complementary axes: effectiveness, i.e., how this capability is measured, and efficiency, i.e., how it is learned. On effectiveness, we systematically analyze tool-calling evaluation pipelines and show that results can be highly sensitive to seemingly minor, often undocumented implementation choices including the random seed, system prompt, multi-turn template construction, and how prior interaction/reasoning history is carried forward. These choices can lead to substantial differences in reported performance, especially in multi-turn settings where without rigorous standardization, leaderboard rankings are unreliable. On efficiency, we examine standard reinforcement learning (RL) for tool-calling and identify two sources of computational waste: (i) during rollouts, many prompts produce no learning signal, and (ii) during policy updates, optimization incurs high computational cost. Guided by these findings, we introduce two techniques that accelerate RL-based tool-calling training, achieving substantial wall-clock speedup without degrading performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines tool-calling from two connected perspectives: whether evaluations measure it reliably and whether reinforcement learning teaches it efficiently. Tool use lets agents act beyond the knowledge stored in their parameters, making both the credibility of reported scores and the cost of training practically important.

The evaluation analysis finds that apparently minor implementation choices can substantially change results. These include random seeds, system prompts, the construction of multi-turn templates, and the way previous interactions or reasoning are retained. Sensitivity is especially pronounced in multi-turn settings. Without rigorous standardization, reported leaderboard positions can therefore reflect differences in evaluation setup as well as differences in model capability.

The training analysis identifies waste in two stages. During rollouts, many prompts provide no learning signal; during policy updates, optimization is computationally expensive. The authors introduce two techniques motivated by these observations and report substantial reductions in wall-clock training time without lower performance. Together, the findings connect better-controlled measurement with more efficient learning, addressing how tool-calling capability is both judged and acquired.
summary.tldr: Tool-calling scores depend strongly on evaluation details, while two proposed techniques accelerate reinforcement learning without reported performance loss.

title: On Effectiveness and Efficiency of Agentic Tool-calling and RL Training

abstract: Sample inefficiency remains a challenge in pixel-based visual reinforcement learning (RL), primarily due to ineffective state representation learning. While recent advances employ auxiliary tasks to improve representation learning, their representation goals (e.g., mask reconstruction, state prediction) are misaligned with the ultimate RL goal of maximizing return, constraining further improvements in representation quality. To achieve efficient visual reinforcement learning, we propose Return-Critic (RC), an auxiliary framework that bridges goal discrepancy by return prediction. RC samples partial frames from an episode, processes them through a shared visual encoder, and employs a lightweight Transformer to predict the episode’s return, forcing the encoder to learn return-relevant representation. The attention weights naturally highlight important frames, enabling a key function for prioritized learning. Extensive experiments on both online (DMControl) and offline (V-D4RL) benchmarks demonstrate that RC significantly enhances the sample efficiency, particularly achieving 68% performance boost on average across nine challenging tasks from DMControl.

paragraphs: Learning from pixels requires a reinforcement-learning agent to discover which visual information matters for obtaining reward. Auxiliary tasks can help build representations, but reconstructing images or predicting states does not directly match the goal of maximizing return. Return-Critic changes the auxiliary target to the episode’s return.

The framework samples a subset of frames from an episode and passes them through the same visual encoder used for representation learning. A lightweight Transformer then predicts the episode return from those encoded frames. This training signal encourages the encoder to retain information relevant to task outcomes. Its attention weights also highlight important frames, providing a mechanism for prioritized learning.

Experiments evaluate the approach in online learning on DMControl and offline learning on V-D4RL. The authors report substantial improvements in sample efficiency, including an average 68% performance increase across nine challenging DMControl tasks. These findings support aligning representation learning with return prediction so that visual features are trained around the same outcome the agent ultimately seeks to improve.
summary.tldr: Return-Critic trains visual representations to predict episode return, improving reinforcement-learning sample efficiency in online and offline benchmarks.

title: Return-Critic: Bridging Goal Discrepancy for Efficient Visual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Music recordings often suffer from audio quality issues such as excessive reverberation, distortion, clipping, tonal imbalances, and a narrowed stereo image, especially when created in non-professional settings without specialized equipment or expertise. These problems are typically corrected using separate specialized tools and manual adjustments. In this paper, we introduce SonicMaster, the first unified generative model for music restoration and mastering that addresses a broad spectrum of audio artifacts with text-based control. SonicMaster is conditioned on natural language instructions to apply targeted enhancements, or can operate in an automatic mode for general restoration. To train this model, we construct the SonicMaster dataset, a large dataset of paired degraded and high-quality tracks by simulating common degradation types with nineteen degradation functions belonging to five enhancements groups: equalization, dynamics, reverb, amplitude, and stereo. Our approach leverages a flow-matching generative training paradigm to learn an audio transformation that maps degraded inputs to their cleaned, mastered versions guided by text prompts. Objective audio quality metrics demonstrate that SonicMaster significantly improves sound quality across all artifact categories. Furthermore, subjective listening tests confirm that listeners prefer SonicMaster’s enhanced outputs over other baselines. The model and demo samples are available through https://github.com/AMAAI-Lab/SonicMaster.

paragraphs: Music recordings can contain several quality problems at once, including distortion, excessive reverberation, clipping, tonal imbalance, and reduced stereo width. Correcting them typically involves separate tools and manual adjustments. SonicMaster brings restoration and mastering into one generative model that accepts natural-language instructions or operates automatically for general restoration.

The researchers create paired degraded and high-quality tracks by applying nineteen simulated degradation functions. These cover five enhancement groups: equalization, dynamics, reverb, amplitude, and stereo. The model trains through flow matching to transform degraded audio into cleaned and mastered output, with text prompts guiding the requested enhancement.

Objective audio-quality measurements show significant improvements across all artifact categories, and subjective listening tests find that listeners prefer SonicMaster’s outputs over the evaluated baselines. These two forms of evaluation support both measurable improvement and listener preference. The approach matters because one model can address a broad range of recording problems while allowing the user to specify a targeted change or request general restoration.
summary.tldr: SonicMaster unifies music restoration and mastering with text-guided or automatic enhancement, improving measured quality and listener preference.

title: SonicMaster: Towards Controllable All-in-One Music Restoration and Mastering

abstract: Cross-view geo-localization (CVGL) aims to retrieve the corresponding satellite image given a street query and is critical for autonomous navigation. Although recent methods perform well on benchmarks, they often fail to generalize to unseen environments. A key limitation is the use of contrastive learning, which assigns equal labels to all negative samples and induces similarity-amplified repulsion. But should all negatives be treated equally? In CVGL, semi-positive samples that are geographically proximate to the positive often share important semantic cues. Treating them as ordinary negatives forces the model to overfit noise, leading to a collapse in generalization. To address this issue, we propose an uncertainty-aware framework grounded in Deep Evidential Regression (DER), modeling the Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) distribution as a conjugate prior to quantify environmental complexity $u$ in a single forward pass. The estimated $u$ adaptively softens labels for hard negatives in Soft InfoNCE, mitigating excessive repulsion on semi-positive samples. An Uncertainty Head with cls-to-spatial cross-attention and attention statistics is designed to accurately fit the NIG distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, including an average 18% R@1 improvement in zero-shot cross-dataset transfer, filling the critical gap between laboratory benchmarks and robust real-world deployment.

paragraphs: Cross-view geolocation matches a street-level image to the corresponding satellite image. A training difficulty arises when an incorrect candidate is geographically close to the correct location and shares useful visual meaning. The paper argues that treating these partially relevant candidates as ordinary negatives can push their representations apart too strongly and harm transfer to unfamiliar environments.

The proposed framework estimates environmental complexity through Deep Evidential Regression, using a Normal-Inverse-Gamma distribution in a single forward pass. An uncertainty head combines attention between a global classification token and spatial features with attention statistics. Its uncertainty estimate controls label softening for difficult negatives within a Soft InfoNCE objective.

This adaptive softening reduces excessive repulsion of nearby, semantically related candidates. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance, including an average 18% improvement in top-ranked retrieval accuracy for zero-shot transfer across datasets. The result supports the paper's premise that negative examples need different treatment depending on uncertainty and partial relevance. The approach connects uncertainty estimation directly to how the retrieval model learns similarities, rather than using uncertainty only after prediction.
summary.tldr: Uncertainty-based softening of difficult negative examples improves cross-view geolocation transfer by reducing excessive separation of nearby, semantically related locations.

title: Must All Negatives Be Pushed Away Equally? Uncertainty-Aware Cross-View Geo-Localization via Normal Inverse Gamma Distribution

abstract: Post-training compression is currently divided into two contrasting regimes. On the one hand, fast, data-free, and model-agnostic methods (e.g., NF4 or HQQ) offer maximum accessibility but suffer from functional collapse at extreme bit-rates below 4 bits. On the other hand, techniques leveraging calibration data or extensive recovery training achieve superior fidelity but impose high computational constraints and face uncertain robustness under data distribution shifts. We introduce EntQuant, a framework that unites the advantages of these distinct paradigms. By matching the performance of data-dependent methods with the speed and universality of data-free techniques, EntQuant enables practical utility in the extreme compression regime. Our method decouples numerical precision from storage cost via entropy coding, compressing a 70B parameter model in less than 10 minutes. We demonstrate that EntQuant does not only achieve state-of-the-art results on standard evaluation sets and models, but also retains functional performance on more complex benchmarks with instruction-tuned models, all at modest inference overhead.

paragraphs: Compressing a trained model often involves choosing between convenience and fidelity. Fast methods that need no data can lose functionality at very low bit rates, while methods using calibration data or recovery training require more computation. EntQuant aims to combine the accessibility of data-free compression with the performance of data-dependent approaches.

Its central mechanism is entropy coding, which separates the numerical precision used to represent values from the storage cost of encoding them. This gives compression another degree of freedom beyond reducing the precision of every stored value. The framework is data-free and model-agnostic, and the authors report compressing a model with 70 billion parameters in less than ten minutes.

The reported evaluations show state-of-the-art results on standard models and evaluation sets, alongside retained functionality on more complex benchmarks using instruction-tuned models. These results come with modest inference overhead. The contribution is a practical route to extreme compression that combines rapid post-training processing with useful model behavior, rather than requiring calibration examples or extensive recovery training to obtain that combination.
summary.tldr: EntQuant uses entropy coding to deliver rapid, data-free extreme model compression while retaining useful performance.

title: Float8@2bits: Entropy Coding Enables Data-Free Model Compression

abstract: Semi-supervised statistical inference plays a key role in biomedical research, where labeled data often have higher quality but are limited due to costly clinical annotation. Yet, existing semi-supervised statistical inference methods rely heavily on structured variables and strictly matched covariates between labeled and unlabeled datasets – limitations ill-suited for the heterogeneity and unstructured nature of real-world biomedical data. Modern biomedical studies increasingly collect unstructured data (clinical notes, patient audio and video recordings), with inconsistent protocols across datasets causing covariate misalignment (for instance, detailed medication histories may be recorded in one study but not another). Recent advances in pre-trained multimodal large language models (LLMs), which excel at handling unstructured data, present an attractive potential solution. To transform this potential into rigorous semi-supervised statistical inference methods for biomedical research, two key challenges must be addressed: (1) How can we reliably integrate LLMs to enhance semi-supervised inference efficiency without compromising statistical validity? (2) How can those efficiency gains persist despite mismatched covariates between labeled and unlabeled datasets? In this paper, we tackle these challenges by systematically calibrating pseudo-labels provided LLMs with a novel prediction-invariance identification strategy. Our resulting semi-supervised inference framework improves parameter estimation efficiency while maintaining full statistical validity, as demonstrated through our theoretical results and illustrated in a case study for identifying key biomarkers in Alzheimer’s disease detection with speech data.

paragraphs: Biomedical studies often have a small amount of carefully labeled data alongside larger collections without labels. Combining these sources is difficult when they contain unstructured material, such as speech or clinical notes, or record different sets of variables. This paper develops a statistical inference framework designed to use language models despite these mismatches.

The method systematically calibrates pseudo-labels supplied by language models and introduces a prediction-invariance identification strategy. Calibration is central because useful model-generated labels must contribute to parameter estimation without compromising statistical validity. The framework also addresses the requirement that efficiency gains persist when the labeled and unlabeled datasets have different available covariates.

The authors provide theoretical results showing improved estimation efficiency while maintaining statistical validity within their framework. They illustrate the approach through a study of speech data used to identify key biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease detection. The contribution concerns rigorous population-level inference: it connects the ability of language models to process unstructured observations with a statistical procedure for using their predictions.
summary.tldr: Calibrated language-model pseudo-labels improve semi-supervised statistical estimation while accommodating unstructured data and mismatched covariates.

title: Language Model Augmented Semi-Supervised Statistical Inference

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual-language reasoning, yet remain confined to their native modalities and cannot directly process structured, non-visual data such as human skeletons. Existing methods either compress skeleton dynamics into lossy feature vectors for text alignment, or quantize motion into discrete tokens that generalize poorly across heterogeneous skeleton formats. We present SkeletonLLM, which achieves universal skeleton understanding by translating arbitrary skeleton sequences into the MLLM’s native visual modality. At its core is DrAction, a differentiable, format-agnostic renderer that converts skeletal kinematics into compact image sequences. Because the pipeline is end-to-end differentiable, MLLM gradients can directly guide the rendering to produce task-informative visual tokens. To further enhance reasoning capabilities, we introduce a cooperative training strategy: Causal Reasoning Distillation transfers structured, step-by-step reasoning from a teacher model, while Discriminative Finetuning sharpens decision boundaries between confusable actions. SkeletonLLM demonstrates strong generalization on diverse tasks including recognition, captioning, reasoning, and cross-format transfer—suggesting a viable path for applying MLLMs to non-native modalities. Code is available in the Supplementary Material.

paragraphs: Human skeleton sequences describe motion in a structured format that multimodal language models cannot directly process through their native visual inputs. Existing conversions can lose motion information or generalize poorly between skeleton formats. SkeletonLLM addresses this by turning skeleton sequences into images that the model can interpret.

The central component, DrAction, is a differentiable renderer designed to work across skeleton formats. It converts skeletal motion into compact image sequences. Because gradients can pass through the renderer, training signals from the multimodal model can shape the visual representation itself, encouraging images that retain information useful for the task.

Two training components strengthen the resulting system. Causal Reasoning Distillation transfers structured reasoning from a teacher model, while Discriminative Finetuning helps distinguish easily confused actions. The authors report strong generalization across recognition, captioning, reasoning, and transfer between skeleton formats. These results suggest that a learnable visual translation can help multimodal models handle structured inputs outside their original modalities, with skeleton understanding providing the demonstrated application of that broader possibility.
summary.tldr: SkeletonLLM learns to render skeleton motion into task-informative images, enabling multimodal language models to recognize, describe, and reason about motion across formats.

title: Universal Skeleton Understanding via Differentiable Rendering and MLLMs

abstract: Formal verification of system software with complex heap manipulations remains challenging. Standard automated solvers frequently fail to discharge separation logic verification conditions even when correct specifications like loop invariants are provided, forcing verification engineers to manually construct proofs. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in proof synthesis, specialized approaches for separation logic remain unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce SL-VC (Separation Logic Verification Conditions), a benchmark of 289 verification conditions from textbook implementations of data structures and algorithms together with real-world C code, including the LiteOS kernel’s linked list library and the mini-gmp library. Experimental results on SL-VC demonstrate that SPLIT consistently outperforms existing approaches, showing that LLM-assisted proof synthesis is a promising solution for separation logic verification of real-world system software.

abstract: Autonomous web agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon tasks, yet their ability to adhere to real-world policies remains critically underexplored compared to standard safety objectives. To address this gap, we introduce PolicyGuardBench, a benchmark of 60k policy-trajectory pairs designed to evaluate compliance through both full-trajectory and novel prefix-based violation detection tasks. Using this dataset, we train PolicyGuard, a lightweight guardrail model that achieves strong detection accuracy while maintaining high inference efficiency. Notably, our model demonstrates robust generalization capabilities, preserving high performance even on unseen domains. These contributions establish a comprehensive framework for studying policy compliance, showing that accurate and generalizable guardrails are feasible at small scales.

These two views make it possible to study compliance over finished executions and over partial sequences, extending evaluation beyond a single final response.

It achieves strong detection accuracy while keeping inference efficient, and retains high performance on unseen domains in the reported evaluations. title: Learning Efficient Guardrails for Compliance

abstract: Large language model (LLM)-driven multi-agent systems typically require multiple model invocations and complex coordination during inference, and their execution strategies directly affect system accuracy, latency, and computational cost. Parallel execution provides a means to improve inference-time efficiency. From the perspective of inference-time execution, this paper models parallelism in multi-agent systems as two distinct levels of decision processes: Replica Parallelism, which explores multiple complete solution paths at the task level, and Structural Parallelism, which enables concurrent execution within a single solution path through task decomposition. However, the roles of different forms of parallelism and their interrelationships still lack systematic study in terms of unified organization and coordination. We therefore propose TIPEX, a controllable execution framework that unifies these two levels of parallelism and coordinates their roles within the inference process under a unified execution semantics while supporting systematic combinations and analyses of different parallel strategies and parameter configurations. Systematic experiments on the GAIA benchmark demonstrate that inference-time parallelism can significantly improve accuracy and reduce end-to-end latency at the cost of increased token consumption. Further analysis shows that Replica and Structural Parallelism exhibit complementary effects across task complexities, with tasks of intermediate difficulty benefiting most from their coordination, while overly aggressive parallel strategies do not necessarily yield better performance.

paragraphs: Multi-agent language-model systems make many model calls, and how those calls are scheduled affects accuracy, latency, and cost. This paper distinguishes two ways to run work in parallel. The results therefore frame scheduling as a tradeoff among solution quality, elapsed time, and token use, with the best coordination depending on task difficulty.
summary.tldr: TIPEX coordinates parallel solution attempts and parallel subtasks, revealing accuracy and latency gains that come with higher token use.

title: A Two-Tier Perspective on Inference-Time Parallelism in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

abstract: Instruction following in LLMs captures models’ ability to change their visible behaviors as requested by users. Instead, we study models’ ability to control their chain-of-thought (CoT). This capability – CoT controllability – is undesirable because it could allow models to suppress signs of misbehavior in their CoT, thereby undermining our ability to monitor them. To measure this, we introduce the CoT-Control evaluation suite. We show that reasoning models are less able to follow instructions in their CoT than in their outputs: on instructions like reasoning about a genetics problem without mentioning the word “chromosome", Claude-Sonnet-4.5 complies only 5% of the time. We also find that CoT controllability is higher for larger models and decreases with more RL training, test-time compute, and increased problem difficulty. CoT controllability failures extend even to situations in which models are given incentives (as opposed to direct requests) to evade CoT monitors, although models that are told they’re being monitored exhibit slightly higher controllability. Similarly, eliciting controllability by adversarially optimizing prompts doesn’t meaningfully increase controllability. Our results leave us cautiously optimistic: reasoning models generally seem characterized by low CoT controllability. However, the mechanism behind this phenomenon is not well understood. Given its importance for maintaining CoT monitorability, we recommend that frontier labs keep tracking controllability for future models.

title: Reasoning Models Struggle to Control their Chains of Thought

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated evaluators that assign numeric scores to model outputs, a paradigm known as LLM-as-a-Judge. However, standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods typically rely on binary rewards (e.g., 0-1 accuracy), thereby ignoring the ordinal structure inherent in regression tasks; for instance, they fail to recognize that predicting 4 is significantly better than predicting 1 when the ground truth is 5. Conversely, existing regression-aware approaches are often confined to Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), limiting their ability to explore optimal reasoning paths. To bridge this gap, we propose REAL (Regression-Aware Reinforcement Learning), a principled RL framework designed to optimize regression rewards, and also proven to be optimal for correlation metrics. A key technical challenge is that the regression objective is explicitly policy-dependent, thus invalidating standard policy gradient methods. To address this, we employ the generalized policy gradient estimator, which naturally decomposes optimization into two complementary components: (1) exploration over Chain-of-Thought (CoT) trajectory, and (2) regression-aware prediction refinement of the final score. Extensive experiments across model scales (8B to 32B) demonstrate that REAL consistently outperforms both regression-aware SFT baselines and standard RL methods, exhibiting significantly better generalization on out-of-domain benchmarks. On Qwen3-32B specifically, we achieve gains of +8.40 Pearson and +7.20 Spearman correlation over the SFT baseline, and +18.30/+11.20 over the base model. These findings highlight the critical value of integrating regression objectives into RL exploration for accurate LLM evaluation.

title: REAL: Regression-Aware Reinforcement Learning for LLM-as-a-Judge

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is computationally efficient but often yields inferior generalization compared to reinforcement learning (RL). This gap is primarily driven by RL’s use of on-policy data. We propose a framework to bridge this chasm by enabling On-Policy SFT. We first present Distribution Discriminant Theory (DDT), which explains and quantifies the alignment between data and the model-induced distribution. Leveraging DDT, we introduce two complementary techniques: (i) In-Distribution Finetuning (IDFT), a loss-level method to enhance generalization ability of SFT, and (ii) Hinted Decoding, a data-level technique that can re-align the training corpus to the model’s distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves generalization performance on par with prominent offline RL algorithms, including DPO and SimPO, while maintaining the efficiency of an SFT pipeline. The proposed framework thus offers a practical alternative in domains where RL is infeasible. We will open-source the code and data on GitHub.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning is computationally efficient, but the paper argues that its generalization often trails reinforcement learning because of differences in how training data aligns with the current model. The authors seek to bring the benefits of on-policy data alignment into an SFT pipeline without giving up its practical efficiency.

They introduce Distribution Discriminant Theory to explain and quantify alignment between training data and the distribution induced by a model. Two techniques act on different parts of the pipeline.
